preface.title: Preface
preface.p: Calculus connects local change, accumulated change, and approximation. This book begins with velocity and distance, develops derivatives and integrals together with their hypotheses, and uses them to study models, numerical methods, differential equations, and series.

The prerequisites are algebra, coordinate geometry, and trigonometry in radians. Appendices A–C review those tools. Worked examples, conceptual checkpoints, warning examples, and projects keep calculation, explanation, and application in contact.

preface.title: How to Read This Book
preface.p: Read the chapter introductions for the guiding questions. Work through each example with pencil and paper before reading its calculation, then answer the checkpoints in your own words. A formula should be read together with its domain and hypotheses.

Use the warning examples to test the limits of a rule. Use computing sections and projects to compare exact reasoning with numerical evidence; report an error bound whenever an approximation is used. The later previews show where single-variable calculus leads, and may be read after the core derivative, integral, and series material.

Sections headed Additional topics are optional extensions. Richardson and Romberg integration and adaptive quadrature follow numerical integration; Runge–Kutta methods follow differential equations; contraction iteration follows sequences; and the Weierstrass M-test follows uniform convergence. The local existence and uniqueness theorem is placed at the end of the book because its proof uses the Cauchy criterion, contraction theorem, and uniform convergence. It can be read after those topics without the intervening complex-number material.
Return to Appendices A–C for prerequisite review, Appendix D for proof details, Appendix E for technology notes, and Appendix F for formula and test summaries.

chapter.title: Velocity, Distance, and the First Shape of Calculus

introduction.p: Velocity describes how position changes with time. Accumulating velocity over a time interval gives the change in position. This chapter develops these two relationships using motion, slopes, areas, finite differences, and finite sums.
Look at two instruments on a car dashboard.
The odometer records distance. It tells how many miles the car has accumulated.
The speedometer records speed. It tells how fast the odometer reading is changing.
For the moment, imagine that the car moves only forward along a straight road. Then speed and velocity agree. Later, when the car can reverse direction, we will need signed velocity.

figure.caption: The odometer records accumulated distance. The speedometer records how fast that distance is changing.

description.p: The odometer records accumulated distance. The speedometer records how fast that distance is changing.

introduction.p: Let t denote time, measured in hours after the start of a trip. Let

The notation d(t) means: the distance depends on the time. When the input is a time t, the output is a distance d(t). We will soon give this kind of rule a name: a function. For now, the notation lets us keep track of the trip.

subsection.title: Distance as accumulated motion
subsection.p: Suppose the odometer reads 18{,}246.3 miles at 9{:}00 and 18{,}346.3 miles at 11{:}00. During those two hours, the car has accumulated
miles.

The odometer does not say how the car traveled those 100 miles. The driver might have gone steadily. Or slowly at first and quickly later. The odometer remembers the total effect, not the moment-by-moment history.
If we reset the trip odometer at the start, then d(0)=0. After 2 hours in this example,
The distance function d(t) is a memory of the trip.

exercise.title: What does an odometer remember?

statement.p: Two trips can produce the same odometer change even if one is steady and the other is stop-and-go. In your own words, what information does the final distance reading d(T) remember, and what information does it throw away? How does knowing the entire record d(t) give more information?

hint.p: The final value d(T) is one running total. Different trips can have the same final total. The entire function d(t) records how that total changed throughout the trip; when differentiable, it determines speed.

subsection.title: Velocity as changing distance
subsection.p: Velocity measures how fast distance changes.
If the car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, then its average velocity over that time is
Using d(t), this is

This number is an average over an interval. It does not say that the car was moving at exactly 50 miles per hour at every instant. It only says that the total change, spread evenly over two hours, would be 50 miles per hour.
A speedometer asks a sharper question:

p.me: \text{How fast is the distance changing right now?}

subsection.p: That word “right now” is where calculus enters.

exercise.title: What does an average velocity hide?

statement.p: If a car travels 100 miles in 2 hours, the average velocity is 50 miles per hour. In your own words, why is that number not yet a speedometer reading, and what extra question does the word right now add?

hint.p: An average spreads a total change over a whole interval. A speedometer asks about one instant inside that interval.

subsection.p: The units point to the mathematics.

The numerator measures change in distance. The denominator measures change in time. Their quotient measures change per unit time.

exercise.title: What do the units already tell you to do?

statement.p: Distance is measured in miles and velocity in miles per hour. In your own words, why do those units force velocity to be a ratio of a change in distance to a change in time, and why does multiplying velocity by time return a distance?

hint.p: Treat units as instructions: division by hours makes a rate; multiplication by hours undoes that division.

subsection.title: The first question: distance to velocity
subsection.p: Suppose we know the whole odometer record d(t). Can we recover the velocity v(t)?
For a long interval, we can compute only an average velocity. For example,

To know the velocity near t=2, we should look closer:

exercise.title: How can a whole distance record produce a velocity at one instant?

statement.p: Starting from a known function d(t), we look at fractions such as \frac{d(2.001)-d(2)}{2.001-2}. In your own words, what are those fractions measuring, and why should shorter and shorter time intervals be better clues to the velocity at t=2?

hint.p: Each fraction is still an average, just over a smaller window. Ask what that window is trying to collapse onto.

subsection.p: Now reverse the question.
Suppose we know the whole speedometer record v(t). Can we recover the distance d(t)?
If the velocity is 60 miles/hour for 2 hours, then the car travels
miles.
If the velocity changes, we can break the trip into smaller pieces. Suppose a car travels

Each product

This is the second great problem of calculus:
Geometrically, this will become the problem of finding area under a graph.

exercise.title: How can a velocity record rebuild distance?

statement.p: If velocity is not constant, we break a trip into pieces and add products of the form velocity times time. In your own words, why does each such product give a piece of distance, and why does adding the pieces reconstruct the odometer change?

hint.p: When velocity changes little over a short interval, constant velocity gives a useful approximation to that interval's displacement. Adding these approximations estimates the total displacement.

subsection.title: The two questions together
subsection.p: The two questions are opposite in spirit.
means: measure the instantaneous rate of change.
means: accumulate many small changes.
The first process will be called differentiation. The second will be called integration. The deepest early theorem in calculus will say that these two processes undo each other.

exercise.title: Why are the two dashboard questions inverses?

statement.p: For motion along a line, differentiating position gives velocity, and accumulating velocity over an interval gives the change in position. Explain why these operations are related and what additional starting information is needed to recover position.

hint.p: If you accumulate a rate of change, you should recover the original change. If you measure how fast an accumulated quantity is changing, you should recover the original rate.

subsection.p: We first compute both quantities for constant velocity.

exercise.title: Why are slope and area inverse clues?

statement.p: From the distance graph we read velocity as a slope; from the velocity graph we read distance as an area. In your own words, why are those two readings inverse operations rather than two unrelated pictures?

hint.p: One process extracts a rate from an accumulated quantity. The other process rebuilds the accumulated quantity from the rate.

subsection.title: Why the word “constant” matters
subsection.p: The formula
This formula requires constant velocity. For changing velocity, a single velocity value does not generally determine the total displacement.
Suppose a car travels

The total distance is

The average velocity over the full hour is 50 miles/hour, but the car was never moving at 50 miles/hour during either half of the trip.
The velocity graph is no longer one horizontal line. It has two steps. The distance graph is no longer one straight line. It has two line segments, one with slope 30 and one with slope 70.

subsection.p: This example is still simple because the velocity is constant on each half-hour piece. We can add two rectangle areas.
But real motion rarely changes only once. A driver speeds up, slows down, stops, and starts again. The velocity graph may have many pieces, or no flat pieces at all.
The next step is to allow motion forward and backward. Then area below the time axis must count with a sign. That sign is not a technicality; it is how calculus remembers direction.

exercise.title: What does the word constant buy us?

statement.p: The slope and rectangle-area calculations here used constant velocity. Explain which calculation changes when velocity varies and why approximating over shorter intervals is useful.

hint.p: Rectangles and a single slope are exact only when the height of the velocity graph does not move. Changing height forces smaller pieces, then a limiting process.

introduction.p: When motion can reverse direction, speed alone does not describe it. Signed velocity records both how fast an object moves and which direction it moves.
Velocity has a sign.
Choose one direction on a straight road and call it positive. For example, east may be positive and west negative. A car moving east at 40 miles/hour has velocity
A car moving west at the same speed has velocity
The speed is the size of the velocity:
So speed is never negative, but velocity can be negative. This sign is how calculus remembers direction.

subsection.title: Positive and negative velocity

If s(0)=0, then:

The change

hint.p: A speedometer reports how fast the odometer is ticking. It does not report whether the car is heading forward or backing up.

hint.p: Signed area is not painting a wall. It is accumulating change, and backward motion decreases position.

subsection.p: A formula such as

Piecewise-defined functions are not artificial. They describe many real situations:

cell.p: a car stops at a red light
an elevator goes up, stops, then goes down
a thermostat turns heat on and off
different rates on different income intervals

The signed calculation tells where the car ends. The absolute-value calculation tells how much road the car has covered.

subsection.title: What the sign prepares us for
subsection.p: Signed area is not ordinary geometric area. Ordinary geometric area is never negative. Signed area is different because it is designed to represent accumulated change.
If v(t)>0, the signed position increases.
If v(t)<0, the signed position decreases.
If v(t)=0, the signed position does not change.
That is why the graph of s(t) rises, falls, or stays flat according to the sign of v(t).

For piecewise-constant velocity, rectangles give exact displacement. If instead we have signed positions at equally spaced times, adding consecutive position changes recovers the final position from the initial one.
That is calculus before limits.

But real motion is usually not made of perfect steps. A car does not hold one exact velocity for a while, jump instantly to another, and hold that forever. Its velocity changes while the clock is running.
For a changing velocity, rectangles are no longer exact. They become estimates. The natural response is to use shorter intervals, then shorter ones still.
That is where limits enter.

exercise.title: How can calculus exist before limits?

statement.p: Finite differences compute position changes, and summing consecutive differences recovers the total change. Explain this cancellation and why instantaneous velocity still requires a limiting process.

hint.p: Finite differences and finite sums undo each other exactly, with a starting position supplied. They give interval changes and average rates, rather than an instantaneous rate. Multiplying a sampled instantaneous velocity by a finite step is generally only an estimate when velocity varies within the step.

section.title: Changing velocity and the need for limits

introduction.p: When velocity is constant on each of finitely many time intervals, rectangles give the exact displacement. When velocity changes continuously, rectangles give approximations. We will refine those approximations by using shorter intervals. The same limiting process turns average velocity into instantaneous velocity.

subsection.title: Average velocity over a time interval
subsection.p: Let s(t) be signed position at time t. If a\neq b, the average velocity from time a to time b is
This is the same formula we have used since the dashboard:
The denominator cannot be zero. Average velocity needs an interval of time, not a single instant.

exercise.title: Why must the time interval shrink?

statement.p: Average velocity over a long interval can hide a lot of speeding up and slowing down. In your own words, why does shrinking the interval give a better clue to the velocity at one instant, and why is h=0 still forbidden in the difference quotient?

hint.p: A smaller window mixes fewer different velocities. Setting the window width to zero would ask you to divide by zero, so the instant has to be approached rather than plugged in.

example.p: Suppose a toy motion has signed position
The formula is chosen because the arithmetic is simple. The average velocity from t=2 to t=3 is
The average velocity from t=2 to t=2.1 is
The shorter interval gives a number closer to what we expect the velocity to be at the instant t=2.
To see the pattern, write the nearby time as 2+h. Then
The number h is the time step. It may be positive or negative, but it cannot equal 0 inside this fraction.
As h gets closer to 0, the average velocities get closer to 4. So the instantaneous velocity at t=2 should be
We have just used the idea of a limit. We have not yet defined limits carefully, but the picture is already clear:

p.em: instantaneous velocity = the value approached by average velocities over shrinking intervals.

example.p: The notation \lim_{h\to 0} means that h is allowed to get closer and closer to 0, while h itself remains nonzero during the calculation.

subsection.title: The word “if” matters
subsection.p: The average velocities must approach a single number. That does not always happen.
Recall the forward-then-backward motion from Section~. In one simplified model,
Before t=2, the slope is 40. After t=2, the slope is -30. The graph has a corner at t=2.
If we approach t=2 from the left, the average velocities approach 40. If we approach from the right, they approach -30. There is no single velocity at the switching instant in this idealized model.

note.p: A derivative is born only when the nearby average rates settle toward one value.

subsection.p: This is why calculus needs limits. The phrase “gets close to” must become precise enough to decide whether one number is really being approached.

subsection.p: Average velocity has a geometric twin: secant slope.
For a graph y=s(t), the average velocity from t=a to t=a+h is
This is the slope of the secant line through the two points
If these secant slopes approach one number as h\to0, the limiting line is called the tangent line.
For s(t)=t^2 at t=2, the limiting slope is 4. The tangent line passes through (2,4), so its equation is

subsection.p: At this stage, the tangent line is not merely a line that touches the curve. Some tangent lines cross the curve. Some lines can touch a graph without being the right tangent. The tangent line is the line obtained from limiting secant lines.
This changes the question from geometry to arithmetic:

exercise.title: Why do tangent slope and area become the same two questions?

statement.p: The first dashboard question becomes the slope of a tangent line. The second becomes area under a graph. In your own words, why are those geometric problems the same two questions as distance to velocity and velocity to distance?

hint.p: Slope is rise over run, which is change in output over change in input. Area is height times width, which is a rate times a time interval, then added.

subsection.title: The area problem
subsection.p: Now suppose velocity is known and displacement is required.
If the velocity is constant on each time interval, rectangles give the exact answer. But suppose the velocity changes continuously, for example
from t=0 to t=2.
The graph is curved. No finite collection of rectangles naturally gives the exact area under it. But rectangles can estimate the area.

subsection.title: Why finite arithmetic is no longer enough
subsection.p: Finite differences and finite sums worked perfectly for step motion.
If velocity is constant on each of finitely many intervals, then displacement is exactly
But if velocity changes at every instant, no finite list of rectangles can fully capture the graph. We need an idea that lets infinitely many improving finite estimates settle toward one number.
That idea is a limit.
Limits will let us define:
and
These two limiting processes serve as the entry points to calculus. Before constructing them in detail, it’s helpful to take a step back and view the entire picture.

exercise.title: Why are finite rectangles no longer enough?

statement.p: For a changing velocity, a finite rectangle sum is generally an approximation; an exact match may occur by coincidence. In your own words, what does a limit add that a better-but-still-finite partition cannot, and why is that extra idea necessary rather than optional?

hint.p: Each finite partition is an estimate. A limit is the claim that those estimates settle toward one number as the pieces become arbitrarily fine.

section.title: A first map of the book

introduction.p: Slope measures a rate of change, and signed area measures an accumulated change. Finite differences and finite sums give discrete versions of these operations. Limits will connect them to derivatives and integrals.

subsection.title: Derivative: from position to velocity
subsection.p: The derivative is the precise version of instantaneous rate of change.
Starting with signed position s(t), the derivative answers:

p.me: \text{How fast is }s(t)\text{ changing at this instant?}

subsection.p: The formula will be
when that limit exists.

The derivative is local. It studies what happens near one input a. On a graph, it gives the slope of the tangent line. In motion, it gives velocity. In an applied model, it gives sensitivity: how much the output changes when the input is nudged.
For s(t)=t^2, we found
Later we will learn how to compute s'(t) for many functions without starting from the limit every time.

subsection.title: Integral: from velocity to position
subsection.p: The integral is the precise version of accumulated signed change.
Starting with velocity v(t), the integral answers:

p.me: \text{How much signed position has accumulated over an interval?}

subsection.p: The notation will be
This means the signed accumulation of v(t) from t=a to t=b. If v(t) is above the time axis, it contributes positively. If v(t) is below the time axis, it contributes negatively.

The integral is global. It uses the whole interval, not just one instant. On a graph, it is signed area. In motion, it is displacement. In applications, it can represent accumulated mass, work, energy, probability, cost, or growth.
The central theorem of calculus will say that these two processes undo each other:

subsection.title: Approximation: how to work when exact formulas fail
subsection.p: Calculus gives exact definitions, but it also teaches controlled approximation.
The derivative begins with approximate slopes:
The integral begins with approximate sums:
A tangent line gives a local approximation:
This simple formula will become one of the most useful ideas in the book. It says that a differentiable function looks almost linear when we zoom in far enough.
Later, the same idea will grow into Taylor polynomials:

Approximation is not a temporary trick before the exact answer arrives. In science, engineering, economics, and computation, approximation is often the answer we can actually use. The real question is:
Calculus gives ways to estimate that error.

subsection.title: Differential equations: when the law gives the derivative
subsection.p: Sometimes a problem does not give the function directly. It gives a law for how the function changes.
For example, a population P(t) might grow at a rate proportional to its current size:
This equation does not tell us P(t) outright. It tells us the derivative of P. To solve the problem, we must find a function whose rate of change behaves in the required way.
A cooling cup of coffee can be modeled by
The farther the coffee temperature is from room temperature, the faster it cools. Again, the law is written in the language of derivatives.
Equations involving derivatives are called differential equations. They are one of the main reasons calculus became the language of science.

To do that carefully, we need a language for distance on the number line, intervals around a point, functions, graphs, and eventually limits. The next chapter builds that language. It may look like a review at first, but it is not a detour. It is the measuring tape calculus needs.

introduction.p: Calculus uses functions to describe dependence and limits to describe approximation. Before defining limits, we need the real number line, intervals, distances, and error bounds. This chapter develops that language and uses it to describe graphs and mathematical models.

Numbers do two jobs for us. They locate points, and they measure distances between points. The same number 3 can mean a position on a line, a length, a time, a temperature, or an error bound. Calculus depends on moving between these meanings without confusion.

subsection.title: Points as numbers
subsection.p: We picture the real numbers on a horizontal line. Positive numbers lie to the right of 0. Negative numbers lie to the left.

subsection.p: The word error does not mean a mistake. It means the difference between a quantity and the value we want.

Calculus uses inequalities to force errors to become small.

subsection.p: Rational numbers measure many distances, but they do not represent every point required by geometry and limiting processes. The next section explains why the real numbers are needed.
The answer is yes for the real numbers. It is no for the rational numbers. That difference is one reason calculus is built on \mathbb R, not just on fractions.

section.title: Completeness and the idea of no gaps

introduction.p: Rational numbers do not supply every point needed for limits. Completeness is the property of the real numbers that ensures bounded increasing approximations have a real limit.
Fractions are already very rich. Between any two fractions there is another fraction. For example, between 1.41 and 1.42 lies
Still, fractions alone leave gaps. Geometry finds one of those gaps in a unit square.

note.title: First-reading note
note.p: This section explains why the real numbers, not only rational numbers, are the right setting for calculus. You may read the proof details lightly on a first pass. The main idea is simple: calculus needs an unbroken number line because limits can point to numbers that no finite decimal or fraction exactly equals.

subsection.title: Least upper bound property
subsection.p: Completeness can be stated in several equivalent ways. The most useful form for proofs is the least upper bound property.
First we need two definitions.

for every x\in S.
A number L is the least upper bound of S if

The least upper bound is also called the supremum of S, written

example.p: Then 1 is an upper bound for S, because every number in (0,1) is less than 1.
So is 2. So is 100. But 1 is the least upper bound:

note.title: Maximum versus least upper bound
note.p: A maximum must belong to the set.
A least upper bound may or may not belong to the set.

subsection.p: Now we can state the completeness property.

note.title: Completeness Property of the Real Numbers
note.p: Every nonempty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

subsection.p: This property is what fills the gaps. It is not true for the rational numbers.

paragraphs.title: The rational counterexample
paragraphs.p: This is a nonempty set of rational numbers. For example,
It is bounded above. For example, 2 is an upper bound.
But A_{\mathbb Q}, viewed only inside the rational numbers, has no least upper bound. The boundary should be \sqrt2, but \sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q.
The rational line has a hole exactly where the least upper bound should be.

exercise.title: How is a least upper bound different from a maximum?

statement.p: The open interval (0,1) has least upper bound 1, even though 1 is not in the set. In your own words, what is a least upper bound, and why can a set fail to contain the number that caps it from above?

hint.p: A maximum must belong to the set. A least upper bound is the smallest ceiling, whether or not the set reaches that ceiling.

subsection.title: Nested intervals
subsection.p: The decimal approximations to \sqrt2 give a sequence of smaller and smaller intervals:
and so on. Each interval contains the next, and the lengths shrink:

figure.caption: Nested intervals trap one number. For the real line, that trapped point exists. For the rational numbers alone, this example traps a missing point.

description.p: Nested intervals trap one number. For the real line, that trapped point exists. For the rational numbers alone, this example traps a missing point.

subsection.p: This picture leads to a principle.

note.title: Nested Interval Principle
note.p: Suppose
is a nested sequence of closed intervals
and the lengths
become arbitrarily small. Then there is exactly one real number that lies in every interval I_n.

subsection.p: For the intervals above, that one real number is \sqrt2.

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: move to the right or stay fixed. The right endpoints
move to the left or stay fixed. Since every left endpoint is still to the left of every right endpoint, the left endpoints are bounded above.

The real numbers have a least upper bound for the left endpoints. Call it L. Then L lies in every closed interval. If two different numbers x<y lay in every interval, then every interval would have length at least y-x. But the interval lengths become arbitrarily small. Therefore there can be only one such number.
This proof depends on the fact that the left endpoints have a least upper bound. That fact is one form of completeness (absence of holes) of real numbers.

paragraphs.title: What goes wrong with rational numbers
paragraphs.p: Take the same nested intervals, but allow only rational numbers. Each interval contains many rational numbers. Their lengths shrink toward 0. But the only real number common to all of them is \sqrt2, and \sqrt2 is not rational.
So inside the rational numbers alone, these nested rational intervals have no rational point in common.

exercise.title: What do nested intervals trap?

statement.p: The decimal approximations to \sqrt2 give nested closed intervals whose lengths tend to zero. State what the Nested Interval Principle guarantees and explain why their common point is unavailable if only rational numbers are allowed.

hint.p: Each interval contains the next, and the lengths become arbitrarily small. The question is whether a common point is guaranteed to exist inside the number system you are using.

subsection.title: Completeness creates \sqrt2
subsection.p: The completeness property does more than describe \sqrt2. It guarantees that such a number exists.

note.title: What the proof showed
note.p: The existence of \sqrt2 is not a decimal accident. It follows from the no-gaps property of the real numbers.

subsection.title: Why calculus needs the real numbers
subsection.p: Calculus builds exact numbers from limiting processes.

A tangent slope is approached by slopes of secant lines. An area is approached by sums of thin rectangles. A root can be trapped by bisection inside smaller and smaller intervals. An infinite decimal is approached by its finite decimal truncations.
Each step in such a process may use rational numbers. But the number approached may be irrational.
The rational numbers are excellent for computation. They are not complete enough for calculus.

example.title: bisection finds a missing rational point
example.p: the solution, if it exists, should lie between 1 and 2.
Continuing forever gives nested intervals whose lengths shrink to 0. The real number trapped by this process is \sqrt2. If we allowed only rational numbers, the process would point to a hole.

paragraphs.title: The calculus lesson
paragraphs.p: A convergent limiting process has a destination. Completeness guarantees a real destination when the approximations satisfy appropriate conditions, such as nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink to zero, or a bounded monotone sequence. It does not make every sequence converge.
A gap in the number system can prevent these approximations from having a limit within that system.

The real line gives us numbers and distances. The next step is to let one number determine another. A temperature depends on time. A position depends on time. An error depends on a step size h. Those dependencies are called functions.

exercise.title: Why does a limiting process need an unbroken number line?

statement.p: Tangent slopes, areas, bisection roots, and infinite decimals are defined through approximations. Explain how completeness supplies real limiting values when the appropriate convergence conditions hold.

hint.p: Each step of the process may use rational numbers. Completeness is about whether the number being approached is allowed to exist even when it is not rational.

introduction.p: A function assigns one output to each allowed input. For example, a time can determine a position, a radius can determine an area, and a step size can determine an approximation error. We will specify both the assignment and the set of inputs on which it is defined.

subsection.title: Input, output, domain, and range
subsection.p: Imagine a trip along a straight road. At each time t, the car has a position s(t). The input is time. The output is position.
For example, if the car moves at 50 miles/hour starting from position 0, then
This formula assigns one position to each time.

figure.caption: A function assigns an output to each input in its domain.

description.p: A function assigns an output to each input in its domain.

subsection.p: The word “assigns” is important. A function is not merely a formula. It is a rule that gives exactly one output for each allowed input.

statement.p: A function f from a set D to the real numbers is a rule that assigns to each input x\in D exactly one real number f(x).
The set D is called the domain of f.
The set of all outputs is called the range of f:

subsection.p: We often write
This means that the inputs come from D, and the outputs are real numbers.

because every square is nonnegative, and every nonnegative number is the square of some real number.
For instance, 9 is in the range because
But -4 is not in the range because no real number has square -4.

paragraphs.p: The formula alone does not always determine the function. Compare
The formulas are the same, but the domains are different. So the functions are different.

A function is a rule together with its allowed inputs.

exercise.title: Why is a formula not yet a function?

statement.p: The formulas f(x)=x^2 on \mathbb R and g(x)=x^2 on [-1,1] look the same, but they are different functions. In your own words, what extra information besides a formula does a function need, and why can two functions share a formula yet have different ranges?

hint.p: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. Changing the allowed inputs can change the set of outputs that actually appear.

subsection.title: Functions from formulas, graphs, tables, and words
subsection.p: A formula is the most familiar way to describe a function, but it is not the only way.

paragraphs.title: A function from a formula
paragraphs.p: The area A of a circle depends on its radius r:
If the radius is measured in centimeters, then the area is measured in square centimeters. The natural domain is
because a radius cannot be negative.

paragraphs.title: A function from a table
paragraphs.p: A thermometer may record the temperature of a cup of tea every minute.
This table defines a function on the domain
The table does not tell us the exact temperature at t=2.5. It may suggest one, but it does not assign one unless we add more information.
This distinction will matter later. Data can suggest a model, but the model is a new function.

paragraphs.title: A function from a graph
paragraphs.p: A graph can also describe a function. The input x is read along the horizontal axis. The output f(x) is read along the vertical axis.

A graph represents a function only when each input gives exactly one output. This is the reason for the vertical line test: a vertical line corresponds to one input x. If it hits a curve in two places, then that input has two possible outputs, so the curve is not the graph of a function of x.

paragraphs.title: A function from words
paragraphs.p: Sometimes the rule is best described in words.

hint.p: A function only has to answer for inputs in its domain. Ask whether 2.5 is one of the recorded inputs, or an extra interpolation you might be tempted to invent.

subsection.title: The natural domain of a formula
subsection.p: When a formula is given without an explicit domain, we usually take the domain to be all real numbers for which the formula makes sense. This is called the natural domain.

hint.p: Think about division by zero and even roots of negative numbers. A formula cannot assign an output where those operations fail.

subsection.title: Piecewise-defined functions
subsection.p: Many real processes follow one rule for a while and then another rule later.

A car may move forward, stop at a light, then reverse into a parking space. A tax bill may use one rate for the first part of income and another rate for the next part. A postage cost may stay constant over a range of weights, then jump.
These functions are often described piece by piece.

hint.p: Nearby behavior is not the same as the value at the joining point. Limits later watch that neighborhood, so the assignment at the endpoint must be unambiguous.

subsection.p: Functions let one quantity depend on another. Graphs let us see that dependence all at once. Before we can study limits on graphs, we need to learn how graphs move, stretch, reflect, and reveal information.

A graph can show things a formula hides: where a function is positive, where it is zero, where it grows large, and where it has symmetry. It also helps us build new functions from old ones.

Symmetry is not only pretty. It saves work. If an even function is known for x\ge 0, then it is known for x\le 0. If an odd function is known for x\ge 0, then the other half is determined by sign change.

exercise.title: What does even or odd symmetry remember?

hint.p: Evenness is mirror symmetry across the vertical axis. Oddness is a 180^\circ rotation about the origin. Each rule tells you how the output at -x is determined by the output at x.

subsection.p: A graph is a picture of outputs. But many questions about a function are really questions about intervals of inputs.
The graph answers these questions visually.

For now, we only need the first graph-reading skills: intercepts, sign, domain, range, and transformations.

subsection.title: A graph can suggest, but not prove
subsection.p: A graph can suggest a property of a function, but the plotted image alone does not prove it.
A graphing window can hide behavior. A curve may cross the axis just outside the window. A tiny wiggle may disappear if the scale is too large. A vertical asymptote may look like a steep line.
For example, the functions
and
can look almost identical in a wide viewing window. But the second function has many small oscillations.
The lesson is not to distrust graphs. The lesson is to use them correctly.

subsection.p: Transformations let us build many new functions from one familiar function. Next we will build functions in a more algebraic way: by adding, multiplying, dividing, and composing them. Composition is the most hidden of these operations, and later it will force one of the most important derivative rules in calculus.

introduction.p: We can form new functions by adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing their outputs. Composition forms a new function by using the output of one function as the input of another. Each operation also imposes requirements on the domain.

hint.p: Algebra can rewrite values where both formulas are defined. It cannot restore an input that the original expression never allowed.

Composition and inverses will matter throughout calculus. The chain rule will describe how a composition changes. The derivative of an inverse function will describe how undoing a function changes rates.

But before calculus can use functions well, we need to know the families that appear most often. A formula is more than symbols: it has a shape, a natural domain, a growth pattern, and often a physical meaning.

introduction.p: Several function families occur frequently in calculus. Lines describe constant rates, polynomials and rational functions describe algebraic relationships, trigonometric functions describe periodic behavior, and exponentials describe constant proportional growth or decay. Logarithms invert exponentials. This section reviews their formulas, domains, and graphs.

subsection.title: The catalog at a glance
subsection.p: This table is not a substitute for understanding the shapes. It is a map. When a problem mentions constant rate, think linear. When it mentions repeated percentage change, think exponential. When it mentions periodic motion, think trigonometric. When it mentions undoing an exponential, think logarithm.

A function family is a first guess, not a proof. The next step is modeling: choosing a function because units, data, and behavior suggest it. That will be our last preparation before limits turn “near” into a precise mathematical tool.

introduction.p: The catalog gave us familiar function families. A model is the next step: we choose one of those families because a situation asks for it.
A mathematical model represents selected features of a situation under stated assumptions. Its units should be consistent, and its predictions should be checked against data.

statement.p: A mathematical model is a function, equation, graph, or table used to represent a real quantity.
A model should be judged by four questions:

p.me: \text{How well does it fit the information we have?}

introduction.p: Calculus will later tell us how models change and how their effects accumulate. Before calculus begins, we should learn the main shapes that models can take.

subsection.title: Linear growth
subsection.p: Suppose water is poured into a tank at a steady rate of 3 liters per minute. At the moment we start watching, the tank already contains 12 liters.
After t minutes, the amount of water is
The number 12 is the starting amount. The number 3 is the rate of change.
Each time t increases by 1, the output increases by 3.
This is the signature of a linear model: equal input changes produce equal output changes.

paragraphs.title: Finding a linear model from two points
paragraphs.p: Suppose a candle has height 18 cm at time t=0, and height 14 cm after 2 hours. If we assume the candle burns at a constant rate, then its height is linear.
This model predicts that the candle reaches height 0 when
The model says the candle lasts 9 hours.
But this prediction depends on the assumption that the burn rate stays constant. If the candle shape changes or the flame weakens, the model may fail before 9 hours.

note.title: Modeling lesson
note.p: A formula can be algebraically correct and still be physically wrong outside the range where its assumptions make sense.

exercise.title: What four questions should a model survive?

statement.p: A model represents a situation under stated assumptions. What four checks should be made, and why can an algebraically correct formula give an incorrect physical prediction outside its assumed range?

hint.p: Check assumptions, units, agreement with data, and the applicable range. Algebraic consistency alone does not establish agreement with the modeled situation.

subsection.title: Power-law scaling
subsection.p: Linear models are about constant additive change. Power-law models are about scaling.
Imagine enlarging a square photograph. If every length is multiplied by 2, then the area is multiplied by 4.

subsection.title: Exponential growth and decay
subsection.p: Some quantities do not add the same amount in equal time steps. They multiply by the same factor.
Suppose a bacterial culture grows by 50\% every hour. If it starts with 100 bacteria, then after each hour the population is multiplied by 1.5.
The differences are not constant:
But the ratios are constant:
This is exponential growth. These are values of a continuous population model, rather than exact counts of individual bacteria; fractional values represent an approximation to the population.

If a>1, the model grows.
If 0<a<1, the model decays.

If the starting amount is M_0, then a model for the amount after t days is

paragraphs.title: A warning
paragraphs.p: Exponential growth can be a good short-term model and a terrible long-term model.

A bacterial population cannot grow forever in a closed dish. A rumor cannot spread to more people than exist. A bank account cannot earn the same interest rate through every possible economic condition.
A model may be useful because it is locally accurate, even when it is not globally permanent. Calculus will often help us decide what “locally” means.

exercise.title: How do you tell linear growth from exponential growth in data?

statement.p: A linear model adds the same amount in equal time steps. An exponential model multiplies by the same factor. In your own words, what should you look for in a table of values, and why can exponential growth be a good short-term model and a terrible long-term one?

hint.p: Constant differences suggest an additive model, whereas constant ratios suggest a multiplicative model. Resource limits or changing rates may invalidate an exponential model beyond the observed data.

subsection.title: Periodic motion
subsection.p: Some quantities repeat.
A Ferris wheel turns. A tide rises and falls. A weight on a spring moves up and down. A point on a rotating tire returns to its starting height again and again.
The basic models for repeating motion use sine and cosine.

If a rider starts at the midline and is moving upward at time t=0, then the height can be modeled by

subsection.title: Choosing a model from units and data
subsection.p: A model is a choice. The choice should be guided by the situation.

table.title: Choosing a model from units and data

example.title: linear or exponential?
example.p: A small plant is measured once per week.
not constant. But the ratios are approximately
The symbol \approx matters. Data are often measured with error, and real processes rarely follow a model perfectly.

paragraphs.title: Residuals: the errors a model leaves behind
paragraphs.p: At input x_i, the prediction error is
These errors are called residuals. A good model should leave small residuals without using a formula that is more complicated than the situation deserves.

note.title: A modeling habit
note.p: Do not ask only:

p.me: \text{Can I find a formula through the data?}

note.p: Ask also:

p.me: \text{Does the formula behave reasonably outside the data?}

example.title: a model that fits too well
example.p: Given five data points, it is often possible to find a polynomial of degree 4 that passes exactly through all of them. That does not mean the polynomial is the best model.
A high-degree polynomial may wiggle wildly between data points or make absurd predictions just outside the measured interval. Exact fit is not the same as understanding.
For calculus, the simplest useful model is often better than a complicated perfect fit.

Models give us functions to study. Technology gives us quick graphs of those functions. But a graph on a screen is not the function itself. It is a picture made with choices: a window, a scale, and a finite number of sampled points.
Those choices can hide the truth.

exercise.title: Why is an exact fit not the same as understanding?

statement.p: Residuals are the errors a model leaves behind, and a high-degree polynomial can pass through every data point. In your own words, why should we ask whether a formula explains a pattern rather than only whether it hits the measured points, and what can go wrong just outside the data?

hint.p: Exact interpolation can wiggle wildly between points or make absurd predictions nearby. A good model should leave small residuals without being more complicated than the situation deserves.

introduction.p: A graphing calculator or computer can draw in a second what would take minutes by hand. That speed is useful. It is also dangerous.
A screen does not show a function. It shows a sampled picture of a function in a chosen window.
The picture may be excellent. It may also miss a hole, hide a turn, smooth out an oscillation, or round away a small but important difference.
Check features suggested by a plotted graph using the formula, the sampling resolution, and the chosen viewing window.

p.alert: Use technology to see. Use mathematics to check

subsection.title: Windows can lie
subsection.p: A graphing window is a rectangle:

p.me: x_{\min}\le x\le x_{\max}, \qquad y_{\min}\le y\le y_{\max}.

subsection.p: Anything outside that rectangle is invisible. The same function can look simple in one window and complicated in another.

exercise.title: What can a graphing window hide?

statement.p: A screen shows a sampled picture of a function in a chosen rectangle, not the function itself. In your own words, why can the same function look simple in one window and complicated in another, and what can a graph suggest that it cannot prove?

hint.p: Anything outside the rectangle is invisible. A picture can hint at a zero, a turn, a hole, or an asymptote; it cannot by itself prove that there is exactly one, or none, or always.

subsection.title: Sampling can miss behavior
subsection.p: A computer cannot check infinitely many points. It samples finitely many input values, plots the corresponding output values, and connects or displays them.
Usually this works well. Sometimes it fails spectacularly.

exercise.title: Why can sampling make an oscillation look like zero?

statement.p: A computer plots finitely many sample points and then displays them. In your own words, why can a rapidly oscillating function look identically zero under unlucky sampling, and what does that say about trusting a graph at a scale the sampling cannot see?

hint.p: If every sampled input happens to hit a root of the oscillation, the plotted points are all zero. The missing wiggles were never asked about.

example.p: This function oscillates 50 full times on the interval [0,1].

The sampled graph may look like the horizontal line y=0, even though the true function swings from -1 to 1 again and again between the sampled points.

example.p: Oscillations appear in sound, light, vibration, and signal processing. Sampling matters.

warning.title: Sampling warning
warning.p: A graph drawn from samples is trustworthy only at the scale the sampling can see.

subsection.title: Numerical evidence versus proof
subsection.p: Numerical evidence is useful. It helps us guess patterns. It helps us find examples. It helps us notice mistakes.
But a long list of checked cases is not a proof.

exercise.title: Why is a long list of checked cases not a proof?

statement.p: Numerical evidence helps us guess patterns and notice mistakes. In your own words, what does a computation actually show, and what extra claim does a proof have to make that checking a thousand points cannot make?

hint.p: A computation reports the inputs it tested. A proof explains why the statement must hold for every allowed input, including the ones never typed into a calculator.

example.title: a graph suggests positivity
example.p: appears to lie above the x-axis. That suggests
A graph supports the claim, but algebra proves it:
The proof tells us more than the graph. It tells us that the function is not merely positive; it is at least 1.

example.title: a sign change suggests a root
example.p: The outputs change from negative to positive between x=1 and x=2. A graph suggests that the curve crosses the x-axis somewhere between them.
Later, after we define continuity, the Intermediate Value Theorem will make this exact. It will say that a continuous function that changes sign on an interval must have a zero inside that interval.
For now, the important lesson is this:

p.me: \text{a theorem explains when the clue is reliable.}

example.title: many correct cases do not prove an identity
example.p: Suppose a calculator suggests that two formulas give the same output for many inputs. That does not prove the formulas are identical.
At each of those inputs, the product term is 0, so
But the functions are not the same. At x=0,
Checking five points was not enough. Checking a thousand points is still not a proof of equality for all real numbers.

warning.title: Proof warning
warning.p: A computation can show that a statement is true at the inputs tested.
A proof shows why the statement must be true for every allowed input.

subsection.title: A first warning about roundoff
subsection.p: There is another way technology can mislead: numbers are rounded.
A calculator screen may show 10 digits. A computer may store more. But still, it stores only finitely many digits. Most real numbers cannot be stored exactly.
Usually this causes no visible trouble. But when two nearly equal numbers are subtracted, important digits can disappear.

example.title: subtracting nearly equal numbers
example.p: This expression will appear naturally when we study the derivative of \sqrt{x}. For small h, the numerator
subtracts two numbers very close to each other.
is extremely close to 1. A rounded calculation may lose the small difference.
But algebra gives a safer expression. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate:
Now there is no subtraction of nearly equal numbers.
As h becomes small, this safer expression is close to

warning.title: Roundoff warning
warning.p: Two algebraically equal formulas can behave differently when approximately computed on a calculator.
The problem is not the mathematics. The problem is the finite storage of decimal or binary approximations.

paragraphs.title: Why this matters for calculus
paragraphs.p: Calculus is built from small changes:
When h is small, the numerator subtracts nearly equal numbers. Rounding can then affect the computed quotient substantially.
This does not mean we should avoid numerical computation. It means we should understand what the computation is doing.
Sometimes, algebra can make a formula more (numerically) stable. Sometimes a graph needs a better range for variables. Sometimes, a numerical pattern needs a precise definition.
The next chapter provides the missing language. It will make the phrase
into mathematics. That language is the limit.

exercise.title: Why can subtracting nearly equal numbers lie?

statement.p: Calculus is built from small changes such as \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}. In your own words, why can a tiny step h make the numerator subtract two nearly equal numbers, and why is that a storage problem rather than a failure of the mathematics?

hint.p: Machines store only finitely many digits. When two close approximations are subtracted, the digits that carried the small difference can disappear, even though the exact algebraic difference is still meaningful.

introduction.p: Chapter 1 began with motion. It asked how to pass between velocity and distance, slope and area, difference and sum.

Chapter 2 built the language that this question needs. We used the real line to measure nearness, functions to record dependence, graphs to see geometric behavior, and models to connect formulas with real applications. We also learned that a graph on a screen is only evidence, not proof.
The next chapter returns to the original motion problem. But now we are ready to say what “near” means.

subsection.p: The last problem is the doorway to the next chapter.

As h gets close to 0, the average velocity gets close to 4. Chapter 2 gave us the language to make that sentence sharper:
So if we want the output error to be less than \varepsilon, we can demand
This is the shape of a limit. The input is allowed to approach a forbidden or special value. The output is forced into any desired error bound.
The next chapter gives this idea its name.

exercise.title: What is already the shape of a limit?

statement.p: For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity from 2 to 2+h is 4+h for h\ne0. Explain how its error from 4 can be made smaller than any positive tolerance without evaluating the quotient at h=0.

hint.p: The condition 0<|h|<\varepsilon keeps the step away from zero and still small enough. That is the measuring-tape language the next chapter will name.

introduction.p: Chapter 2 ended with a small but important calculation. For
the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is
As h gets close to 0, this average velocity gets close to 4. The value h=0 is forbidden in the quotient, but we can move as close to it as we like.
That is the first shape of a limit:

p.me: \text{the input approaches a value, and the output approaches a value.}

introduction.p: The word “approaches” sounds informal. This chapter turns it into mathematics.

A speedometer gives an instantaneous reading. But if all we have is a position formula, we first see only average velocities over intervals. The limit is the act of shrinking the interval until the average rate settles toward one number.

subsection.title: Average velocity as the interval shrinks
subsection.p: Let
be the position of an object moving along a line, measured in meters after t seconds. We want the velocity at the instant t=2.
Over the interval from 2 to 2+h, the average velocity is

Since h\neq0, we may divide by h:

The closer h is to 0, the closer A(h) is to 4. This suggests that the instantaneous velocity at t=2 should be
The important point is not only the answer. The important point is how we got it:

figure.caption: The slopes of the secant lines approach the slope of the tangent line at t=2.

description.p: The slopes of the secant lines approach the slope of the tangent line at t=2.

subsection.p: The same calculation can be read geometrically. The average velocity over an interval is the slope of a secant line. As the second point moves toward t=2, the secant line approaches a tangent line.
This is why limits are needed before derivatives can be defined. A tangent slope is not usually found from two separated points. It is found by letting one point approach another.

exercise.title: Why is instantaneous velocity a limit of averages?

statement.p: For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity over an interval of width h is 4+h whenever h\neq0. In your own words, why is that average not yet a speedometer reading, and why should shrinking the interval be a better clue to the velocity at the instant t=2?

hint.p: An average still spreads a change over a whole window. The speedometer asks about one instant inside that window. Geometrically, secant slopes are trying to settle toward a tangent slope.

subsection.title: Decimal approximations to a number
subsection.p: Limits do not belong only to motion. They also appear whenever approximations close in on a target.
Chapter 2 used nested intervals to trap \sqrt2:
The left endpoints
approach \sqrt2 from below. The right endpoints approach it from above. Neither finite list equals the whole number \sqrt2, but the approximations can be made as close as desired.

note.title: A limit is a target value for a process
note.p: A number can be approached by decimal approximations. A velocity can be approached by average velocities. A tangent slope can be approached by secant slopes.

subsection.p: The same idea appears in different clothing. The mathematics is the same: errors are forced to become small.

exercise.title: What is a limit a target for?

statement.p: Decimal approximations approach a number, average velocities approach an instantaneous velocity, and secant slopes approach a tangent slope. In your own words, what do these processes have in common, and why is a limit a target value for a process rather than a value read off at the missing input?

hint.p: Each process produces a sequence of errors that we try to force toward zero. The target is what the nearby values are heading toward, whether or not the process is allowed to use the exact center.

hint.p: A limit concerns nearby values; the value assigned at the point is separate. Continuity requires those values to agree.

subsection.title: Limits from graphs and tables
subsection.p: A graph can suggest a limit. A table can suggest a limit. But both must be read with care.

subsection.p: The first situation is continuous at the point. The other two distinguish an existing nearby limit from the assigned function value.
The next task is practical. Graphs and tables help us guess limits, but calculus needs reliable ways to calculate them. Algebra gives the first tools.

introduction.p: Limit laws allow us to calculate limits using arithmetic operations on simpler functions. We will also use algebraic simplification and inequalities when direct substitution is unavailable. Tables and graphs can suggest an answer; the calculation must justify it.

paragraphs.title: Warning: the quotient law needs a nonzero limiting denominator
paragraphs.p: As x\to0, the denominator approaches 0, and the quotient does not approach a finite number. From the right it grows without bound; from the left it becomes negative without bound.
So we cannot use a quotient rule when the denominator limit is 0. Sometimes a different algebraic simplification saves the limit. Sometimes no finite limit exists.

paragraphs.title: Warning: limit laws do not work backward
paragraphs.p: It is possible for a sum to have a limit even when the pieces do not.

exercise.title: Why do nearby pieces control a nearby combination?

statement.p: If f(x) approaches L and g(x) approaches M, then their sum approaches L+M. In your own words, why is that believable from error control, and why do the limit laws refuse to run backward: a sum can have a limit even when the pieces do not?

hint.p: The error in a sum is bounded by the sum of the individual errors. Conversely, cancellation may make a sum converge even when its components have no limits.

hint.p: For the polynomial and rational functions considered here, substitution gives the limit when the denominator is nonzero. In general, substitution is justified by continuity at the approach point. The form \frac00 says only that direct substitution failed; factoring, rationalizing, or another method must reveal the nearby behavior.

exercise.title: How can a trapped oscillation still have a limit?

statement.p: The factor \sin(1/x) does not approach one number as x\to0, yet x^2\sin(1/x) does approach 0. In your own words, what is the squeeze idea, and why must the two outside functions approach the same target?

hint.p: If a function is trapped between two others, and those two walls close in on the same number, the trapped graph has nowhere else to go. If the walls headed toward different numbers, there would be a gap to hide in.

subsection.title: A map of the new behaviors
subsection.p: The word “limit” now covers several related ideas.

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{notation} \amp \textbf{input behavior} \amp \textbf{output behavior}\\ \hline \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from both sides} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L\\ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from the left} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L\\ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ approaches }a\text{ from the right} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L\\ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=\infty \amp x\text{ approaches }a \amp f(x)\text{ grows without bound}\\ \displaystyle \lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L \amp x\text{ grows without bound} \amp f(x)\text{ approaches finite }L \end{array}

subsection.p: These ideas help us describe graphs accurately. But the word “approaches” is still informal. The next section turns it into a test that does not depend on the drawing or the table.
The test is based on a challenge: make the output error smaller than any tolerance I name.

exercise.title: How do you tell a hole from a vertical asymptote?

statement.p: Cancellation can turn a forbidden input into a hole, while a denominator approaching zero without cancellation can produce a vertical asymptote. In your own words, what nearby output behavior distinguishes those two pictures?

hint.p: Near a hole, the values settle toward a finite height with one point missing. Near a vertical asymptote, the values refuse to settle and instead grow without bound.

section.title: The precise definition of a limit

introduction.p: The word “approaches” has done a lot of work. It helped us describe average velocities, holes, jumps, asymptotes, and end behavior. But pictures and tables can only suggest a limit. To prove a limit, we need a precise test.
The test begins with error.

statement.p: The definition says that every horizontal band around L must contain the graph over some punctured vertical strip around a. In your own words, why does a jump fail this picture, and why can one-sided versions still succeed when the two-sided test fails?

hint.p: A two-sided strip has to control both sides at once. If the two sides head toward different heights, no single band around one target can hold both nearby pieces. A one-sided test only looks at one half of the strip.

subsection.title: What the definition gives us
subsection.p: The precise definition is not meant to replace intuition. It protects intuition.

It explains why a table can suggest a limit but not prove it. It explains why the value at the point may not matter. It explains why a jump breaks a two-sided limit. It gives us a way to prove limit laws instead of trusting them from graphs.
Most of the time, we will calculate limits using algebra, known limit laws, and continuity. But the \varepsilon-\delta definition is the foundation underneath those shortcuts.

note.title: What a finite limit really says

subsection.p: Now that limits have a precise meaning, we can define a special kind of well-behaved function. It is the case where the nearby limit and the actual value agree. That property is called continuity, and it is the reason many familiar graphs can be drawn without lifting the pencil.

introduction.p: A limit describes nearby function values and may exist even when the function is undefined at the point. Continuity at a requires the function value to exist and equal that limit: \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).

note.p: A function has a removable discontinuity at a if the limit

subsection.p: The word “removable” does not mean the original function was continuous. It means we can make it continuous by changing the value at one point.

exercise.title: When can a hole be repaired?

statement.p: The function \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} is not continuous at x=1 because the value is missing, yet defining the missing height to be 2 produces a continuous extension. In your own words, what makes a discontinuity removable, and why can a jump or a vertical asymptote not be repaired by filling in one point?

hint.p: Repair is possible only when nearby values already agree on a finite target. A jump has two targets. An infinite discontinuity has no finite target at all.

subsection.p: A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of that interval.

exercise.title: Why do endpoints of a closed interval use one-sided continuity?

statement.p: Continuity on [a,b] asks for ordinary continuity inside (a,b), but only a right-hand match at a and a left-hand match at b. In your own words, why are those one-sided conditions the natural ones at the ends of a closed interval?

hint.p: At the left endpoint, allowed inputs of the interval approach only from the right. At the right endpoint, they approach only from the left. There is no other side inside the interval.

exercise.title: Why can a composition have a limit when the inner function is not continuous?

statement.p: If \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L and f is continuous at L, then \lim_{x\to a}f(g(x))=f(L), even if g has a hole or a wrong value at a. Why is the inner limit enough for the composition limit? Why is it not enough for continuity of f\circ g at a?

hint.p: Nearby values of g go to L, and a continuous outer function sends them to values near f(L). Continuity of the composition also needs f(g(a)) to exist and to equal that limit.

exercise.title: Why must the outer function be continuous at L?

statement.p: If \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L but f is not continuous at L, then f(L) may not be the limit of f(g(x)). This is clearest when g(x)=L for every x. Why is a nearby limit of f not enough?

hint.p: A nearby limit of f ignores the value at L. If g equals L, the composition uses that ignored value.

exercise.title: If the inner limit fails, when can the composition still have a limit?

statement.p: The function |x|/x has no two-sided limit at 0. Neither does the identity of that function. Its square does. When does an inner jump remain after composition? When does it disappear?

hint.p: The jump remains if the two sides go to different heights. It disappears if they go to the same height.

exercise.title: Why is continuity easy to build from old continuous pieces?

statement.p: Sums, products, and (when the denominator is nonzero) quotients of continuous functions are continuous, and so is a composition f\circ g when g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a). In your own words, why do these combination rules follow from limit laws, and why does a zero denominator still block continuity?

hint.p: Continuity says nearby values approach the actual values. Limit laws then pass that approach to sums, products, and compositions. A quotient is not even defined where the denominator is zero, so it cannot be continuous there.

subsection.title: Three common discontinuities
subsection.p: Continuity can fail in several ways. The three most common early failures are removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and infinite discontinuities.

figure.caption: Three common ways continuity can fail: a hole, a jump, or a vertical asymptote.

description.p: Panel 1 of 3. Three common ways continuity can fail: a hole, a jump, or a vertical asymptote.
Panel 2 of 3. Three common ways continuity can fail: a hole, a jump, or a vertical asymptote.
Panel 3 of 3. Three common ways continuity can fail: a hole, a jump, or a vertical asymptote.

subsection.p: The names are not just vocabulary. They tell us what kind of repair, if any, is possible.
A removable discontinuity can be fixed by changing one value.
A jump cannot be fixed by changing one value, because the two sides approach different targets.
An infinite discontinuity cannot be fixed by changing one value, because nearby values do not stay near any finite number.

subsection.title: A continuity checklist
subsection.p: When checking continuity at a, ask:

cell.p: If not, the function is not continuous at a.
If the two sides disagree or the values do not settle, the function is not continuous at a.
If not, the nearby behavior and the actual value disagree.

subsection.p: For familiar formulas, continuity often lets us substitute directly. For piecewise functions, endpoints between pieces must be checked. For quotients, denominators must be watched. For roots and logarithms, the domain must be respected.

Continuity is still a local idea: it describes what happens near one point. But it has surprising global consequences. A continuous graph cannot jump over a height, and on a closed finite interval it cannot avoid having a highest and lowest point.
Those two facts are the next payoff.

introduction.p: A continuous function on a closed finite interval takes every value between its endpoint values and attains a maximum and a minimum. The Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem make these statements precise. Both depend on continuity; the extrema theorem also depends on the interval being closed and bounded.

subsection.title: Intermediate values
subsection.p: Suppose the temperature outside is 50^\circF at sunrise and 74^\circF at noon. If the temperature changes continuously, then at some time between sunrise and noon it must have been 60^\circF.
It cannot move from 50 to 74 without passing through the values in between.
The same idea solves equations.

example.p: The value of p(x) changes from negative to positive on the interval [1,2]. Since p is a polynomial, it is continuous. Therefore the graph must cross the x-axis somewhere between 1 and 2.
So there is a number c\in(1,2) such that

statement.p: If a continuous function on [a,b] changes from negative to positive, it must hit zero somewhere in between. In your own words, why does continuity force that crossing, and why is the theorem an existence statement rather than a formula for the root?

hint.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a point with the specified intermediate value. It gives neither uniqueness nor a formula for that point.

subsection.p: This proof idea shows why the real line matters. Bisection produces smaller and smaller intervals. The real numbers guarantee that the intervals trap an actual point.

paragraphs.title: What the theorem does not say
paragraphs.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees existence, not a formula. It tells us a root exists in (1,2), but it does not tell us the exact root.
Bisection gives approximations. If we keep cutting long enough, we can make the interval around the root as short as desired. This is one of the first reliable numerical methods in calculus.

exercise.title: How does bisection turn existence into a trap?

statement.p: Bisection repeatedly keeps the half-interval that still has a sign change. In your own words, why does that process trap a root, and why does completeness of the real line matter for the nested intervals it produces?

hint.p: Each step preserves a sign change and halves the length. Nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink to zero trap one real number. Continuity then forces that trapped number to be a root.

subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity.

subsection.p: The hypothesis of continuity is not decoration. It prevents jumping.

exercise.title: Why is the Intermediate Value Theorem a no-jump theorem?

statement.p: A function that jumps from 0 to 2 can miss the intermediate value 1 even on a closed interval. Explain which hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem fails and why its conclusion need not hold.

hint.p: The theorem’s machine needs a graph that cannot skip heights. If a hypothesis is missing, the output is no longer guaranteed.

subsection.title: Highest and lowest values
subsection.p: Continuity on a closed, bounded interval also ensures that the function attains its extrema.
Suppose h(t) gives the height of a hiker above sea level at time t, for 0\le t\le4. If h is continuous, then during those four hours the hiker reaches a highest elevation and a lowest elevation.
The hiker cannot have a “least upper bound” of heights that is approached but never reached, as long as the time interval includes its endpoints and is finite.
A simple graph shows the idea.

on the interval [0,2]. This function is continuous. Its values include

figure.caption: A continuous function on a closed finite interval reaches its highest and lowest values.

description.p: A continuous function on a closed finite interval reaches its highest and lowest values.

subsection.p: The theorem says this always happens.

statement.p: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a,b].
That is, there are numbers c,d\in[a,b] such that
for every x\in[a,b].

subsection.p: The number f(d) is the absolute maximum value. The number f(c) is the absolute minimum value.
The theorem does not say where the maximum and minimum occur. They may occur at interior points, at endpoints, or at several points.

example.title: Example
example.p: is continuous on [-2,2], so the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [-2,2].
We do not yet have the derivative tools to find them efficiently. But we already know they exist.
This is how the theorem will be used later. Before optimizing a continuous function on a closed interval, we know that the best and worst values are really there.

subsection.title: Why closed and bounded intervals matter
subsection.p: The Extreme Value Theorem has two interval hypotheses:
Both matter.

paragraphs.title: If the interval is not closed
paragraphs.p: The values of f get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).
The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval. So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

paragraphs.title: If the interval is not bounded
paragraphs.p: There is no largest value and no smallest value. The function can grow as large as we like and as negative as we like.
The function is continuous, but the interval is unbounded. The conclusion fails.

paragraphs.title: If the function is not continuous
paragraphs.p: Even on a closed bounded interval, discontinuity can break the conclusion.
The domain is the closed interval [0,1], but K is not continuous at 1.
The values of K(x) get close to 1 as x\to1^-, but K(x) never equals 1. Also,
So K has no absolute maximum on [0,1].

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{missing hypothesis} \amp \textbf{example} \amp \textbf{what fails}\\ \hline \text{closed interval} \amp f(x)=x\text{ on }(0,1) \amp \text{no maximum or minimum}\\ \text{bounded interval} \amp f(x)=x\text{ on }(-\infty,\infty) \amp \text{no maximum or minimum}\\ \text{continuity} \amp K(x)= \begin{cases} x,\amp 0\le x<1\\ 0,\amp x=1 \end{cases} \amp \text{no maximum} \end{array}

paragraphs.p: The theorem is strong because its hypotheses are strong.

exercise.title: Why do closed and bounded intervals matter for highest and lowest values?

statement.p: The Extreme Value Theorem says a continuous function on [a,b] reaches an absolute maximum and minimum. In your own words, why can the conclusion fail on an open interval, on an unbounded interval, or if continuity is dropped, even when a sampled graph appears to attain extrema?

hint.p: Missing endpoints can be approached but never attained. An unbounded interval can let values escape to infinity. A jump can skip the would-be highest or lowest height. The theorem is strong because its hypotheses are strong.

subsection.title: Why these two theorems matter
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem do not usually compute answers. They guarantee that answers exist.
