because \cos1<1. Therefore, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is some c\in(0,1) such that
The theorem does not solve the equation exactly. It tells us a solution must exist. Numerical methods can then approximate it.

example.title: a maximum exists before we know how to find it
example.p: Suppose a continuous function A(x) gives the area of a rectangle built from a fixed amount of fencing, where x is one side length and 0\le x\le L. Since the possible side lengths form a closed interval and A is continuous, the Extreme Value Theorem says that the largest possible area exists.
Later, derivatives will tell us where it occurs. The theorem tells us that the search is not chasing a ghost.

note.title: Existence before formula
note.p: Some theorems do not calculate the desired number. They tell us the desired number is real and reachable. That is often the first step in solving a problem.

subsection.p: The Intermediate Value and Extreme Value Theorems require their stated continuity and interval conditions. The next section gives counterexamples when those conditions are removed.

introduction.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem requires continuity on an interval. The Extreme Value Theorem requires continuity on a closed, bounded interval. The examples below show how their conclusions can fail when these conditions are removed. We will also distinguish a function value from its nearby limit.

subsection.title: Jump discontinuity: unequal one-sided limits
subsection.p: A two-sided limit needs one target. A jump gives two targets.
Define
As x\to0^-, the values of J(x) are always 0. So
As x\to0^+, the values of J(x) are always 1. So
The one-sided limits disagree. Therefore
does not exist.

figure.caption: A jump creates two different one-sided limits, so the two-sided limit fails.

description.p: A jump creates two different one-sided limits, so the two-sided limit fails.

subsection.p: Changing the value at x=0 cannot repair the two-sided limit. The problem is not the point itself. The problem is that the nearby values on the two sides head toward different numbers.

p.me: \text{A two-sided limit is about agreement from both sides.}

exercise.title: Why can changing the value at a jump never repair a two-sided limit?

statement.p: At a jump, the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree. In your own words, why is the problem not the point itself, and why does a two-sided limit demand agreement from both sides?

hint.p: Nearby values on the two sides are already heading toward different numbers. Relabeling the single center point cannot make those two neighborhoods share a target.

subsection.title: A limit that is infinite, not finite
subsection.p: A different kind of failure happens when the values do not settle near any finite number.
Consider
As x gets close to 0, the denominator x^2 gets close to 0, but stays positive. The quotient grows larger and larger.
We write
This notation does not mean that the function has a finite limit. It means the values grow beyond every fixed positive bound.
There is no real number L such that

figure.caption: The values of 1/x^2 grow without bound near 0. This is infinite behavior, not a finite limit.

description.p: The values of 1/x^2 grow without bound near 0. This is infinite behavior, not a finite limit.

subsection.p: A removable discontinuity can be repaired by filling in one value. Infinite divergent behavior cannot. No choice of f(0) can keep the nearby values close to a finite number.

p.me: \infty\text{ describes unbounded behavior. It is not a real-number target.}

exercise.title: Why is \infty not a real-number target?

statement.p: The values of \frac1{x^2} grow beyond every fixed positive bound as x\to0. In your own words, why is that infinite behavior not a finite limit, and why can no choice of a value at the missing point keep the nearby outputs close to a real number L?

hint.p: A finite limit requires outputs to settle inside some \varepsilon-window around a real target. Unbounded growth refuses every such window. Filling one point cannot cage an exploding neighborhood.

subsection.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem fails without continuity
subsection.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem said:

p.em: continuous graph+endpoint values \Longrightarrow all intermediate values are hit.

subsection.p: The word continuous cannot be removed.
Define
On the interval [-1,1],
The number 1 lies between 0 and 2. If we tried to use the Intermediate Value Theorem, we might expect some c\in[-1,1] such that
But no such c exists. The function takes only the values 0 and 2. It jumps over 1.

figure.caption: Without continuity, a function can jump over an intermediate value.

description.p: Without continuity, a function can jump over an intermediate value.

subsection.p: The theorem fails because S is not continuous at 0.

p.me: \text{The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem.}

exercise.title: Which hypothesis of the Intermediate Value Theorem must be checked?

statement.p: The Intermediate Value Theorem is a no-jump theorem: continuous graph plus endpoint values imply that intermediate heights are hit. In your own words, why does dropping continuity let a function skip a height, and what should you check before using the theorem to prove that an equation has a solution?

hint.p: A theorem is a machine with conditions. If the graph can jump, an intermediate value is no longer guaranteed. Check continuity on the closed interval first.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an open interval
subsection.p: The Extreme Value Theorem said:

p.em: continuous on [a,b] \Longrightarrow absolute maximum and minimum are reached.

subsection.p: The closed interval [a,b] includes its endpoints. If the endpoints are missing, the conclusion can fail.
Consider
on the open interval
The function is continuous at every point of its domain. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1, because x=1 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute maximum on (0,1).
The values also get close to 0, but never equal 0, because x=0 is not in the interval.
So f has no absolute minimum on (0,1).

figure.caption: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

description.p: On (0,1), the function f(x)=x approaches its lowest and highest possible values but never reaches them.

subsection.p: The problem is not the formula. The formula f(x)=x is perfectly continuous. The problem is the domain. The endpoints are missing.

p.me: \text{For the Extreme Value Theorem, endpoints matter.}

exercise.title: Which Extreme Value Theorem hypotheses fail in these examples?

statement.p: On an open interval, f(x)=x approaches its apparent highest and lowest values without reaching them. On [0,\infty), the same formula has no largest value. In your own words, why do both closed and bounded matter, and what does it mean to say that a theorem’s output is no longer guaranteed when a condition is missing?

hint.p: Endpoints can be the place where a max or min is attained. An interval that stretches forever can let values escape. The examples are reminders of what the theorem actually says, not exceptions to it.

subsection.title: The Extreme Value Theorem fails on an unbounded interval
subsection.p: A closed interval is not enough if it stretches forever.
Consider
on
The function is continuous on its domain. The interval includes its left endpoint 0, so f has an absolute minimum:
But f has no absolute maximum. Given any value f(x)=x, we can choose a larger input, such as x+1, and get
So no largest value exists.
A physical version is also common. Recall the cooling model
The interval [0,\infty) is unbounded. The temperature starts at
and approaches 70 as t\to\infty. It never reaches 70 for any finite t, because
So this continuous function has an absolute maximum on [0,\infty), but no absolute minimum.

p.me: \text{A function can approach a best value forever without reaching it.}

subsection.p: The word “bounded” in the Extreme Value Theorem prevents this escape to infinity.

subsection.title: A map of the warnings
subsection.p: The examples above are not exceptions to the theorems. They are reminders of what the theorems actually say.

largest or smallest value may escape to infinity

subsection.p: A theorem is a machine with conditions. If a condition is missing, the output is no longer guaranteed.
Limits and continuity have now given us a careful language for functions of a real variable x. But some limiting processes arrive as lists:
or
The input is no longer every nearby real number. The input is the whole-number step n. That leads to sequences.

section.title: Sequences as limits indexed by whole numbers

introduction.p: Limits so far have used a real input approaching a point:
But many approximations arrive one step at a time. Bisection gives a first interval, then a second, then a third. A decimal approximation gives a first decimal, then a second, then a third.
The input is not a continuous variable. It is a counting number:
A limit of such a list is called a limit of a sequence.

subsection.title: Sequence notation
subsection.p: A sequence is a function whose input is a positive integer.
Instead of writing
we usually write
The number a_n is called the nth term of the sequence.

exercise.title: How is a sequence a limit with a counting-number input?

statement.p: Limits so far used a real input approaching a point. A sequence is a function whose input is a positive integer. In your own words, what changes when the input is a counting number n=1,2,3,\ldots rather than a continuous variable x, and why do bisection and decimal approximations naturally produce sequences?

hint.p: The input no longer fills an interval; it arrives one step at a time. Nested intervals and longer decimals are lists indexed by whole numbers.

example.title: Example
example.p: This sequence does not settle down. It alternates forever.

example.title: recursive notation
example.p: Some sequences are not first given by an explicit formula. They are given by a starting value and a rule for the next term.
The terms move toward 2. Each step takes the current value and moves halfway from it to 2.
Recursive sequences will appear later in Newton’s method and Euler’s method. They are how a computer often follows a mathematical process step by step.

subsection.p: The sequence

subsection.p: A sequence that has a finite limit is called convergent. A sequence that does not have a finite limit is called divergent.
The precise definition is the same epsilon idea we used for functions, with \delta replaced by a cutoff index N.

exercise.title: What does a cutoff index N do in place of a \delta?

statement.p: Sequence convergence uses the same epsilon idea, but the response is a whole-number cutoff: after n\ge N, every term stays inside the \varepsilon-window around L. In your own words, why does the order first \varepsilon, then N still matter, and what would it mean for a sequence to diverge?

hint.p: The challenger still names any positive output error. You answer with how far out in the list you must go. Divergence means no finite target survives every such challenge, whether by oscillation or by growing without bound.

subsection.title: Monotone bounded sequences
subsection.p: Some sequences converge because they move steadily in one direction and cannot escape.
The decimal approximations
move upward toward \sqrt2. They never pass \sqrt2. They are increasing and bounded above.
This is a common pattern.

A sequence is monotone if it is increasing or decreasing.

subsection.p: Here “increasing” allows equality. Some books call this nondecreasing.

paragraphs.p: Let (a_n) be increasing and bounded above. Consider the set of its terms:
Since the sequence is bounded above, this set has an upper bound. By the least upper bound property, it has a least upper bound. Call it L.
Let \varepsilon>0 be given. Since L is the least upper bound, the number

Also, since L is an upper bound,
The decreasing case is similar, or can be proved by applying the increasing case to -a_n.

paragraphs.p: Increasing alone is not enough. The sequence
is increasing, but it is not bounded above. It diverges to infinity.
Bounded alone is not enough. The sequence

exercise.title: Why do monotone bounded sequences have to settle?

statement.p: The decimal approximations 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \ldots increase and never pass \sqrt2. In your own words, why does an increasing sequence that is bounded above converge, and why is this one of the first places completeness of the real numbers is doing essential work?

hint.p: The set of terms has a least upper bound L. Increasing terms cannot jump over L, and they cannot stay a fixed distance below it forever. Completeness is what supplies that least upper bound.

subsection.p: The bisection method from the Intermediate Value Theorem produces sequences automatically.
For

where each interval still contains a sign change.

The right endpoints form a decreasing sequence:
The left endpoints are bounded above by 2. The right endpoints are bounded below by 1. Therefore both endpoint sequences converge.
Also, the interval lengths shrink by a factor of \frac12 at each step. If the first interval has length 1, then after n steps the length is
Since
the two endpoint sequences converge to the same number. That number is the root trapped by bisection.
This is why bisection is reliable. It does not guess wildly. It creates sequences that are forced to settle.

subsection.p: Sequences are the bridge from limits to infinite sums. They also bring us back to the question that started the chapter. A tangent slope can be approached by a sequence of secant slopes, for example by taking

A derivative requires the same limit as h approaches zero through all allowed nonzero steps, not just h=1/n.

exercise.title: Why is an infinite sum secretly a sequence problem?

statement.p: We do not add infinitely many terms all at once. We add the first N terms and watch the partial sums as N\to\infty. In your own words, what does it mean for a series to converge, and how is bisection the same kind of settling?

hint.p: A series converges when its sequence of partial sums converges. Bisection creates nested endpoint sequences whose lengths shrink to zero, so those sequences are forced to settle to the trapped root.

introduction.p: This chapter defined limits and continuity, distinguished one-sided limits from two-sided limits, and treated unbounded behavior and sequence limits. The review problems ask you to calculate limits, check hypotheses, and apply the Intermediate Value and Extreme Value Theorems.

subsection.title: The chapter in one picture
subsection.p: A limit is the central idea. The other ideas in the chapter are different ways of asking what a limit is doing.

figure.caption: Limits are the center. Continuity, asymptotes, sequences, and tangent slopes all use the same idea of controlled approach.

description.p: Limits are the center. Continuity, asymptotes, sequences, and tangent slopes all use the same idea of controlled approach.

subsection.p: The most important habit is not memorizing a table of limit forms. It is asking:

p.me: \text{What is the input doing, and what target is the output approaching?}

exercise.title: What one idea sits at the center of the chapter?

statement.p: The chapter began with a forbidden value h=0 that did not stop us from seeing what happens as h gets close to 0. In your own words, what does a limit watch, and why can continuity, one-sided behavior, asymptotes, and sequences all be seen as different ways of asking the same nearby-target question?

hint.p: A limit is a controlled approach to a target. Sometimes the input is a real number, sometimes a whole-number index, sometimes only one side, and sometimes the target is infinite rather than finite.

subsection.title: A decision guide for limits and continuity
subsection.p: When you face a limit problem, begin with the simplest test. Then move only as far as the problem requires.

table.title: A decision guide for limits and continuity

Use continuity or the limit laws.
Factor, cancel, expand, combine fractions, or rationalize. Then try again.
left and right sides behave differently
Compute one-sided limits. A two-sided limit exists only if they agree.
Check signs from the left and right. The limit may be \infty, -\infty, or may fail to exist.
Divide by the largest power, or compare leading terms.
an oscillating factor is multiplied by something small
a theorem about continuous functions is tempting
Check the hypotheses first: continuity, closed interval, bounded interval, and the right endpoint information.
Use the \varepsilon-N definition, algebraic limit laws, or monotone bounded convergence.

subsection.title: The derivative as a limit
subsection.p: A limit watches a quantity approach a target. In this chapter, the quantity might have been a function value, a sequence term, or an average velocity.
The next chapter chooses one limit and builds a new object from it:
The numerator measures change in output. The denominator measures change in input. The quotient is an average rate of change. The limit, if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change.
That number is the derivative.

exercise.title: What new object is the next chapter about to build from a limit?

statement.p: The next chapter chooses the limit \lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}. In your own words, what do the numerator and denominator measure, why is the quotient still an average, and what extra meaning appears if that limit exists?

hint.p: The numerator is change in output. The denominator is change in input. The quotient is an average rate. The limit, if it exists, is the instantaneous rate: the derivative.

introduction.p: A derivative is the limit of average rates of change over intervals shrinking to a point:

When this finite limit exists, it gives the instantaneous rate of change and the tangent slope at that point. This chapter defines the derivative, develops its first formulas, and explains its use in local approximation and motion.
A limit of average rates cannot be understood until the average rate itself is clear. So we begin with the ordinary slope between two points.
If f is a function and the input changes from a to b, then the output changes from f(a) to f(b). The average rate of change compares these two changes:
This is the slope of the line through the two graph points
That line is called a secant line.

exercise.title: Why is an average rate a secant slope rather than a local slope?

statement.p: The average rate of change of f from a to b is the slope of the line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). In your own words, why does that number describe the whole interval at once, and why is it not the slope of the graph at every point in between?

hint.p: A secant uses two points. On a curved graph, nearby pairs of points can produce different slopes.

subsection.p: The same quotient appears in motion.
Let s(t) be the position of an object at time t. If s is measured in meters and t is measured in seconds, then

That is a velocity.

paragraphs.title: Displacement, not distance traveled
paragraphs.p: Average velocity uses signed change in position:
If an object moves forward and then backward, its displacement can be small even if it traveled a long distance.
For example, suppose a runner starts at 0 meters, runs to 100 meters, and then returns to 0 meters in 20 seconds. The average velocity over the full trip is
That does not mean the runner was standing still. It means the net change in position was 0. Average velocity measures net signed change per unit time.

exercise.title: Why can average velocity be zero even if the object moved?

statement.p: A runner who goes out and back in 20 seconds has average velocity 0. In your own words, why does that not mean the runner stood still, and what quantity is average velocity actually using?

hint.p: Average velocity uses signed change in position. Distance traveled counts every step, forward or back.

subsection.title: Average rate from data
subsection.p: A formula is not required. If we have a table, we can still compute average rates.
Recall the cooling coffee data from Chapter 2:
The average rate of change of the coffee temperature from t=0 to t=5 is
The units are degrees Celsius per minute. So during the first 5 minutes, the coffee cooled at an average rate of
The negative sign means the temperature decreased.
From t=15 to t=25, the average rate is
So between 15 and 25 minutes, the coffee cooled at an average rate of
The coffee cools more slowly later. The average rate depends on the interval.

figure.caption: Average rates from data are secant slopes between measured points.

description.p: Average rates from data are secant slopes between measured points.

subsection.p: A table gives only certain points. We can compute average rates between those points, but we cannot know the exact instantaneous rate from the table alone. We can estimate it by using nearby data, but the estimate depends on the quality and spacing of the measurements.

exercise.title: Why does reversing the endpoints leave the secant slope unchanged?

statement.p: Computing from b back to a changes the sign of both the numerator and the denominator. In your own words, why is the average rate the same either way, and what geometric object is being measured?

hint.p: A line through two points has one slope. Changing the order of the two points does not change the line.

note.title: Meaning before formulas
note.p: An average rate of change is always a comparison:

p.me: \frac{\text{how much the output changed}}{\text{how much the input changed}}.

note.p: The units tell what kind of comparison it is.

subsection.p: Average rates are useful, but they still describe an interval. A speedometer does not report the average velocity over the last hour. It reports what is happening now.
To get that number from position, we must make the interval shrink.

exercise.title: Why do units and the chosen interval both matter?

statement.p: An average rate always has the form output units per input unit, and its value depends on which two data points we compare. In your own words, why do the units tell the meaning of the comparison, and why can a table give average rates without giving an exact instantaneous rate?

hint.p: A quotient inherits units from numerator and denominator. A table only supplies certain points, so any rate computed from it still belongs to an interval.

introduction.p: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time. Instantaneous velocity is the limit of this quotient as the nonzero time interval shrinks to zero. We take a limit; we do not evaluate the quotient with a zero denominator.

exercise.title: Why is an instantaneous rate a limit rather than a ratio?

statement.p: The difference quotient \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is an average rate. In your own words, why must h approach 0 rather than be set equal to 0, and what idea does the resulting limit name?

paragraphs.p: It is tempting to say that a tangent line is a line that touches the graph at one point and does not cross it. That picture works for some curves, but it is not a definition.
So the tangent line at (0,0) is

exercise.title: Why is a tangent a limiting secant rather than a line that merely touches?

statement.p: As h\to 0, secant slopes may approach a single number, which we call the tangent slope. In your own words, why is touches at one point and does not cross an unreliable definition, and what example in this section shows the trouble?

hint.p: Look at y=x^3 at the origin. The tangent line is still the limiting position of secants even if the curve crosses it.

subsection.title: The derivative as a limit
subsection.p: The derivative is a limit of slopes:
This formula has three layers.
First, the quotient
is an average rate of change over an interval.
Second, the limit
shrinks the interval toward a single input.
Third, the result f'(a), if it exists, is the instantaneous rate of change at a.
The limit must exist as one finite number. If the slopes approach different values from different sides, there is no derivative.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: the corner in |x|
paragraphs.p: The right-side slopes approach 1. The left-side slopes approach -1. There is no single limiting slope.

figure.caption: At a corner, the left and right limiting slopes can disagree. Then the derivative does not exist.

description.p: At a corner, the left and right limiting slopes can disagree. Then the derivative does not exist.

paragraphs.p: The graph has a sharp corner at the origin. The corner is not the real reason the derivative fails; it is the picture of the reason. The reason is that the limiting slopes do not approach one common value.

note.title: What can go wrong?
note.p: The derivative at a exists only when
exists as a finite number.
If the left and right slopes disagree, or if the slopes grow without bound, then f'(a) does not exist.

paragraphs.p: One derivative gives one slope at one point. But a curve has many points. If we let the point a move, the derivative itself becomes a new function. That new function will tell us how the whole graph is changing.

exercise.title: Why does a corner prevent a derivative?

statement.p: For f(x)=|x|, the right-hand slopes near 0 approach 1 and the left-hand slopes approach -1. In your own words, why does that disagreement mean f'(0) does not exist, and why is the corner a picture of that reason rather than a separate reason?

hint.p: A derivative at a point must be one finite limiting slope. If the two sides settle toward different numbers, there is no such number.

introduction.p: At each input where a function is differentiable, its derivative gives the tangent slope. Collecting these values defines a new function, f\prime. For f(x)=x^2, the derivative function is f\prime(x)=2x, so in particular f\prime(2)=4.

exercise.title: Why may the domain of f' be smaller than the domain of f?

statement.p: The function f(x)=|x| is defined for every real x, but f'(0) does not exist. In your own words, why can a derivative function omit points that the original function includes?

hint.p: f' is defined only where the limiting slope exists. Existence of a height is a weaker demand than existence of a single nearby slope.

exercise.title: Why is the derivative a function and not only a number?

statement.p: At one point, f'(a) is a tangent slope. If the point is allowed to move, we write f'(x). In your own words, what new object is this, and how does its graph differ in meaning from the graph of f?

hint.p: The original graph records height. The derivative graph records slope at each x where the limit exists.

subsection.title: Reading f' from the graph of f
subsection.p: The graph of f contains the graph of f' in hidden form. At each x, the value f'(x) is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f.
This gives several visual rules.

statement.p: Rising, falling, a horizontal tangent, and a sharp corner each have a meaning for f'. In your own words, how would you read those features from the graph of f, and why does the graph of f' not show the height of f?

hint.p: At each x, the value of f' is a slope, not a height. Sign, size, and existence of that slope are what the original graph can reveal.

subsection.title: Reading f from the graph of f'
subsection.p: The derivative graph also gives information in the opposite direction.
If f'(x)>0 throughout an interval, then the tangent slopes are positive there, so f is increasing on that interval. Chapter 6 will justify this conclusion with the Mean Value Theorem.
If f'(x)<0 throughout an interval, then f is decreasing on that interval.
If f'(x)=0, then the graph of f has a horizontal tangent.

This is why derivatives help us understand graphs. A derivative is local information, but when we collect it point by point, it begins to describe the whole curve.

paragraphs.title: What f' does not tell by itself
paragraphs.p: The derivative does not remember vertical shifts.
The two graphs have the same slopes at corresponding x-values, but one graph is 5 units higher.

note.title: The derivative forgets constants
note.p: A derivative records change. Adding a constant changes height, but not slope.

paragraphs.p: This points toward the second half of calculus. If we know all the slopes f'(x), how much of f can we recover? We will eventually need a starting value and a way to accumulate slope information.
Before that larger question, we use the derivative for a more local purpose: near one point, a curve can be replaced by a line.

exercise.title: Why does the derivative forget vertical shifts?

statement.p: The functions x^2 and x^2+5 have the same derivative. In your own words, why must that happen, and what information about f is therefore missing from f' alone?

hint.p: Adding a constant changes height, not slope. Recovering a function from its slopes will later need a starting value.

exercise.title: Why can a tangent line replace a curve nearby?

statement.p: Near a point of tangency, calculus lets us replace a curved graph by a line. In your own words, why is that replacement useful, and why does it fail if we wander too far from the point?

hint.p: A line is simple, and differentiability says the curve and its tangent stay close under enough magnification. Distance from the point of tangency is what the approximation depends on.

subsection.p: Local linear approximation is one of the main reasons derivatives matter. A differentiable function may be curved, but under enough magnification it behaves like a line.

That raises the next question. If a function has a derivative at a point, what does that force the original function to do near that point? In particular, can a differentiable function jump? The answer is no, and the reason is hidden inside the same local linear formula.

hint.p: At an endpoint there is no other side inside the domain. One-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the two-sided derivative.

subsection.title: Units and signs in motion problems
subsection.p: The hardest part of many motion problems is not differentiating. It is deciding what the signs mean.
A position is measured relative to an origin. A velocity is measured relative to a positive direction. Acceleration tells whether velocity is increasing or decreasing in that chosen direction.
Acceleration does not directly tell which way the object is moving. Velocity does that.
Acceleration tells how velocity is changing.

paragraphs.title: Speeding up and slowing down
paragraphs.p: an object speeds up when the magnitude of velocity increases.

p.me: \text{if \(v\) and \(a\) have the same sign, the object is speeding up,}
\text{if \(v\) and \(a\) have opposite signs, the object is slowing down.}

paragraphs.p: The signs are opposite, so the ball is slowing down as it rises.
The signs are the same, so the ball is speeding up as it falls.

paragraphs.title: Same physical motion, different sign convention
paragraphs.p: Suppose a stone is dropped from a 100-meter tower.
If height above the ground is the position, and upward is positive, then
Both velocity and acceleration are negative after the stone is released, so the stone is speeding up downward.
If instead we measure downward distance from the release point, then the same motion is described by
Now velocity and acceleration are positive because the positive direction has been chosen downward.
The physics did not change. The coordinate choice changed.

The derivative has now returned to its first meaning: instantaneous motion. But even motion can hide traps. A graph may look continuous and still have no velocity at a sharp turn. A derivative may exist and still behave unexpectedly. Before moving to a larger library of differentiation rules, we pause to collect these warning examples.

exercise.title: Why must origin and positive direction be chosen before signs mean anything?

statement.p: The same falling stone can have negative or positive acceleration depending on whether upward or downward is called positive. In your own words, why does that not change the physics, and how do the signs of v and a together tell whether the object is speeding up?

hint.p: Signs are relative to a chosen axis. Speed increases when velocity and acceleration point the same way along that axis.

subsection.p: The warnings in this section protect the meaning of the derivative.

The derivative is now defined, interpreted, and tested. But computing every derivative from the limit definition is too slow. The next chapter builds a faster language: rules for differentiating sums, products, quotients, compositions, and the elementary functions.

exercise.title: Why is a graphing calculator not a proof of differentiability?

statement.p: A finite plot of |x-0.03| can miss the corner if that point is never sampled. In your own words, why can a picture hide a nondifferentiable point, and what test actually decides whether f'(a) exists?

hint.p: A screen shows finitely many samples. The difference quotient examines the point itself, from both sides if needed.

introduction.p: The chapter began with a familiar quotient:
That quotient measured average change. By shrinking the interval, we found a new number:
The same number appeared in several forms. It was an instantaneous rate, a tangent slope, the coefficient in the best linear approximation, and velocity when the function was position.

It tells us what the derivative means. It proves the first formulas. It catches corners, cusps, and jumps. It explains velocity, tangent slope, and local linear approximation.
But it is too slow to use from scratch every time.

These functions are built from simpler pieces by multiplying, dividing, and composing. Their derivatives should be built from the derivatives of those pieces.
The next chapter turns the definition into a working language. The goal is not to replace meaning with rules. The goal is to make the meaning fast enough to use.

exercise.title: Why is the definition the source, but not enough by itself?

hint.p: Expanding a product into a polynomial is not always possible. The derivative of a built function should be built from the derivatives of the pieces.

introduction.p: Differentiation rules let us find derivatives without evaluating the defining limit each time. This chapter develops rules for sums, products, quotients, compositions, implicit relations, and inverse functions, then applies them to the elementary functions. The appropriate rule depends on how the function is formed and where it is defined.

The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Multiplication by a constant also passes through differentiation. We will prove these rules from the limit definition and use them to differentiate polynomials.

These rules handle many expressions built by adding, scaling, multiplying, and dividing.
But one common construction is still missing. Many functions are nested:
The outside function changes because the inside function changes first. The next rule measures change through a chain.

introduction.p: In a composition f(g(x)), a change in x first changes g(x), which then changes the output of f. The chain rule multiplies the derivative of the outer function, evaluated at g(x), by the derivative of the inner function.

hint.p: The chain rule guarantees a derivative when both links are differentiable at the required points. If either hypothesis fails, the rule gives no conclusion; the composite may still be differentiable. For example, |x|^2=x^2 is differentiable at zero although the inner function |x| is not.

subsection.title: When the method warns us
subsection.p: Implicit differentiation assumes that near the point we care about, the curve can be treated as one differentiable function y(x). The equation itself does not always guarantee that.

paragraphs.title: A vertical tangent
paragraphs.p: No finite value of y' can satisfy this equation. That does not mean the circle has no tangent. It means the tangent is vertical, so its slope dy/dx is not a finite number.
The point (5,0) is also where the upper and lower branches meet at the right edge. Near that point, the circle cannot be written as a differentiable function y(x) with a finite derivative.

paragraphs.title: A relation with two branches
paragraphs.p: At (0,0), both branches meet. If we choose the branch y=x, the slope is 1. If we choose the branch y=-x, the slope is -1.
which does not determine y'. The reason is geometric: the equation has not selected one branch.

warning.title: Implicit differentiation warning
warning.p: When the equation does not define one smooth branch y(x) near the point, the algebra may produce no slope, many possible slopes, or an equation that does not determine dy/dx.

paragraphs.p: These warnings are useful. They do not break the method. They tell us what the geometry is doing.

exercise.title: When does the algebra warn that there is no finite y'?

statement.p: At (5,0) on the circle, the differentiated equation cannot be solved for a finite slope; at the origin of y^2=x^2, it becomes 0=0. In your own words, what is the geometry doing in each case, and why is that a warning rather than a broken method?

hint.p: A vertical tangent has no finite dy/dx. Two branches meeting at a point have not selected one function y(x).

note.p: Implicit differentiation avoids solving for y. It uses the chain rule to differentiate the relation directly, then solves for dy/dx.

subsection.p: The chain rule and implicit differentiation now let us handle complicated algebraic layers and many curves. But some of the most important functions in calculus are not algebraic. The next step is periodic motion: sine, cosine, and the derivatives that make waves and rotation calculable.

statement.p: Implicit differentiation often produces a formula for y' that still involves y. In your own words, why is that natural for a curve, rather than a defect of the method?

hint.p: A point on a curve has two coordinates. The tangent direction can depend on where the point sits, not only on its x-coordinate.

introduction.p: Sine and cosine describe periodic behavior such as rotation and oscillation. Their derivatives are (\sin x)\prime=\cos x and (\cos x)\prime=-\sin x when angles are measured in radians. We will derive these formulas from limits and use them to differentiate the remaining trigonometric functions.

On the unit circle, an angle of h radians cuts off an arc of length h. That is why radians are the natural angle unit for calculus. A small angle h is also a small distance traveled along the circle.
Degrees do not have this property. A degree is a human subdivision of a full turn. A radian is built from length.

Trigonometric functions describe quantities that repeat. Another family describes quantities that grow or decay by multiplying: populations, radioactive substances, and continuously compounded money. Their derivatives lead to the number e.

section.title: Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions

introduction.p: The function e^x equals its own derivative. Consequently, exponentials describe quantities whose rates of change are proportional to their current values. We will derive exponential and logarithmic derivative formulas, with their domains stated explicitly.

subsection.title: The derivative table so far
subsection.p: We now have the main elementary derivative formulas:

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{function} \amp \text{derivative}\\ \hline x^n \amp nx^{n-1}\\ \sin x \amp \cos x\\ \cos x \amp -\sin x\\ \tan x \amp \sec^2x\\ e^x \amp e^x\\ a^x \amp (\ln a)a^x\\ \ln x \amp \dfrac1x\\ \log_a x \amp \dfrac1{x\ln a} \end{array}

subsection.p: Together with the sum, product, quotient, and chain rules, these formulas let us differentiate a wide range of functions.

But one idea has appeared twice without being named fully. We found \ln x by reversing e^x. Earlier, trigonometry gave us sine and cosine; reversing those functions will give \arcsin x, \arccos x, and \arctan x. The next question is general: when a function has an inverse, how is the derivative of the inverse related to the original derivative?

section.title: Inverse functions and inverse trigonometric functions

introduction.p: The derivative of an inverse function is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input, provided that derivative is nonzero. We will justify this relation and apply it to inverse trigonometric functions. Choosing the inverse branch is necessary to specify both its domain and its derivative.

Inverse functions reverse input and output. The next section returns to powers, where the exponent need not be an integer. That extension also depends on reversing functions, because real powers are most naturally handled with logarithms.

introduction.p: For x>0, logarithms extend the power rule to every real exponent: (x^r)\prime=rx^{r-1}. This section proves that result, defines hyperbolic functions using exponentials, and develops their identities, inverses, and derivatives.

exercise.title: Why do logarithms prove the general power rule?

subsection.title: Inverse hyperbolic functions: branches and derivatives
subsection.p: The identity \cosh^2 t-\sinh^2 t=1 gives the derivatives of the inverses once we choose their branches. We use the names \operatorname{arsinh}, \operatorname{arcosh}, and \operatorname{artanh} to avoid confusing an inverse with a reciprocal. For example, \operatorname{arsinh}x is an inverse function, whereas \operatorname{csch}x=1/\sinh x.
Complete the family by defining \coth t=\cosh t/\sinh t and \operatorname{csch}t=1/\sinh t for t\ne0. The quotient and reciprocal rules give

Since \cosh t>0, \sinh is strictly increasing from \mathbb R onto \mathbb R. The function \tanh is strictly increasing from \mathbb R onto (-1,1). The even functions \cosh and \operatorname{sech} must be restricted to t\ge0 to have inverses. For \coth and \operatorname{csch}, the positive and negative branches have disjoint ranges, so both branches can be inverted together.
Solving the exponential definitions gives logarithmic formulas on precisely these domains:

For example, write x=\sinh y and set z=e^y>0. Then z^2-2xz-1=0, whose positive root is x+\sqrt{x^2+1}. Taking its logarithm proves the first formula. For x=\cosh y, the roots are x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}; the branch y\ge0 selects the plus sign. Solving x=(e^{2y}-1)/(e^{2y}+1) proves the formula for \operatorname{artanh}. The other formulas follow by taking reciprocals in these three inverse relations.

figure.caption: The three basic inverse branches. The branch of \operatorname{arcosh} begins at (1,0); \operatorname{artanh} has vertical asymptotes at x=\pm1.

description.p: Separate plots of arsinh on the real line, arcosh for x at least one, and artanh between minus one and one, with dashed vertical asymptotes for artanh.

subsection.p: For y=\operatorname{arsinh}x, implicit differentiation gives 1=\cosh y\,y'. Since \cosh y=\sqrt{1+x^2}>0, the first derivative follows. For y=\operatorname{arcosh}x with x>1, we have y>0 and \sinh y=\sqrt{x^2-1}. For \operatorname{artanh} and \operatorname{arcoth}, the logarithmic formulas immediately give 1/(1-x^2). Finally, \operatorname{arsech}x=\operatorname{arcosh}(1/x) and \operatorname{arcsch}x=\operatorname{arsinh}(1/x); the chain rule gives the last two formulas. In the last calculation, \sqrt{1+1/x^2}=\sqrt{1+x^2}/|x|, so the absolute value cannot be dropped.

warning.title: The endpoints still matter
warning.p: The functions \operatorname{arcosh} and \operatorname{arsech} are defined at x=1, but they have no finite one-sided derivative there. Also, \operatorname{arcosh}(\cosh t)=|t|, whereas \operatorname{arsinh}(\sinh t)=t. The restriction used to define an inverse remains part of the answer.

chapter.title: Shape, Extremes, and the Mean Value Theorem
chapter.shorttitle: Shape and the Mean Value Theorem

introduction.p: Derivatives describe more than rates of change. Their signs determine intervals of increase and decrease, and second derivatives describe concavity. This chapter connects derivative information to extrema and graph shape, proves Rolle's Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem, and applies these results to limits and estimates.

Velocity tells both how fast a car is moving and its direction. Its sign tells the direction of motion; a speedometer reports the nonnegative speed. Positive velocity means position is increasing. Negative velocity means position is decreasing.
The same idea works for any differentiable function.

When h>0, moving to the right by a small amount, a positive f'(x) gives a positive change in f. A negative f'(x) gives a negative change in f.
The Mean Value Theorem will explain why this local information controls the whole interval.

statement.p: A sign chart splits the line at the places where f' is zero or undefined, then records the sign of f' on each piece. In your own words, why do those split points belong on the chart, and what graph information is the chart trying to make visible without drawing the graph?

subsection.p: The numbers where the derivative is zero or undefined deserve a name.

exercise.title: Why is a critical number a candidate rather than a conclusion?

statement.p: A number c in the domain is critical when f\prime(c)=0 or the derivative is undefined. Explain why these points require checking and why either condition can occur without a local extremum.

hint.p: Think of x^3 at 0, or of |x| at 0. One is critical and does not turn around; the other is critical because of a corner.

introduction.p: The sign chart for x^3-3x showed a graph that rises, then falls, then rises. At the point where rising changes to falling, the graph has a high point nearby. At the point where falling changes to rising, the graph has a low point nearby.
Those points are called extrema.

subsection.title: Local maximum and local minimum
subsection.p: A high point nearby is not necessarily the highest point everywhere. A mountain can have many peaks. A small peak is still a peak if the graph is lower on both sides nearby.

note.title: Local extrema
note.p: A function f has a local maximum at c if
for all x sufficiently close to c.
A function f has a local minimum at c if
for all x sufficiently close to c.

subsection.p: The phrase “sufficiently close” means that we only compare f(c) with nearby values of the function. Local extrema are neighborhood ideas.
Now compare this with the global idea.

note.title: Absolute extrema
note.p: A function f has an absolute maximum at c on a set D if
for every x\in D.
A function f has an absolute minimum at c on a set D if
for every x\in D.

subsection.p: Absolute extrema compare against the whole domain under discussion. Local extrema compare only nearby.

exercise.title: Why is a local maximum not automatically an absolute maximum?

statement.p: A local maximum only asks that nearby values be no larger. An absolute maximum asks that every value on the domain under discussion be no larger. In your own words, why can a nearby peak lose to an endpoint, and what is the difference between a neighborhood comparison and a whole-domain comparison?

hint.p: A mountain can have many peaks. The highest point on a trail may sit at the end of the trail rather than at a nearby summit.

example.p: The derivative changes from positive to negative at x=1, so x=1 is a local maximum. The derivative changes from negative to positive at x=3, so x=3 is a local minimum.
But the absolute maximum on the interval occurs at the endpoint x=5. A local maximum does not have to be the absolute maximum.

subsection.title: Why Fermat’s hypotheses matter
subsection.p: Fermat’s theorem is short, but every condition is doing work.

There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points, not endpoints. At an endpoint, the graph can be highest or lowest simply because the interval stops.

does not exist. Again, Fermat’s theorem is not contradicted. The theorem says that if the local extremum occurs at a differentiable interior point, then the derivative is 0.
Corners can have extrema without horizontal tangents.

But x^3 is increasing through 0. It has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum there.

p.em: Every differentiable interior extremum is critical, but not every critical number is an extremum.

subsection.title: The first derivative test
subsection.p: A critical number becomes more meaningful when we look at the sign of f' on both sides.

note.title: First derivative test
note.p: Suppose c is a critical number of f, and f is continuous at c.

subsection.p: The reason is simple. If the function increases before c and decreases after c, then c is a high point nearby. If it decreases before c and increases after c, then c is a low point nearby.
This test depends on the first derivative sign rule, whose full proof comes from the Mean Value Theorem. The picture is already clear; the next theorem will make it secure.

hint.p: Rising into a point and falling away from it makes a nearby high point. A horizontal tangent that does not change the direction of travel does not.

subsection.title: Absolute extrema and the closed interval method
subsection.p: Local extrema are nearby comparisons. Absolute extrema are whole-domain comparisons. To find them, we need a guarantee that they exist.
The guarantee comes from continuity on a closed, bounded interval.

statement.p: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a,b].

subsection.p: This theorem is a deep fact about the real line. It rests on the idea that the real line has no gaps. For now, its meaning is more important than its proof:

p.em: a continuous graph on a closed finite interval cannot escape its highest and lowest values.

subsection.p: The hypotheses matter.

paragraphs.title: Open interval warning
paragraphs.p: has no absolute maximum and no absolute minimum. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1. They get close to 0, but never equal 0.

paragraphs.title: Unbounded interval warning
paragraphs.p: has an absolute minimum at 0, but no absolute maximum.

paragraphs.title: Continuity warning
paragraphs.p: on [0,1]. This function has no absolute maximum. The values approach 1, but the function never reaches 1. At the endpoint, it jumps down to 0.
The interval is closed and bounded, but the function is not continuous.

subsection.title: The closed interval method
subsection.p: Fermat’s theorem tells us where an interior extremum can occur. The Extreme Value Theorem tells us that absolute extrema exist on a closed interval. Together they give a practical method.

hint.p: Fermat’s theorem only constrains interior differentiable extrema. An endpoint can be best or worst simply because the interval stops.

subsection.p: We have used the derivative to read the shape of a function:

Fermat’s theorem was proved directly from the derivative definition. But the first derivative sign rule still needs its real proof.

The missing idea is surprisingly simple. If a car’s average velocity over a trip is 50 miles per hour, then at some instant its speed should have been 50 miles per hour. If a smooth graph starts and ends at the same height, then somewhere in between it should have a horizontal tangent.
That idea is Rolle’s Theorem, and just beyond it is the Mean Value Theorem.

section.title: Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem

introduction.p: Rolle’s Theorem combines the existence of absolute extrema with the zero-derivative condition at an interior extremum. The Mean Value Theorem extends the result to unequal endpoint values.
For example, a car moving from mile marker 10 at noon to mile marker 160 at 3{:}00 has average velocity
miles per hour. If its position is continuous throughout the trip and its velocity exists between the endpoint times, then at some instant its velocity is
The car’s velocity may vary during the trip. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees an instant when it equals the average velocity.

exercise.title: Why do the hypotheses of Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem matter?

statement.p: Explain the roles of continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on its interior, and equal endpoint values in Rolle's Theorem. Which hypotheses fail for a jump or a corner?

hint.p: A jump can skip the needed height, a corner can turn without a horizontal tangent, and a steadily rising graph has no reason to flatten if it starts and ends at different heights.

subsection.title: Consequences of the Mean Value Theorem
subsection.p: The Mean Value Theorem turns information about derivatives into information about functions. That is why it is so useful.

statement.p: If f'(x)=0 for every x in an interval I, then f is constant on I.

exercise.title: Why does a zero derivative on an interval force a constant function?

statement.p: If f'(x)=0 everywhere on an interval, then f is constant there. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem turn that local information into a global conclusion, and why do two functions with the same derivative differ only by a constant?

hint.p: Between any two inputs, some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is zero, the net change between those inputs must be zero.

statement.p: A positive derivative at one point is local information. Increasing on a whole interval is a comparison of values. In your own words, how does the Mean Value Theorem turn a sign of f' throughout an interval into the inequality f(x_2)>f(x_1) whenever x_1<x_2?

hint.p: Write the difference f(x_2)-f(x_1) as f'(c)(x_2-x_1). The second factor is positive; the first factor keeps a constant sign.

subsection.p: The Mean Value Theorem also turns a bound on the derivative into a bound on total change.

That idea will return when we estimate errors.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: The Mean Value Theorem explains why the sign of f' controls increasing and decreasing behavior. It also explains why a zero derivative on an interval forces a function to be constant.
But there is more shape left to read.

Two graphs can both be increasing and still look very different. One can rise faster and faster. Another can rise more and more slowly. The first derivative tells us whether the graph rises or falls. The next question asks whether the first derivative itself is increasing or decreasing.
That is the second derivative.

introduction.p: The first derivative describes whether a function increases or decreases. The second derivative describes how its slope changes. An increasing slope gives concave-up behavior, and a decreasing slope gives concave-down behavior. For motion, this distinction separates positive velocity from positive acceleration.

exercise.title: Why can two increasing graphs still have different shapes?

statement.p: A car can move forward while speeding up, or move forward while slowing down. In both cases velocity is positive. In your own words, why does the first derivative miss this distinction, and what extra question does the second derivative ask?

hint.p: f' tells whether the graph is rising or falling. f'' tells whether those slopes themselves are increasing or decreasing.

subsection.title: Concave up and concave down
subsection.p: The word concavity describes the direction a graph bends.
If the slopes are increasing as we move left to right, the graph is concave up. It bends like a cup.
If the slopes are decreasing as we move left to right, the graph is concave down. It bends like a cap.

note.title: Concavity
note.p: Suppose f is differentiable on an interval I.
The function f is concave up on I if f' is increasing on I.
The function f is concave down on I if f' is decreasing on I.

subsection.p: This definition says that concavity is really a statement about how the tangent slopes change.
Because the second derivative is the derivative of f', the first derivative sign rule applied to f' gives the main test.

note.title: Second derivative sign rule
note.p: Suppose f'' exists on an interval I.
If
on I, then f is concave up on I.
If
on I, then f is concave down on I.

subsection.p: The reason is direct. If f''>0, then f' is increasing. If f''<0, then f' is decreasing.

figure.caption: Concave up means slopes increase. Concave down means slopes decrease.

description.p: Concave up means slopes increase. Concave down means slopes decrease.

exercise.title: Why is concavity a statement about changing slopes?

statement.p: Concave up means f' is increasing; concave down means f' is decreasing. In your own words, why is that not the same as f being positive, and why does the sign of f'' become a test for concavity?

hint.p: Apply the first derivative sign rule to f' itself. A cup-shaped graph is one whose tangent slopes are getting steeper as you move right.

subsection.title: Inflection points
subsection.p: A point where the concavity changes is called an inflection point.

note.title: Inflection point
note.p: A point (c,f(c)) on the graph of f is an inflection point if f is continuous at c and the concavity of f changes there.

statement.p: An inflection point is a point where concavity actually changes. In your own words, why might we look where f'' is zero or undefined, and why can f''(c)=0 fail to produce an inflection, as with x^4 at the origin?

statement.p: If f'(c)=0 and f''(c)>0, then c is a local minimum. In your own words, why does a positive second derivative at a critical number force the first derivative to change from negative to positive, and why does f''(c)=0 give no conclusion?

subsection.title: When the second derivative test is inconclusive
subsection.p: The last line of the test matters:
Three different things can happen.

paragraphs.title: A local minimum
paragraphs.p: The second derivative test gives no conclusion. But x^4\ge0 for all x, so f has a local minimum at 0.

paragraphs.title: A local maximum
paragraphs.p: Again the test gives no conclusion. But -x^4\le0 for all x, so g has a local maximum at 0.

paragraphs.title: No extremum
paragraphs.p: But x^3 is increasing through 0, so there is no local maximum or local minimum there.

p.me: f''(c)=0 \text{ does not mean the test says ``minimum.''}

paragraphs.p: It means the test is silent. We must return to the first derivative test, the shape of the graph, or another argument.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: The first derivative tells where the graph rises and falls. The second derivative tells where the graph bends upward and downward.
Together, they give a much richer picture:

But a graph can also have asymptotes, holes, intercepts, and end behavior. The next step is to put all the evidence together into a graph-sketching method that is guided by calculus rather than by guesswork.

introduction.p: A graph sketch combines the domain, intercepts, limits, derivative signs, extrema, and concavity. We will organize this information to draw a graph consistent with the function's formulas and limiting behavior.

exercise.title: Why do we need both f' and f'' to sketch a graph?

statement.p: The first derivative gives direction; the second gives bending. In your own words, why is a sign chart for f' not enough by itself, and what extra truth does a sign chart for f'' add to a sketch?

hint.p: Two graphs can both rise and still look different: one can bend like a cup, the other like a cap. Local extrema and inflection points come from different sign changes.

subsection.title: Asymptotes and end behavior
subsection.p: Polynomials do not have vertical asymptotes. Rational functions often do.
Derivative information describes shape where the function exists. Limits describe what happens near missing points and far away.

statement.p: Derivatives describe shape where the function exists. Vertical, horizontal, and slant asymptotes are statements about missing points and about far-away behavior. In your own words, why must a complete sketch ask what happens as x approaches a break and as x\to\pm\infty?

hint.p: A derivative cannot see a hole or an infinite jump that sits outside the domain. Those features are limits.

subsection.title: A complete curve-sketching workflow
subsection.p: A calculus sketch should gather evidence in an organized way.

The workflow is not a rigid machine. Sometimes symmetry saves work. Sometimes a limit matters more than a derivative. Sometimes a derivative is too complicated to factor nicely. But the questions are steady.

hint.p: The goal is not a perfect drawing. The goal is a picture that tells the truth about rising, falling, bending, and end behavior.

subsection.title: When technology helps and when it misleads
subsection.p: A graphing calculator or computer can help check a sketch, but it should not replace the analysis.
Technology draws what it samples. It can miss a hole, hide an asymptote, or make a bad viewing window look convincing.

paragraphs.title: A hidden hole
paragraphs.p: A graphing device may draw the line
without showing the missing point at
But the original function is not defined at x=1. The correct graph is a line with a hole.

p.me: \text{Algebra and domain information can reveal what a plotted graph hides.}

paragraphs.title: A misleading window
paragraphs.p: has vertical asymptotes at x=-1 and x=1. But if we only graph it on the window
we see only the middle branch. The graph may look like a small decreasing curve with a flat point at the origin. That window hides the asymptotes and the outer branches.
A graphing device answers the question we ask it. Calculus helps us ask better questions:
A good sketch uses both tools: computation for speed, and calculus for judgment.

exercise.title: Why can a graphing device hide a hole or an asymptote?

statement.p: Technology draws what it samples. In your own words, why might a calculator draw a line with no hole, or a window that conceals vertical asymptotes, and why does calculus help us ask better questions of the picture?

hint.p: Algebra and domain information can reveal what a plotted graph hides. A device answers the question we ask it, including a bad viewing window.

subsection.p: Graph sketching often leads back to limits. A vertical asymptote is a limit. A horizontal or slant asymptote is a limit. End behavior is a limit.

subsection.p: l’Hospital’s Rule gives a clean way to compare common growth rates.

paragraphs.p: Sometimes l’Hospital’s Rule gives no conclusion, even though the original limit exists.
But the quotient of derivatives is

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original quotient has that same limit. It does not say that the derivative quotient must have a limit whenever the original quotient does.

exercise.title: When can l’Hospital’s Rule not be used, or give no conclusion?

statement.p: Differentiating a quotient that is not indeterminate can produce the wrong limit. Even for an indeterminate quotient, the derivative ratio may fail to have a limit while the original quotient still does. In your own words, why is the rule a one-way implication, and what must we check before using it?

hint.p: Check the indeterminate form, differentiability, and the nonvanishing denominator derivative on the punctured interval. Under the theorem’s hypotheses, a limit of the derivative quotient gives a limit of the original quotient. The converse does not follow from the theorem.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: l’Hospital’s Rule turns some hard limits into derivative limits. It works because, near a point, differentiable functions are controlled by their local linear parts.

But every theorem in this chapter has boundaries. Fermat’s theorem needs an interior point and differentiability. The Mean Value Theorem needs continuity and differentiability. The second derivative test can be silent. l’Hospital’s Rule needs an indeterminate form and a derivative quotient that settles.
The next warning examples collect those boundaries, because knowing when a theorem cannot be used is part of knowing the theorem.

introduction.p: The conclusions of Rolle's Theorem, the Mean Value Theorem, derivative tests for extrema, and l'Hospital's Rule depend on their hypotheses. The examples below show failures caused by missing continuity, differentiability, endpoint conditions, or sign conditions.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

exercise.title: Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

hint.p: A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.

subsection.title: A theorem-use checklist
subsection.p: The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

cell.p: Is the extremum at an interior point? Is the function differentiable there?
Is the function continuous on [a,b]? Is it differentiable on (a,b)?
Does f' actually change sign around the critical number?
Is f'(c)=0? Is f''(c) positive or negative, not zero?
Is the quotient really 0/0 or \infty/\infty? Does the derivative quotient have a limit?

subsection.p: A theorem is not only a conclusion. It is a package:
If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

These warnings prepare the chapter review. We now gather the ideas into one working map: how to read shape from derivatives, how to prove global facts from the Mean Value Theorem, and how to tell when a tempting shortcut is legal.

introduction.p: These problems use derivatives to determine monotonicity, extrema, and concavity; sketch graphs; prove estimates with the Mean Value Theorem; and evaluate limits with l'Hospital's Rule when its hypotheses hold.

subsection.title: The chapter’s map
subsection.p: Here is the main dictionary.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.
But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.

p.me: \text{How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?}

subsection.p: The next chapter applies derivatives to related rates, optimization, and mathematical models.

introduction.p: Applications of derivatives begin by expressing the relevant quantities as functions. We will build models for related rates, optimization, measurement error, growth, and least-time paths. In each case, interpret the result using the model's domain, assumptions, and units.

When changing quantities satisfy an equation, differentiating that equation with respect to time relates their rates of change. For example, a balloon's radius, surface area, and volume change together. The chain rule allows one known rate to determine another.

exercise.title: Why does an equation relating quantities become an equation relating rates?

statement.p: If two quantities are linked by a formula that remains true as time passes, the chain rule turns that formula into a relation among derivatives. In your own words, why is that the idea of a related rates problem, and why must we remember that each quantity is secretly a function of time?

hint.p: An equation relating quantities implies an equation relating their rates. The bridge is the chain rule, not a new kind of derivative.

subsection.p: Related rates tell how quantities change together. The next problem is different. Instead of asking how fast something changes, we ask which choice is best.

exercise.title: Why is a rate not just a number?

statement.p: A related-rates answer carries units and a sign. In your own words, why do matching units catch many algebra mistakes, and why does a positive \frac{dy}{dt} for a ladder sliding down the wall mean the labels, not the calculus, have gone wrong?

hint.p: Before trusting an answer, ask whether the sign makes sense and whether the units make sense. A rate remembers direction as well as size.

introduction.p: An optimization problem asks for a maximum or minimum under given constraints. First choose variables, determine their allowed values, and express the quantity to be optimized as a function. Then use derivatives and endpoint checks to compare all relevant candidates.

exercise.title: Why does a constraint reduce an optimization problem to one variable?

statement.p: Many problems begin with two quantities linked by a restriction, such as a fixed amount of fencing. In your own words, why do we use that restriction to eliminate a variable, and what would go wrong if we differentiated an objective that still contained two independent inputs?

hint.p: The constraint is what makes the choices depend on one another. After substituting, the objective becomes an ordinary one-variable function.

subsection.p: Geometry problems are good training because the constraints are visible.

example.title: the shortest reflected path
example.p: A point A is located a units above a straight mirror, and a point B is located b units above the same mirror. Their horizontal separation is L. A light ray travels from A to the mirror and then to B. Where should it hit the mirror to make the total distance as small as possible?
Place the mirror on the x-axis. Let

Here a,b,L>0. The second derivative is D''(x)=a^2/(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}+b^2/((L-x)^2+b^2)^{3/2}>0, and the critical point lies in (0,L), so it is the unique absolute minimum. This condition is the familiar reflection rule: the incoming and outgoing angles are equal. The derivative has found the law of reflection from a shortest-path principle.

subsection.title: Endpoint checks and physical feasibility
subsection.p: Optimization problems are not finished when we find a critical number.
A critical number is a candidate. It may give a maximum, a minimum, neither, or it may not be physically allowed.
The correct conclusion depends on the domain.

note.title: Closed interval method for applications
note.p: If the objective function is continuous on a closed interval, then:

li.p: Find the critical numbers inside the interval.
Evaluate the objective function at those critical numbers.
Evaluate the objective function at the endpoints.
Compare the values.

subsection.p: In the open-box problem, the domain was
The endpoints gave

So x=2 gave the absolute maximum.

But endpoints do not always lose. If a problem asks for a minimum, an endpoint may win. If a domain is open, the best value may not be attained at all. If a critical point lies outside the physical domain, it is irrelevant.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: a critical point outside the domain
paragraphs.p: Suppose a company models profit from selling q units by
If the company can produce any number of units between 0 and 50, then q=20 is a real candidate. But if a contract requires
then q=20 is not physically allowed. On the interval [30,50],
So P is decreasing throughout the allowed interval. The maximum allowed profit occurs at the endpoint
The derivative found the best point for the wrong domain.

note.title: The domain is part of the problem
note.p: A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. The domain tells the formula which choices are allowed.

paragraphs.p: Related rates asked how fast quantities change together. Optimization asked which choice is best. Both depended on building a model and then reading a derivative.

But real measurements are rarely exact. A radius may be 3 cm only to the nearest millimeter. A length may have a small error. The next question is not the best exact choice, but how sensitive an answer is to small changes.

exercise.title: Why is the domain part of the problem, not an afterthought?

statement.p: A critical number may give a max, a min, neither, or a value that is not physically allowed. In your own words, why must we check endpoints and feasibility, and why can the derivative find the best point for the wrong domain?

hint.p: A formula alone does not know what choices are possible. Endpoints can win, and a critical point outside the allowed interval is irrelevant.

exercise.title: Why is relative error a different question from absolute error?

statement.p: Absolute error keeps the units of the quantity. Relative error compares the error to the size of the quantity itself. In your own words, why can a small absolute error still be a large relative error, or the reverse, and why do power laws make relative error especially readable?

hint.p: An error of one centimeter is huge for a bacterium and tiny for a planet. For y=cx^n, relative error in y is about |n| times relative error in x.

subsection.p: The derivative measures sensitivity.

subsection.title: Convergence when the starting point is good
subsection.p: Newton's method uses a local linear approximation. Its convergence depends on the root, the derivative, and the starting value.
The method works best when:

li.p: the starting guess is close to the root,
the function is smooth near the root,
the derivative at the root is not zero.

subsection.p: The third condition means the graph crosses the axis with a real slope, not with a flat touch.

note.title: Newton convergence principle
note.p: Suppose f has a zero r, so
If f has two continuous derivatives near r, and
then Newton’s method converges to r whenever the starting guess is close enough to r.

subsection.p: The phrase “close enough” is important. The theorem does not say every starting point works. It says that near a good root, Newton’s method behaves well.

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: Let x_n be close to the root r. We can obtain a quadratic error formula using Rolle’s Theorem twice, without assuming a later Taylor formula. Choose C so that F(t)=f(t)-f(x_n)-f'(x_n)(t-x_n)-C(t-x_n)^2 satisfies F(r)=0. We also have F(x_n)=F'(x_n)=0. Rolle’s Theorem first gives a zero of F' between x_n and r, and then a zero of F'' between that point and x_n. Thus C=f''(c_n)/2 for a point c_n between x_n and r. (If x_n=r, the root has already been found.) Therefore
for some point c_n between x_n and r.
Solve this for the Newton correction. Because
So the next error is roughly a constant times the square of the previous error:
This is why Newton’s method can suddenly become very accurate. If an error is about 10^{-3}, its square is 10^{-6}. If an error is about 10^{-6}, its square is 10^{-12}.

This behavior is called quadratic convergence. To make the convergence claim precise, continuity bounds |f''| above and |f'| away from zero in a small interval about r. Hence |x_{n+1}-r|\le C|x_n-r|^2 there for a fixed C. Choose the starting error small enough that C|x_0-r|\le1/2 and the starting point lies in that interval. Each next error is at most half the previous one, so all iterates remain in the interval and converge to r.

note.title: The reason Newton can be fast
note.p: Near a simple root, Newton’s method does not merely reduce the error. It roughly squares the error.

exercise.title: Why is Newton’s method a local method?

statement.p: The method is fast when the starting guess is close, the function is smooth, and f' is nonzero at the root. In your own words, why does close enough matter, and why does a flat touch at the root (a multiple root) slow or spoil the process?

hint.p: Near a simple root, under suitable smoothness conditions, Newton's error is approximately squared at each step. A multiple root requires a different convergence analysis.

subsection.title: Failure modes: cycles and bad tangents
subsection.p: Newton’s method depends on tangent lines. A bad tangent can send the method to the wrong place, make it cycle, or stop it entirely.
The hypotheses are not decoration.

paragraphs.title: Failure mode 1: a horizontal tangent
paragraphs.p: then the tangent line is horizontal. It does not cross the x-axis in the way the method needs.
The Newton formula cannot even produce x_1. The function has roots, but this starting point gives a horizontal tangent.

paragraphs.title: Failure mode 2: a cycle
paragraphs.p: But the function does have a real root. Since
the Intermediate Value Theorem tells us that there is a root between -2 and -1.
Newton’s method failed because the tangent lines from 0 and 1 point back to each other.

figure.caption: For f(x)=x^3-2x+2, Newton’s method starting at 0 cycles between 0 and 1.

description.p: For f(x)=x^3-2x+2, Newton’s method starting at 0 cycles between 0 and 1.

paragraphs.title: Failure mode 3: a multiple root
paragraphs.p: then Newton’s method may still converge, but often more slowly.
This moves halfway toward 1 each time. It converges, but the error is cut in half rather than squared. The fast convergence is lost.

exercise.title: Why can a bad tangent send Newton’s method astray?

statement.p: A horizontal tangent makes the iteration undefined. A cycle can bounce between two wrong points. In your own words, why are these failures not contradictions of the method, and what do they show about depending on tangent lines?

hint.p: The hypotheses are not decoration. A tangent can fail to cross the axis, or it can point somewhere the original curve never intended.

subsection.title: How to use Newton’s method safely
subsection.p: Newton’s method is most reliable when it is used with a picture or with a bracket.
A practical workflow is:

li.p: Graph f, or use signs to locate an interval where a root should lie.
Choose a starting point near the root.
Compute x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
Stop only when both x_n has stabilized and f(x_n) is small.
If the method behaves strangely, try a different starting point or use bisection.

subsection.p: The bisection method is slower, but if f is continuous and changes sign on an interval, bisection is dependable. Newton’s method is faster when it behaves well.

note.title: Newton’s method in one sentence
note.p: Replace the curve by its tangent line, solve the linear problem, and repeat.

subsection.p: Linear approximation has now done two jobs. It estimated how errors move through a formula, and it solved equations by tangent-line correction.

The next models take one more step. Sometimes the rule we know is not a formula for y, but a formula for y'. Growth, decay, cooling, and population change are often written first as laws about derivatives.

exercise.title: Why should we demand both a stable iterate and a small function value?

statement.p: A practical workflow graphs the function, starts near a root, and stops only when x_n has settled and f(x_n) is small. In your own words, why is one of those checks not enough, and why is bisection a slower but more dependable backup?

hint.p: Iterates can wander or cycle while still looking busy. A sign-changing continuous function on an interval is what makes bisection trustworthy.

introduction.p: The exponential model P\prime=rP, with r>0, allows a positive population to grow without bound. To model limited resources, the logistic equation reduces the per-capita growth rate as the population approaches a carrying capacity.
