subsection.p: The logistic equation appears whenever two ideas are both reasonable:
and
For populations, the current amount is the population P, and the limiting factor is the carrying capacity K.
For a rumor, the current amount may be the number of people who have heard it. The limiting factor is the number of people who have not yet heard it.

The rumor spreads slowly at first because few people know it. It then spreads quickly when many people know it and many people remain to hear it. Finally it slows again because most people have already heard it.
This slow--fast--slow shape is the signature of a logistic curve.

subsection.title: What logistic models assume
subsection.p: The logistic model is more realistic than pure exponential growth, but it is still a model.
It assumes:
Those assumptions may be useful, but they are not automatic.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: early data can be misleading
paragraphs.p: So early logistic growth and exponential growth can look almost the same.
That means early data may reveal r, but it may not reveal K. To estimate the carrying capacity, we need data from the stage where growth begins to slow.

note.title: Check the model’s assumptions
note.p: Exponential growth assumes a constant relative growth rate.
Logistic growth assumes a fixed carrying capacity and a relative growth rate r(1-P/K), approximately r when P\ll K.
Check whether these assumptions describe the situation before using the model to predict its behavior.

paragraphs.p: This chapter used derivatives to answer practical questions: rates related to rates, best choices, local approximations, root finding, and models whose laws are written as differential equations.

But we have postponed the other half of calculus. If a derivative tells how fast something changes, how do we recover the total change? If velocity is known at every instant, how do we rebuild distance?
That question leads back to the first chapter, where area under a velocity graph was waiting for us. The next chapter begins the integral.

exercise.title: Why can early data hide the carrying capacity?

statement.p: When P\ll K, the logistic model closely approximates exponential growth. Explain why early data may estimate r while providing little information about K.

hint.p: To estimate the ceiling, we need data from the stage where growth begins to slow. Before that, the slowing factor is nearly invisible.

introduction.p: Some optimization problems choose a path rather than a dimension or price. Reflection and refraction can be derived by minimizing travel time within a specified family of paths. We will write the travel time as a function of the crossing or reflection point and use its derivative to find the minimizing path.

subsection.title: The seed of the calculus of variations
subsection.p: In reflection and refraction, the unknown was one number:

p.me: x=\text{the point where the ray hits a line}.

subsection.p: A more general problem varies an entire path.

Imagine a landscape where the speed depends on position. Perhaps the ground is easy to cross in one region and slow in another. A traveler wants to move from A to B in the least time. Which path should the traveler choose?
A straight line may not be best. A path that detours through faster ground might take less time.
If we approximate a path by many small straight pieces, then the travel time is approximately
where
is the length of the ith small piece, and v_i is the speed along that piece.
A path is no longer described by one variable. It is described by many choices:
or, in the limit, by a whole function.
The quantity being minimized is not an ordinary function of one number. It is a rule that takes a path as input and returns a number as output:
Such a rule is called a functional.
Using the integral notation that will be developed in the next chapters, the travel time along a path is written symbolically as
This formula says:

p.me: \text{add up } \frac{\text{small distance}}{\text{speed}} \text{ along the whole path}.

subsection.p: The notation is only a preview for now. The idea is already visible from the finite sum.

note.title: Extremal principle
note.p: A physical path is often characterized by making some quantity stationary:

p.me: \text{small changes in the path produce no first-order change in the quantity.}

note.p: For light in simple settings, the quantity is travel time.

subsection.p: A stationary path has zero first-order change in travel time under the allowed small path variations. This condition does not by itself establish an absolute minimum.
That is the same idea we used for ordinary critical points. There, a number x was chosen so that
Here, a path is chosen so that the first-order change of a whole accumulated quantity is zero.

This is the beginning of the calculus of variations. We will not develop that subject here. But it points to the next major need. To measure time, work, area, mass, and probability, we need a way to add infinitely many small contributions.
That is the integral.

exercise.title: Why is a path a different kind of unknown from a number?

statement.p: The reflection and refraction examples vary one crossing point. A functional instead takes an entire path as input and returns a number such as time or length. Explain how this changes the optimization problem.

hint.p: A path is described by many small choices, or in the limit by a whole function. The usual derivative with respect to one number is no longer enough.

introduction.p: Derivative calculations must respect the model's domain and constraints. A critical point may be infeasible or only a local optimum, and Newton's method may fail to converge. These examples show how to check those possibilities.

hint.p: Check endpoints, check the physical domain, and ask whether the result is local or absolute. A first-derivative test is a neighborhood test.

subsection.title: Formulas to remember
subsection.p: The formulas below are not separate tricks. Each is a compact version of an idea from the chapter.

p.me: \begin{array}{c|c} \textbf{idea} \amp \textbf{formula}\\ \hline \text{linear approximation} \amp f(a+\Delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\Delta x\\ \text{differential estimate} \amp dy=f'(x)\,dx\\ \text{Newton's method} \amp x_{n+1}=x_n-\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\\ \text{exponential growth or decay} \amp y'=ky,\qquad y(t)=y_0e^{kt}\\ \text{doubling time} \amp D=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k>0)\\ \text{half-life} \amp H=-\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\quad(k<0)\\ \text{Newton's law of cooling} \amp T(t)=T_s+\bigl(T(0)-T_s\bigr)e^{-kt}\\ \text{logistic growth} \amp P'=rP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{K}\right)\\ \text{logistic solution} \amp P(t)=\dfrac{K}{1+\left(\dfrac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}} \end{array}

subsection.title: Skills: related rates and optimization
subsection.p: Related rates and optimization are the two main problem-solving skills of this chapter. They look similar because both begin with translation, but they ask different questions.

paragraphs.title: Related rates checklist

li.p: Draw a picture, if geometry is involved.
Name the changing quantities as functions of time.
Write an equation relating the quantities.
Differentiate with respect to time.
Substitute values for the instant in question.
Solve for the desired rate.
Check sign and units.

paragraphs.p: The most common mistake is substituting the instant-specific numbers too early. The variables must remain variables until after the relation has been differentiated.

paragraphs.title: Optimization checklist

li.p: Name the quantity to optimize.
Name the variables.
Write the objective function.
Write the constraint.
Use the constraint to get one variable.
Find the physical domain.
Find critical numbers and check endpoints.
Translate the result back into the situation.

paragraphs.p: The most common mistake is finding a critical point and stopping. A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion.

exercise.title: Why do related rates, optimization, and models use the same derivative differently?

hint.p: Ask whether the problem wants a rate, a best choice, a small-error estimate, a root, or a function obeying a rate law.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter showed how much can be done with a derivative.
A derivative can relate changing quantities. It can find a best choice. It can estimate error. It can turn a tangent line into a root-finding method. It can express a physical law such as
or
But a derivative is still local. It tells how fast something is changing at an instant.
Many questions ask for the accumulated result of those changes.
If velocity is known at every instant, how far did the object travel?
If a force changes with position, how much work was done?
If density varies along a rod, what is the rod’s total mass?
If a rate law tells how a quantity changes, how much total change has occurred over an interval?
Those questions return us to the dashboard from the beginning of the book. The speedometer gives rate. The odometer gives accumulation.
The next chapter builds the second great operation of calculus: adding up infinitely many small changes.

introduction.p: An integral measures an accumulated quantity. Velocity determines displacement, power determines energy use, and density determines mass. We will approximate each total by dividing an interval into small pieces and adding their contributions, then define the definite integral as a limit of these sums.
A derivative tells how fast a quantity is changing. To recover the quantity itself, we must add up many small changes.
If s(t) is position and v(t)=s'(t) is velocity, then for a short time interval of length \Delta t,
This is the local linear idea in reverse. The derivative says
So the small position change is approximately
The integral begins by adding many expressions of this kind.

exercise.title: Why do we pretend velocity is constant on short intervals?

subsection.title: Signed displacement versus total distance
subsection.p: Velocity has a sign. Positive velocity means motion in the positive direction. Negative velocity means motion in the negative direction.

subsection.title: Upper and lower sums
subsection.p: Left and right rectangles are easy to compute, but they are not always upper or lower estimates. If a function decreases, the left rectangles lie above the curve and the right rectangles lie below it. If a function rises and falls, both can be mixed.

For a continuous function, a more reliable idea is to use the largest and smallest function values on each small interval. We assume continuity in this construction; later we will use least upper bounds and greatest lower bounds for general bounded functions.

For now, the main point is this:

p.me: \text{Area under a graph is an accumulation of thin rectangular pieces.}

subsection.p: There is one caution. Not every wild function behaves well enough for this process. If a function jumps too violently at every scale, upper and lower sums may refuse to come together. Continuous functions do behave well, and we will return to that fact later.
The next obstacle is notation. Rectangular sums quickly become long:
To define the integral cleanly, we need a compact language for finite sums. That is where sigma notation enters.

paragraphs.p: This telescoping technique generalizes to any integer power p \ge 1. To find a closed-form formula for \sum_{i=1}^{n} i^p, we start with the binomial expansion of the difference of (p+1)-th powers. Here \binom{N}{k}=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1)/(1\cdot2\cdots k) for 1\le k\le N, and \binom{N}{0}=1; these are the coefficients obtained by expanding (k+1)^{p+1} by multiplication:
Summing both sides from k=1 to n telescopes the left side entirely:

p.me: \text{The definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums.}

introduction.p: A Riemann sum approximates accumulation by adding function values multiplied by subinterval widths. The definite integral is their common limit, when it exists, as the largest subinterval width tends to zero. The limit must be independent of the partitions and sample points.

subsection.title: Why the sample point should not matter
subsection.p: The definition of the integral asks for more than the convergence of one special sum. It asks that all sufficiently fine Riemann sums approach the same number.
Why such a strong requirement?
Because the integral should belong to the function and the interval, not to our particular choice of sample points.

For a smooth graph, this is natural. If a subinterval is very narrow, the values of f inside it are close to one another. A left endpoint, a right endpoint, and a midpoint give nearly the same height. The rectangle heights may differ a little, but the differences become negligible as the widths shrink.

p.em: When all fine rectangular sums are forced toward one number, that number is the integral.

exercise.title: Why should the sample point not matter for a well-behaved function?

statement.p: On a very narrow subinterval, the values of a continuous function stay close together. In your own words, why do left, right, and midpoint heights then become interchangeable, and why does that force all fine rectangular sums toward one number?

hint.p: When all fine rectangular sums are forced toward one number, that number is the integral. The sample choice is a finite-sum detail that the limit is trying to erase.

subsection.title: Integrability, informally first
subsection.p: The definition says:

p.me: \text{all fine Riemann sums must approach one common value.}

subsection.p: This is a strong condition, but most functions we meet in first-year calculus satisfy it.

statement.p: If f is continuous on [a,b], then f is integrable on [a,b].

subsection.p: We will discuss this more carefully later. The intuition is that a continuous function cannot jump wildly inside tiny intervals. When the subintervals are small, the function values inside each subinterval are forced to stay close together.
Continuity is not required, though. A function with a finite number of jump discontinuities can still be integrable.
For example, the step function
is integrable on [0,2]. The jump at x=1 affects only one point. Riemann sums still settle down to the total area:
But not every bounded function is integrable.

paragraphs.title: Warning example: too much oscillation
paragraphs.p: Define a function D on [0,1] by

Every interval, no matter how small, contains rational numbers and irrational numbers. So on every subinterval, we can choose a rational sample point and get height 1, or choose an irrational sample point and get height 0.
If every sample point is rational, the Riemann sum is
If every sample point is irrational, the Riemann sum is
These two outcomes do not approach one common number. They remain separated by 1, no matter how fine the partition is.
Therefore D is not Riemann integrable on [0,1].

note.title: Moral
note.p: The definite integral is not just any limit of convenient sums. It exists only when fine Riemann sums are forced toward the same value, regardless of the sample points.

paragraphs.p: Boundedness alone does not imply Riemann integrability. Continuous functions and bounded piecewise-continuous functions on a closed finite interval are integrable, but a bounded function can fail to have convergent Riemann sums.
We now have the central object of integral calculus:

When f\ge0, it is area under the graph. But the original motivation came from velocity, and velocity can be negative. The next step is to understand the integral as signed accumulation: area above the axis counts positively, area below the axis counts negatively.

exercise.title: Why can a bounded function fail to be integrable?

statement.p: Continuity on a closed interval is enough for integrability, and a finite number of jumps can still be all right. In your own words, why is boundedness not enough by itself, and what goes wrong if a function oscillates too violently at every scale?

hint.p: Integrability requires all sufficiently fine Riemann sums to approach one value. For the function that is one on rationals and zero on irrationals, every subinterval allows either sample height, so the sums can stay a full interval length apart.

introduction.p: The definite integral was built from Riemann sums:
Each term has two parts. The width \Delta x_j is positive when we move from left to right. The height f(x_j^*) can be positive, zero, or negative.
That one fact changes the meaning of area.

If the graph lies above the x-axis, the rectangles contribute positively. If the graph lies below the x-axis, the rectangles contribute negatively. So the definite integral is not ordinary area first. It is signed accumulation.

p.me: \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \text{area above the axis} - \text{area below the axis}.

introduction.p: Ordinary area is never negative. A definite integral can be negative, because it is designed to remember direction.

For example, suppose f(x)=2 on [0,5]. Then the graph is a horizontal line, and the area is a rectangle:
The integral is positive because the graph is above the axis.

More generally, if f(x)\ge0, then the integral accumulates positive amount. In a motion problem, this might mean forward displacement. In a density problem, it might mean mass. In a power problem, it might mean energy used.
The same rectangle picture from the beginning of the book is still present:
The integral adds infinitely many such pieces.

exercise.title: Why is a definite integral signed accumulation rather than ordinary area?

statement.p: In a Riemann sum the widths are positive when we move left to right, but the heights can be negative. In your own words, why does that make the integral equal to area above the axis minus area below, and why can an integral be negative when ordinary area cannot?

hint.p: Ordinary area is never negative. A definite integral is designed to remember direction, just as velocity remembers forward and backward motion.

subsection.title: Cancellation and meaning
subsection.p: Signed area can cancel.
For example, consider
on [-1,1]. The graph lies below the axis on [-1,0] and above the axis on [0,1]. The two triangles have the same ordinary area:
The signed integral is
But the graph is not zero. The function does not vanish. The integral is zero because the negative and positive contributions balance exactly.

note.title: An integral can be zero for two different reasons
note.p: It may be zero because there is no accumulation.
It may also be zero because positive and negative accumulation cancel.

subsection.p: This distinction is crucial in motion.
If a car travels 40 miles east and then 40 miles west, its displacement is 0. But it did not stay still. It traveled 80 miles.
The signed integral measures net change. It does not measure total activity.

exercise.title: Why can an integral be zero for two different reasons?

statement.p: The integral of x from -1 to 1 is zero, even though the graph is not the zero function. In your own words, why might an integral vanish because nothing accumulated, and why might it vanish because positive and negative accumulation cancelled?

hint.p: A car that travels forty miles east and forty miles west has displacement zero, but it did not stay still. The signed integral measures net change, not total activity.

exercise.title: Why does integrating velocity give displacement, while integrating speed gives distance?

statement.p: \int_a^b v(t)\,dt is net change in position. \int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt is total distance traveled. In your own words, why does the absolute value remove cancellation, and why must we always ask what the sign of the integrand means?

hint.p: Net signed accumulation is positive contributions minus negative ones. Total accumulation is the same two contributions added.

subsection.p: The same distinction appears outside motion.
Suppose f(x) represents a signed rate of change. Positive values increase a quantity. Negative values decrease it.

But

The definite integral is therefore more flexible than ordinary area. It can measure area, displacement, accumulated signed change, or cancellation. To use it well, we must always ask what the sign means.
The next section collects the algebraic rules that make integrals useful. These rules will look familiar because they come from the same place as the integral itself: finite sums.

exercise.title: Why is net change no substitute for total change?

statement.p: The two formulas \int_a^b f and \int_a^b |f| answer different questions. In your own words, why can the total be strictly larger than the absolute value of the net, and what does that difference tell you about cancellation along the way?

hint.p: Cancellation is removed when we integrate the absolute value. Write the positive and negative accumulated amounts as P and N. Then the total is P+N and the absolute net is |P-N|; the inequality is strict precisely when both amounts are positive.

introduction.p: The basic integral properties follow from Riemann sums and their limits. Integrals are linear, can be split at an intermediate endpoint, and preserve inequalities. Symmetry can also simplify calculations when the interval and integrand satisfy the required conditions.

statement.p: Accumulation from a to b is accumulation from a to c plus accumulation from c to b. Reversing the limits multiplies by -1. In your own words, why do these rules treat the interval as oriented, and why is there no accumulation from a point to itself?

Continuous functions do. So do many functions with jumps. But not every bounded function is integrable. The next section explains where the line is.

introduction.p: A bounded function has a Riemann integral when its upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close. This section uses that criterion to establish integrability for continuous functions, monotone functions, and bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities. Boundedness alone is insufficient.

subsection.title: Continuous functions are integrable
subsection.p: A continuous graph on a closed interval cannot jump. If we look at a short enough piece of the graph, the output values stay close together.
That is exactly what the upper-lower test needs.

statement.p: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: A continuous function on a closed interval has a special kind of steadiness:

p.me: \text{if }x\text{ and }y\text{ are close enough, then }f(x)\text{ and }f(y)\text{ are close,}

paragraphs.p: and the same meaning of “close enough” works everywhere on the interval. This property is called uniform continuity. To see why it follows here, suppose it failed for some fixed output gap \eta>0. Bisect the closed interval repeatedly, each time retaining a half that still contains pairs of arbitrarily close inputs with output gap at least \eta. Such a half must exist: otherwise the two halves have distance thresholds, and continuity at their common endpoint also controls pairs straddling it. The retained intervals are nested and their lengths tend to zero, so completeness gives a common point c. Eventually a retained interval lies wholly in a neighborhood of c where continuity makes every value differ from f(c) by less than \eta/2. No two values there can have gap at least \eta, a contradiction.
More precisely, for every \eta>0, there is a \delta>0 such that
Now choose a partition whose subinterval widths are all less than \delta. Then on each subinterval,
By the upper-lower test, f is integrable.

subsection.p: Continuity is enough for integrability, but it is not necessary.

A function may jump and still be integrable. The simplest reason is monotonicity: a monotone function can move only one way. It may jump, but it cannot oscillate up and down forever inside every small interval.

subsection.title: Functions with finitely many jump discontinuities
subsection.p: A function may have several jumps and still be integrable. The reason is the same: finitely many points can be covered by intervals whose total width is as small as we wish.

statement.p: If f is bounded on [a,b] and is continuous except at finitely many points, then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: Suppose the discontinuities occur at finitely many points. Put tiny intervals around those points. Since there are only finitely many of them, we can make the total width of all the tiny intervals very small.
On those tiny intervals, the function may behave badly, but it is bounded. So the upper-lower contribution is at worst
On the rest of the interval, the function is continuous on closed pieces. So the upper-lower contribution there can also be made small.
Putting the two parts together, the total upper-lower gap can be made smaller than any chosen \varepsilon. Hence the function is integrable.

note.title: Safe classes of integrable functions
note.p: The following functions are Riemann integrable on closed intervals:

The general rule. The ultimate test for Riemann integrability was proven by Henri Lebesgue. A bounded function is integrable if and only if its set of discontinuity points has measure zero---meaning that, for every \varepsilon>0, those points can be covered by a finite or countable collection of open intervals whose lengths sum to less than \varepsilon. This criterion is stated here for perspective; its proof requires a later course in analysis.

subsection.p: The integral is now on solid ground. We know what it means, how to estimate it, what signs do, what algebraic rules it obeys, and which common functions actually have one.
The next chapter studies accumulation functions with a moving endpoint. For a continuous integrand, differentiating the accumulation recovers the integrand.

exercise.title: Why do the algebraic properties of the integral come from finite sums?

introduction.p: For a continuous function f, the accumulation function A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt has derivative A\prime(x)=f(x). Conversely, an antiderivative F evaluates a definite integral by \int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a). This chapter proves these two parts of the Fundamental Theorem and develops antiderivatives and substitution.
A definite integral with fixed endpoints gives one accumulated amount. But if the upper endpoint moves, the accumulated amount changes. That changing amount is a function.

This is the same idea as recovering position from velocity. At each time, the position change is the accumulated signed velocity up to that time. If we know the velocity graph, that change is an area-with-sign whose right endpoint moves. An odometer instead accumulates speed, so its reading never decreases.

subsection.p: The problem is exactly what the theorem avoids. Near 0, the function f has no single nearby height. From the left it is 0. From the right it is 1. The average height over a shrinking interval depends on the side from which we approach.
Continuity gives one nearby height. That is why it appears in the theorem.

subsection.p: Continuity is a safe hypothesis, not the weakest possible one. But it is the right hypothesis for a first version of the theorem because it matches the geometry exactly: short intervals around x have heights close to f(x).

exercise.title: Why does Part I need continuity?

statement.p: For the step function that jumps from 0 to 1 at t=0, the accumulation function has a corner, so A'(0) does not exist. In your own words, why does a jump in f prevent the average height of a shrinking strip from settling on a single nearby height?

hint.p: Continuity gives one nearby height. From the left of a jump the nearby height is one number; from the right it is another.

subsection.title: What Part I gives us
subsection.p: Part I says that every continuous function f is the derivative of some function, namely
That is a remarkable statement.

A function F with F'=f is called an antiderivative of f. Before this theorem, such a function was something we might hope to find by guessing. Now we know an antiderivative exists for every continuous function, even if no elementary formula can describe it.
For example,

note.title: A new kind of function
note.p: An integral with a moving endpoint is not merely a way to compute area. It is a way to create functions whose derivatives are known.

hint.p: An antiderivative is a function whose derivative is f. Existence is a different question from writing a familiar closed-form expression.

introduction.p: The first part of the Fundamental Theorem produces an antiderivative by integration. The second part evaluates an integral using any antiderivative: if F\prime=f on the interval and f is continuous, then \int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a). This avoids calculating a limit of Riemann sums separately for every integral.

subsection.p: The word net matters. Positive and negative changes can cancel.

exercise.title: Why is the integral of a rate a net change?

statement.p: The net change theorem says \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a). In your own words, why does that recover final amount minus initial amount, and why does the word net matter when the rate changes sign?

hint.p: Positive and negative rates cancel in the integral. The result is the leftover change, not the total of all upward and downward motion counted as positive.

example.p: Suppose the temperature of a metal plate changes at the rate
Find the net temperature change from t=0 to t=5.
The rate T'(t) becomes negative after t=3. So the temperature first rises, then falls. The integral counts both effects with signs.

subsection.p: The theorem applies the rate-accumulation relation to motion.
If s(t) is position and v(t)=s'(t) is velocity, then
The integral of velocity is displacement.

statement.p: If v(t) is velocity, then \int_a^b v(t)\,dt is displacement, while \int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt is total distance. In your own words, why does the first integral allow cancellation, and why must the second refuse it?

hint.p: Displacement is net change of position. Distance counts every piece of motion as positive, so backward motion cannot cancel forward motion.

exercise.title: Why is having an antiderivative different from finding a formula?

hint.p: Existence means some function has the desired slope. A usable elementary formula is an extra gift that the basic library does not always provide.

introduction.p: Substitution follows from the chain rule. When x=g(u), the expression dx=g\prime(u)\,du records the factor that converts the integrand to the new variable:

note.title: Substitution rule, read geometrically
note.p: Let f be continuous on an interval J, and let g have a continuous derivative on the interval between \alpha and \beta, with all its values in J. When x=g(u),
where

To prove the rule, choose an antiderivative F of f, which exists by Part I. The chain rule gives (F\circ g)'(u)=f(g(u))g'(u). Part II makes the right-hand integral F(g(\beta))-F(g(\alpha))=F(b)-F(a), exactly the left-hand integral. No monotonicity of g is needed: oriented contributions cancel if it doubles back. The derivative g'(u) converts du-steps into oriented dx-steps.

subsection.p: The limits are part of the substitution. They are not decoration.

The next section collects places where these ideas are easy to misuse. The warnings do not weaken the formulas. They make the formulas safer.

introduction.p: These examples examine four common errors: applying the Fundamental Theorem across a discontinuity, retaining old endpoints after substitution, treating an integral as a product, and confusing a signed integral with ordinary area.

subsection.p: Part I of the Fundamental Theorem said:

Continuity matters.

Changing a function at a single point does not affect its integral. Therefore

note.title: Moral
note.p: The formula

exercise.title: Why can a jump in f create a corner in A?

statement.p: Part I is often written as if differentiating an accumulation always returns the integrand. In your own words, why does a discontinuity in f threaten that conclusion, and what should you check before claiming A'(x)=f(x)?

hint.p: The thin-strip argument needs one nearby height. A jump leaves two nearby heights, so the accumulation function may fail to be differentiable there.

subsection.title: Forgetting the new limits in substitution
subsection.p: A definite integral has endpoints. When we change variables, the endpoints must change too.

hint.p: The definite integral accumulates from a starting value of the current variable to an ending value of that same variable. After x=g(u), those values are u-values.

subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem has connected derivatives and integrals. Substitution has given us the first serious method for computing integrals. Differential notation has shown why orientation and change of variables belong inside the symbols.

Now integrals are ready to measure more than area under one graph. They can measure area between curves, volume, mass, work, pressure, and average value. The same accumulation idea will keep reappearing, but the small pieces will change shape.

introduction.p: The Fundamental Theorem relates differentiation to integration. For continuous f, differentiating \int_a^x f(t)\,dt gives f(x); integrating a continuous derivative gives F(b)-F(a). The review problems apply these results to accumulation functions, antiderivatives, and substitutions, with attention to domains and hypotheses.

subsection.p: The most common mistakes come from forgetting one of these meanings. A definite integral is signed accumulation. An indefinite integral is a family of functions. A substitution changes both the integrand and the limits. A formula for an antiderivative must be valid on the interval where it is used.

hint.p: One direction starts with a rate and builds a running total. The other starts with a running total and reads its rate. Each undoes the other.

exercise.title: What must you carry along when you change variables or reverse direction?

statement.p: A substitution changes the integrand, and reversing an interval changes the sign. In your own words, why are orientation and the new limits part of the meaning of the integral rather than extra bookkeeping?

hint.p: The small piece being added is height times oriented step. Changing the coordinate or the direction changes that step, so the description of the accumulation must change with it.

introduction.p: To set up an integral for a total quantity, identify the contribution of a small piece and add those contributions over the relevant interval. For volume, the contribution is cross-sectional area times thickness. For mass, it is density times length or area. This chapter develops that approach for geometric quantities, work, fluid force, averages, and probability, with units used to check each formula.

The area between two curves can be computed by adding thin strips. For vertical strips, the height is the upper function minus the lower function; for horizontal strips, the width is the right boundary minus the left boundary. Split the region where the order of the boundaries changes.

subsection.title: When shells beat washers
subsection.p: The washer method uses slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. The shell method uses slices parallel to the axis of rotation.
That one choice can turn a difficult setup into a simple one.
A quick way to remember it is:

p.me: \text{slices perpendicular to the axis make disks or washers;}
\text{slices parallel to the axis make shells.}

exercise.title: Why do slices parallel to the axis make shells instead of washers?

statement.p: Disks and washers come from slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. In your own words, why does a strip parallel to that axis sweep out a thin cylindrical wall, and how does that one choice of direction change the small piece?

hint.p: A strip perpendicular to the axis rotates in place and traces a disk or washer. A strip parallel to the axis is carried around the axis and traces a cylinder.

hint.p: One adds thin cylindrical walls. The other adds thin cross-sectional washers. Both are ways of assembling the same three-dimensional object.

section.title: Mass, density, and center of mass

introduction.p: Area and volume describe geometry without telling us how mass is distributed. Real objects are often heavier in one place than another.
A metal rod may be denser near one end. A wire may be made from two different materials. A thin plate may have paint or coating that varies from point to point.
Then length alone does not determine mass. We need density.

The small piece is force times displacement. The integral will measure energy transferred through motion.

exercise.title: Why does M_y give \bar x?

statement.p: For a lamina, \bar x=M_y/m and \bar y=M_x/m. In your own words, why do the subscripts look backwards at first, and why is a moment about the y-axis the one that uses horizontal distance?

hint.p: The signed coordinate measured from the y-axis is x, while the signed coordinate measured from the x-axis is y. Ordinary distance would use absolute values, but moments retain the side of the axis.

introduction.p: Work measures energy transferred by a force through displacement. For a force along a line, a small displacement contributes approximately F(x)\,\Delta x. Integrating the signed force over the displacement gives the total work.

But forces are often not constant. A spring pulls harder the more it is stretched. A rope or chain may require more work to lift one part than another. Water in a tank must be lifted different distances depending on where the water is.
So we return to the same idea:

paragraphs.title: Signed work
paragraphs.p: Work can be negative. For motion in the increasing x-direction, a force pointing opposite the motion has F(x)<0, and
is negative. Negative work means the force removes energy from the moving object rather than adding energy to it.
For now, most examples use positive forces in the direction of motion. The sign is still part of the formula.

exercise.title: Why does a variable force require an integral?

statement.p: For constant force along the motion, work equals force times displacement. Explain why using only the final force is invalid for a varying force and how \int F(x)\,dx accounts for the variation.

hint.p: On a short piece of the path the force is almost constant, so the old product is a good local estimate. The integral adds those local products.

subsection.title: Springs and Hooke’s law
subsection.p: A spring gives the first natural example of a variable force.

When a spring is at its natural length, it does not need any force to hold it there. When it is stretched, it pulls back. For many springs, at ordinary stretches, the force needed to hold the spring stretched x units is proportional to x:
The constant k is called the spring constant. This relation is called Hooke’s law.
A stiffer spring has a larger k. It takes more force to stretch it the same distance.

example.p: The same spring is already stretched 0.20 meters. How much additional work is required to stretch it to 0.50 meters beyond its natural length?
Stretching from 0.20 to 0.50 meters takes more work than stretching from 0 to 0.20, because the spring is already pulling harder.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: In Hooke’s law, x is the extension from the natural length, not necessarily the total length of the spring.
If a spring has natural length 10 cm and is stretched to length 18 cm, then the extension is 8 cm, not 18 cm.

hint.p: The top pieces travel less than the bottom pieces. Treating every gram as if it were lifted the full length pretends the chain is a single point.

subsection.title: Energy stored by work
subsection.p: Work transfers energy.

When we stretch a spring, the work we do is stored as elastic potential energy. When we lift a chain, the work becomes gravitational potential energy. When we pump water up and out of a tank, the work raises the water.
This is why work appears so often in physics and engineering. A force acting through a distance can change the energy of a system.
For this chapter, the calculus point is the same as before:
The next problem still involves water, but the water does not move. It simply pushes. The force from still water is not the same at every depth. Deeper water pushes harder.
That gives a new small piece:

exercise.title: What energy is work transferring?

statement.p: Stretching a spring, lifting a chain, and pumping water all store or raise energy. In your own words, why is work accumulated force over distance, and why can the same integral be negative if the force opposes the motion?

hint.p: Positive work adds energy to the system. Negative work means the force is removing energy rather than supplying it.

introduction.p: Fluid pressure increases with depth. To compute the force on a submerged surface, divide it into strips narrow enough that the pressure is nearly constant on each strip. Multiply the pressure by the strip area and integrate.

subsection.title: Choosing strips
subsection.p: Hydrostatic pressure depends on depth. So horizontal strips are natural.
A vertical strip would contain many depths at once, and the pressure would vary along the strip. A horizontal strip stays at one depth, up to a tiny error that disappears in the limit.

p.me: \text{For hydrostatic force on a vertical plate, use horizontal strips.}

paragraphs.title: Same area, different force
paragraphs.p: Now turn the same triangular plate upside down: vertex at the surface, base 4 feet long at depth 6 feet.
The area of the triangle is the same. But more area is now deeper, where pressure is larger.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: Hydrostatic force is not determined by area alone. Depth matters.
Two plates with the same area can feel different total forces if one has more of its area deeper in the water.

exercise.title: Why can two plates with the same area feel different forces?

statement.p: Turning a triangular plate upside down keeps the area the same but can double the force. In your own words, why is hydrostatic force not determined by area alone, and what does it mean to put more area deeper?

hint.p: Deeper water pushes harder. A plate with more of its area at large depth accumulates more force, even if the total area has not changed.

subsection.title: Dams and windows
subsection.p: Dams and underwater windows are the most common places where hydrostatic force matters.
A dam is wide, and the water depth changes from top to bottom. A window may be small, but the pressure can still be large if it is deep.

exercise.title: Why is pressure not the same as total force?

statement.p: Pressure is force per unit area. In your own words, why may you multiply pressure by area only when the pressure is constant over that area, and why does a vertical wall force you to integrate?

hint.p: On a vertical plate, deeper strips feel more pressure than shallow ones. One pressure times the whole area would pretend the depth never changes.

subsection.p: We have now used integrals to measure area, volume, mass, center of mass, work, and force. One more common question remains:

p.me: \text{What single number represents a varying quantity over an interval?}

subsection.p: That question leads to average value. From there, the same integral language will begin to measure probability.

introduction.p: The average value of an integrable function on [a,b], with a<b, is its integral divided by the interval length. Weighted averages replace equal weighting by a density or weight function. Probability densities provide an important application of this distinction.

subsection.p: In words:

p.me: \text{A continuous function reaches its average value somewhere.}

paragraphs.title: Idea of the proof
paragraphs.p: Because f is continuous on [a,b], the Extreme Value Theorem says that f has an absolute minimum m and an absolute maximum M on the interval.

Thus the average value lies between the minimum and the maximum. Since f is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem says that f takes every value between m and M. Therefore f takes its average value at some point c.

paragraphs.title: Why continuity matters
paragraphs.p: The average value can exist even when the function is not continuous. But without continuity, the function may not actually equal its average anywhere.
But f(x) is only 0 or 1. It is never equal to \frac12.

hint.p: There are infinitely many values, so we imitate the finite average with a Riemann sum. The integral accumulates the values; dividing by the length of the interval turns that total into an average height.

note.title: The lesson of arc length
note.p: The integral is not merely an antiderivative problem. It is a way to define and measure quantities. Some of those quantities require new functions or numerical approximation.

subsection.p: This chapter has asked what integrals measure. We have measured area, volume, mass, center of mass, work, hydrostatic force, average value, probability, length, and surface area.

hint.p: Setting up an integral and evaluating it by an antiderivative are different jobs. A quantity can be exactly the value of an integral even when we must approximate that value.

subsection.title: Skills: choose the small piece
subsection.p: The hardest step is usually not the antiderivative. The hardest step is choosing what to add.

subsection.p: The unit check is often the best error detector.
For example, if a work integral has units
then the integrand should contain a force times a distance. If a hydrostatic force integral has units
then the integrand should contain pressure times area.

exercise.title: Why are units a test of the setup?

statement.p: A work integrand should produce force times distance; a hydrostatic-force integrand should produce force. In your own words, why is a unit check often the best error detector, and what would a mismatch tell you about the small piece you wrote?

hint.p: The factors in the integrand must multiply to the quantity you claim to be accumulating. Missing a length, an area, or a density shows up first in the units.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter has shown why integrals matter.
They measure area, volume, mass, center of mass, work, hydrostatic force, average value, probability, arc length, and surface area.
But setting up an integral is not the same as evaluating it.
Even simple applications can produce integrals such as

Substitution will not handle all of these. Some require reversing the product rule. Some require trigonometric identities. Some require a clever triangle. Some require partial fractions. Some have no elementary antiderivative at all.
That is the next problem.

p.em: The small piece tells us what to integrate. Now we need better ways to integrate it.

subsection.p: The next chapter develops techniques for finding antiderivatives when substitution alone is not enough.

introduction.p: Different integrands require different methods. Substitution reverses the chain rule, integration by parts reverses the product rule, and identities or partial fractions simplify the expression before integration. We will also treat improper integrals as limits and distinguish convergence from the availability of an elementary antiderivative.

Integration by parts follows from the product rule. It rewrites the integral of one product in terms of another, which may be easier to evaluate. Integrands such as xe^x, x\cos x, and x^2\ln x are typical applications.

statement.p: For \int x e^x\,dx, taking u=x simplifies the remaining integral, while taking u=e^x makes it worse. In your own words, why is the choice not cosmetic, and what should you want to happen to u when it is differentiated?

hint.p: Differentiate the factor that becomes simpler, and integrate the factor that stays manageable. A poor choice raises the power or complicates the remaining integral.

example.title: no visible product
example.p: There is no visible product, but we can write
This example is a useful reminder. Integration by parts can apply even when the integrand does not look like a product. The hidden factor may be 1\,dx.

example.p: The sign comes from the antiderivative of \sin x. A quick derivative check confirms the result:

p.me: \frac{d}{dx}(x\sin x+\cos x) = \sin x+x\cos x-\sin x = x\cos x.

subsection.title: Repeated integration by parts
subsection.p: Sometimes one use of integration by parts is not enough. A power may need to be reduced one degree at a time.

exercise.title: Why is one use of parts sometimes not enough?

statement.p: A power such as x^2 may need to be reduced one degree at a time, and some integrals cycle back to the original. In your own words, why can repeating the method, or naming the original integral and solving for it, still be reversing the product rule rather than starting over?

hint.p: Each pass peels one derivative off a factor. If the original integral returns, it has become an algebraic unknown that can be moved to the other side.

subsection.title: Definite integrals and boundary terms
subsection.p: For definite integrals, integration by parts has the same idea, but the product term is evaluated at the endpoints.

subsection.p: The term \bigl[uv\bigr]_a^b is called a boundary term. It comes from the Fundamental Theorem:
In an indefinite integral, this term appears as uv. In a definite integral, it becomes an endpoint contribution.

exercise.title: What is the boundary term in a definite integral?

statement.p: For definite integrals, integration by parts evaluates uv at the endpoints: \bigl[uv\bigr]_a^b. In your own words, why does that term come from the Fundamental Theorem, and why does it replace the standalone product uv that appears in the indefinite formula?

hint.p: Accumulating d(uv) from a to b is net change of the product. In an indefinite integral that net change has not yet been evaluated.

subsection.p: Integration by parts is one way of recognizing the hidden derivative rule behind an integrand. Products of algebraic and exponential or logarithmic functions often need it.
But another large family of integrals comes from identities rather than product rules. Trigonometric functions bring their own algebra.

introduction.p: Trigonometric functions have two kinds of structure at once.
First, their derivatives cycle:
Second, their values are tied together by identities:
Trigonometric integrals use both facts. We try to save a factor that becomes a differential, and then use an identity to rewrite everything else.

exercise.title: Why do trigonometric integrals begin by saving a differential?

statement.p: For powers of sine and cosine, the book saves one factor that becomes du and rewrites the rest with an identity. In your own words, why is the saved piece the one that matches the derivative of the other trigonometric function, rather than a factor chosen at random?

statement.p: A product such as \sin(5x)\cos(2x) does not fit the power patterns. In your own words, why do identities that turn products into sums make the integral easier, and why is that still a structural response rather than a new kind of calculus?

hint.p: Sums of sines and cosines integrate term by term. The identities are algebra that reveals those sums; the integration step is then ordinary.

subsection.title: Strategy over memorization
subsection.p: Trigonometric integrals can look like a long list of cases. But the cases are guided by a few questions.

subsection.p: That habit is the same one we used in substitution. The difference is that trigonometric identities give us the algebra needed to make substitution possible.

paragraphs.title: A final mixed example
paragraphs.p: The power of sine is odd. Save one \sin x\,dx, and convert the remaining powers of sine into cosines:
The computation looks long, but the idea is short. Save \sin x\,dx, rewrite the rest in terms of \cos x, and substitute.
Trigonometric identities help with powers of trigonometric functions. In the next section, they will do something more surprising: they will remove square roots such as

exercise.title: Why is an odd power more helpful than two even powers?

statement.p: An odd power of cosine lets you save \cos x\,dx and convert the rest by \cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x. In your own words, why does that strategy fail when both powers are even, and why do half-angle identities appear in that case?

hint.p: If a sine or cosine power is odd, saving one factor leaves an even power of that same function, which the Pythagorean identity converts into the other function. If both powers are even, half-angle identities lower the powers instead.

introduction.p: Trigonometric integrals used identities after trigonometric functions were already present. Trigonometric substitution uses those identities earlier. It creates trigonometric functions on purpose.
The reason is square roots.

A trigonometric substitution chooses x so that the square root becomes a simpler trigonometric expression. The identities simplify the square root after a branch has been chosen to give the correct sign.

In your own words, why is the right substitution the one whose Pythagorean identity cancels the square root, rather than a trigonometric function chosen for familiarity?

The condition x>2 is not a small detail. The substitution x=2\sec\theta with 0\le\theta<\pi/2 covers x\ge2. On another interval, such as x<-2, we would choose a different range or adjust the substitution. Antiderivatives are always local to an interval where the integrand is defined.

subsection.title: Returning to the original variable
subsection.p: An indefinite integral should end in the original variable unless the new variable has been clearly defined.
There are two common ways to return.

cell.p: Uses the substitution to draw a triangle and read \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \tan\theta, or \sec\theta.

subsection.p: In many examples, both methods are needed. The angle \theta itself becomes an inverse trigonometric function. Other expressions, such as \sin2\theta or \tan\theta, are easiest to recover from the triangle.

paragraphs.title: Definite integrals: change the limits
paragraphs.p: For definite integrals, there is often no need to return to x. We can change the limits instead.
No x-triangle is needed at the end because the whole calculation stayed in the new variable after the limits changed.

note.title: A common mistake
note.p: Do not mix variables in a definite integral. After substituting x=2\sin\theta, either change the limits to \theta-limits or return the antiderivative to x before evaluating.
The expression
after an x-substitution is meaningless unless 0 and 1 have been converted into the corresponding \theta-values.

paragraphs.p: The differential keeps the direction of the substitution. If increasing the new variable moves x in the opposite direction, the sign of dx records that reversal. This is the same orientation idea we saw in definite integrals.

exercise.title: Why can a definite trigonometric substitution skip returning to x?

statement.p: For a definite integral, we can change the limits to \theta-values and never go back. In your own words, why are the limits part of the substitution, and when would you still need a triangle to return to the original variable?

hint.p: An indefinite answer must be written in x. A definite integral only needs the accumulated amount between the new endpoints.

The hyperbolic substitution gives the logarithmic answer more directly. It is not a new kind of calculus. It is another choice of variable matched to the shape of the square root.

Trigonometric substitution handles square roots by changing the geometry of the variable. The next family of integrals has no square roots at all. It is algebraic: one polynomial divided by another. There the right move is not to create a triangle, but to split one complicated fraction into simpler fractions.

subsection.p: The derivatives in organize several square-root and rational integrals. For a constant a>0, substitution u=x/a gives

The logarithmic form \ln|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}|+C works on either interval x>a or x<-a, with an independent constant on each. The logarithmic form of the rational antiderivative is \frac1{2a}\ln|(a+x)/(a-x)|+C. It also works on each interval separated by x=\pm a. No antiderivative crosses either singularity.
Two reciprocal patterns complete the list:

Differentiate these formulas separately on the positive and negative intervals. The derivative of |x| supplies the sign needed to recover 1/x. Using \operatorname{arcsch}(x/a) without the absolute value would give the wrong sign on the negative interval.

example.p: The chain-rule factors are (-1)(-1/3), and \sqrt{x^2/9-1}=\sqrt{x^2-9}/3. Their product gives the positive integrand. The expression \operatorname{arcosh}(x/3) would not even be real on this interval.

The same method gives \int\operatorname{arcosh}x\,dx=x\operatorname{arcosh}x-\sqrt{x^2-1}+C for x>1, and \int\operatorname{artanh}x\,dx=x\operatorname{artanh}x+\tfrac12\ln(1-x^2)+C for |x|<1. In each case differentiating the answer makes the two extra terms cancel.

We now have several strong methods: substitution, integration by parts, trigonometric identities, trigonometric substitution, and partial fractions. The difficult part is no longer only carrying out a method. It is choosing the method. That is the next question.

exercise.title: Why is partial fractions algebra before calculus?

statement.p: The method begins only after the rational function is proper, and it splits one complicated fraction into simpler pieces. In your own words, why must you divide first when the numerator’s degree is too large, and why is the integration step almost an afterthought?

hint.p: The pieces 1/(x-r) and (Ax+B)/(x^2+1) already have known antiderivatives. The work is rewriting the integrand so those pieces appear.

introduction.p: Before choosing a method, simplify the integrand and look for a derivative factor, a product suitable for integration by parts, a useful identity, or a rational expression suitable for partial fractions. No single technique works for every integral. We will compare these choices on examples.

subsection.title: Recognizing the structure of an integrand
subsection.p: A derivative rule leaves a fingerprint.
The chain rule often leaves a function and its derivative:
The product rule often leaves a product where one factor becomes simpler when differentiated:

p.me: x e^x, \qquad x\ln x, \qquad x\cos x.

subsection.p: Trigonometric identities appear when powers of sine, cosine, tangent, or secant are mixed:
Right-triangle identities appear when a square root has one of the forms
Partial fractions appear when the integrand is a rational function:
The first question is therefore not “What formula do I remember?” It is:

table.title: Recognizing the structure of an integrand

cell.p: A function together with something close to its derivative
A product where one factor simplifies when differentiated
A square root like a^2-x^2, a^2+x^2, or x^2-a^2
Use polynomial division if needed, then partial fractions.
A complicated expression that becomes simpler after expansion, factoring, or rationalizing
Do algebra before choosing a calculus method.

subsection.p: This table is a guide, not a law. Many integrals can be solved in more than one way. The best method is usually the one that reveals the structure most clearly.

exercise.title: Why is a technique a response to the shape of the integrand?

statement.p: A derivative rule leaves a fingerprint: a chain-rule pair, a product that simplifies when differentiated, a Pythagorean square root, a rational function. In your own words, why is the first question what structure do I see? rather than what formula do I remember??

hint.p: Each method undoes a specific kind of differentiation. Matching the method to the fingerprint is recognition, not a search through a bag of tricks.

subsection.title: Substitution first or parts first?
subsection.p: Some integrals look like products but are really substitution problems. Others look like they might have an inside function, but integration by parts is better.
A useful test is this:

p.me: \text{Before using parts, check whether substitution removes the whole problem.}

subsection.p: Integration by parts creates a new integral. Substitution often turns the integral directly into a known form. So substitution is usually the first thing to test.

exercise.title: Why test substitution before integration by parts?

statement.p: The product x e^{x^2} looks like a candidate for parts, but substitution removes the whole problem. In your own words, why is substitution usually the first thing to test, and what is the difference between a product that is really a chain rule and a product that really needs parts?

hint.p: Substitution often turns the integral directly into a known form. Parts always creates a new integral. Check whether the inside function’s derivative is already present.

example.title: a product that is really substitution
example.p: The integrand is a product, but the exponent has inside function
So substitution is the natural choice:
Trying integration by parts would make this worse. The product is not the main structure. The inside function x^2 is.

example.title: a product that really needs parts
example.p: Here the exponent is just x. Its derivative is 1, not a missing factor that simplifies the integral. Substitution does not help.
But x becomes simpler when differentiated, and e^x is easy to integrate. So integration by parts gives
The two examples are close in appearance:
But their structures are different. The first is a chain rule problem. The second is a product rule problem.

example.title: logarithms often want parts
example.p: There is no helpful substitution. The factor \ln x becomes simpler when differentiated:
A logarithm is often a good choice for u, because it simplifies under differentiation.

note.title: Substitution or parts?
note.p: Substitution asks:

p.me: \text{Is there an inside function whose derivative is present?}

note.p: Integration by parts asks:

p.em: Can I differentiate one factor and make it simpler, while integrating the other factor?

note.p: When both seem possible, try substitution first. If it does not simplify the integral, look for parts.

subsection.title: Algebraic simplification
subsection.p: Sometimes the right technique is hidden behind algebra. Before reaching for a new calculus method, simplify the integrand.
Algebra can reveal substitution, partial fractions, cancellation, or a known form.

exercise.title: Why can algebra be the real technique?

statement.p: Dividing, canceling, completing the square, or expanding can reveal a simple integrand that was hiding. In your own words, why should you simplify before reaching for a new calculus method, and what does that say about where the difficulty often lives?

hint.p: Many hard-looking integrals are easy after a rewrite. The calculus step is then a basic formula; the work was algebraic recognition.

The original integrand is not defined at x=1. An indefinite integral is always understood on an interval in the domain, such as (-\infty,1) or (1,\infty).

The substitution did not immediately give a basic antiderivative. It gave an algebraic expression we could simplify.

The calculus was easy after the algebra.

note.p: Before choosing an integration method, ask whether the integrand can be simplified by
A hard-looking integral may become a basic one after the right algebraic move.

subsection.title: A practical decision tree
subsection.p: No decision tree can replace judgment. But a rough order helps.

figure.caption: A practical order of questions. The arrows are not laws; they are a way to begin thinking.

subsection.p: The order matters less than the habit: pause, read the integrand, and identify the structure.

Its derivative is 2x, and the numerator contains x^3\,dx. Rewrite
A trigonometric substitution would work, but it would be longer. The simpler inside function was already present.

example.p: The interval [-2,2] is symmetric about 0. Therefore the positive and negative parts cancel:
We could also use substitution, but symmetry is faster and more revealing.

note.title: For definite integrals, use definite information
note.p: Before finding an antiderivative, check for
A definite integral may have a simple value even when the indefinite integral is hard.

subsection.title: When no elementary antiderivative exists
subsection.p: It is natural to hope that every continuous function has a familiar antiderivative. The Fundamental Theorem tells us that every continuous function f has an antiderivative:
But it does not say that F can be written using the elementary functions we already know.

By elementary functions, we mean functions built from polynomials, rational functions, powers, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, inverse trigonometric functions, and combinations of these by addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and composition.
Many elementary functions have antiderivatives that are not elementary.
Famous examples include
and
This is not a failure of calculus. It is a sign that the family of elementary functions is not closed under antidifferentiation.

paragraphs.title: The Gaussian example
paragraphs.p: is a perfectly good function, and the Fundamental Theorem gives
But G(x) cannot be expressed using elementary functions. So instead of forcing it into old language, mathematicians name it. A scaled version is called the error function:
The name is not a trick. It is a recognition that this accumulation is important enough to become a function in its own right.

paragraphs.title: A definite integral may still be meaningful
paragraphs.p: has no elementary antiderivative, the definite integral
still has a definite value. It measures accumulated area. We can approximate it numerically. Later, we will also approximate it with power series.
The absence of an elementary antiderivative does not stop the integral from existing.

p.em: Exact elementary formulas are useful, but they are not the only way to know an integral.

exercise.title: Why can an antiderivative exist without being elementary?

statement.p: Part I guarantees that every continuous function has an antiderivative F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt. In your own words, why does that not mean F can be written from polynomials, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions, and why is that not a failure of calculus?

hint.p: The family of elementary functions is not closed under antidifferentiation. The accumulation function is still a genuine function; it may simply be a new name, such as the error function, or a quantity we approximate.

subsection.title: Strategy summary
subsection.p: Integration is less mechanical than differentiation. Differentiation has a direct rule for each way of building a function. Integration asks us to recognize what construction might have produced the integrand.
A useful final checklist is:

cell.p: Can the integrand be simplified algebraically?
Factor, cancel, expand, rationalize, complete the square, or divide.
Is there an inside function with its derivative nearby?
Is there a product with a factor that simplifies under differentiation?
Are there trigonometric powers or products?
Is there a square root matching a Pythagorean pattern?
Use polynomial division and partial fractions.
Is it a definite integral with symmetry or geometry?
Use the bounds and the shape before seeking an antiderivative.
Define a new accumulation function, approximate numerically, or use series.

subsection.p: The best way to learn strategy is to practice with mixed examples. But the guiding principle stays simple:

p.me: \text{Do not ask first, ``What technique should I use?''}

subsection.p: Ask instead:

p.me: \text{What is the integrand trying to tell me?}

subsection.p: The next section adds a modern tool. Computer algebra systems and integral tables can find many antiderivatives. But they do not remove the need for thought. They make checking, interpretation, and domain awareness more important.

section.title: Computer algebra systems and integral tables

introduction.p: Integral tables and computer algebra systems can suggest antiderivatives and simplify expressions. Check a proposed answer by differentiating it on the relevant domain. Pay particular attention to absolute values, branch choices, singularities, and assumptions that may be implicit in the output.

subsection.title: Branch and domain issues
subsection.p: An indefinite integral is not a global object on every part of the real line at once. It is usually a family of antiderivatives on intervals where the integrand is defined.
This matters most for logarithms, square roots, and inverse trigonometric functions.

subsection.p: A computer algebra system may return a special function for a definite integral. That is not necessarily less useful than a decimal.

subsection.p: The important question is not always “Can we find an elementary antiderivative?” Often the better question is:

p.me: \text{How accurately do we need the accumulated amount?}

subsection.p: That question leads naturally to numerical integration.

subsection.title: A responsible workflow with tools
subsection.p: When using a table or computer algebra system, work in this order.

cell.p: Inspect the integrand first. Identify possible structure.
Try a human method if the structure is clear.
Use a table or CAS to check, compare, or explore.
Check the interval, branch, and absolute values.
For a definite integral, check whether endpoints or discontinuities cause trouble.
Decide whether an exact form, special-function form, or decimal approximation is most useful.

subsection.p: The last endpoint check points toward the next section. A definite integral over a finite interval with a continuous integrand is safe. But many important integrals are not of that kind. The interval may be infinite. The integrand may blow up. A formal antiderivative may exist while the accumulated amount is not finite.
For example,

but the accumulated area grows without bound.
So the next question is not how to find an antiderivative. It is more basic:

p.me: \text{When does an infinite or singular accumulation have a finite value?}

subsection.p: That is the problem of improper integrals.

introduction.p: An integral over an infinite interval, or with an unbounded integrand near an endpoint or interior point, is defined using limits of integrals over finite nonsingular intervals. It converges when every required limit is finite. This section develops comparison tests and distinguishes absolute convergence from convergence caused by cancellation.

subsection.title: Convergence and divergence
subsection.p: The words convergent and divergent describe the limiting process, not the antiderivative.
An improper integral converges if the limiting accumulated amount approaches a finite number. It diverges if the limiting accumulated amount does not approach a finite number.
The antiderivative may exist on every finite subinterval and the improper integral may still diverge.
For example,

statement.p: For every finite t>1, \int_1^t(1/x)\,dx=\ln t exists, but \int_1^\infty(1/x)\,dx diverges. In your own words, why do the words convergent and divergent describe the limiting accumulated amount, not the existence of an antiderivative?

hint.p: Convergence means the running total approaches a finite number. An antiderivative on each compact subinterval is not the same as a finite total for the whole improper accumulation.

Improper integrals teach a useful discipline. Do not evaluate first and ask questions later. First ask where the integral is improper. Then replace the dangerous endpoint or discontinuity by a limit. Then decide whether the limit is finite.
The next section collects the mistakes this discipline prevents.

subsection.title: Absolute and conditional convergence
subsection.p: Cancellation can make a signed accumulation finite even when the total unsigned area is infinite. An improper integral \int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx is absolutely convergent if \int_a^\infty|f(x)|\,dx converges. It is conditionally convergent if the signed integral converges but the absolute-value integral diverges. Use the same definitions at a singular endpoint, and require convergence on every piece when several endpoints or singularities are involved.

note.title: Absolute convergence implies convergence
note.p: Assume f is continuous on each finite subinterval. Put f_+=\max(f,0) and f_-=\max(-f,0). Both are nonnegative and bounded above by |f|. Comparison shows that their improper integrals converge if the integral of |f| does. Since f=f_+-f_-, the signed integral then converges too. Moreover, for any tail beginning at R,

example.title: Oscillation with finite unsigned area
example.p: For x\ge1, |\sin x|/x^2\le1/x^2. Thus \int_1^\infty \sin x/x^2\,dx converges absolutely, and its tail after R\ge1 has magnitude at most 1/R.

example.p: Consider \int_1^\infty \sin x/x\,dx. Integration by parts on a finite interval gives

To test absolute convergence, use the disjoint intervals

The partial sums of these lower bounds grow without bound: among indices with 2^j\le k+1<2^{j+1}, there are 2^j terms, each at least 1/(3\cdot2^{j+1}), so each group contributes at least 1/6. The unsigned integral diverges. The original integral is conditionally convergent.

Thus it converges conditionally at zero. By contrast, \int_1^\infty\sin x\,dx diverges because \cos1-\cos T has no limit. Oscillation by itself does not ensure convergence.

warning.title: Keep the two tails separate
warning.p: Conditional convergence still requires each improper piece to converge. The symmetric values \int_{-R}^R\sin x\,dx=0 do not make \int_{-\infty}^\infty\sin x\,dx convergent. Such a symmetric limiting procedure is called a Cauchy principal value; it is a different definition.

exercise.title: Classify oscillatory integrals

statement.p: Classify \int_1^\infty\cos x/x\,dx, \int_1^\infty\cos x/x^2\,dx, and \int_0^1\sin(1/x)\,dx as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.

hint.p: The first is conditional: integrate by parts using the bounded antiderivative \sin x, and adapt the lobe lower bound for |\cos x|. The other two are absolute; bound by 1/x^2 and by 1, respectively.

introduction.p: For an improper integral, apply the Fundamental Theorem only on finite nonsingular intervals, then take the required limits. If there is an interior singularity or two infinite tails, treat each piece separately. The examples below show errors caused by skipping these steps.

subsection.title: A CAS gives an antiderivative with the wrong domain
subsection.p: A computer algebra system may return an antiderivative that is correct only on part of the real line, or correct only after choosing a complex logarithm branch.

subsection.p: Improper integrals have given us one last lesson for exact integration: before computing, ask where the integral is defined and what limit is being taken.
This chapter has focused on exact methods and convergence. But exact antiderivatives are not always available, and convergence alone may not give the number we need. The next question is practical:

p.em: How can we approximate an accumulated amount, and how can we control the error?

subsection.p: That question leads to numerical integration.

hint.p: A triangle carries sign information. Separate pieces of the domain, such as (-\infty,-2) and (2,\infty), may need different ranges or different inverse functions.
