subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: When exact integration is unavailable, numerical integration can approximate the value.
Some integrals have elementary antiderivatives:
Some have antiderivatives that require special functions:

Some come from data instead of formulas. A speedometer may give readings every second. A thermometer may give temperatures every hour. A sensor may give force measurements at discrete positions. In those cases, there may be no formula to antidifferentiate.
But the accumulated amount may still be exactly what we need.
is a real number. The length
is a real length. The work computed from measured force data is real work.
So the next question is not

p.me: \text{Can we always find an exact antiderivative?}

subsection.p: The answer is no.
The better question is

p.em: How can we approximate an integral, and how can we know how accurate the approximation is?

subsection.p: That question leads to numerical integration, error estimates, and computation.

exercise.title: When is numerical integration needed?

statement.p: Some integrals have elementary antiderivatives, some require special functions, and some come from data with no formula at all. In your own words, why can the accumulated amount still be exactly what we need even when no elementary antiderivative exists?

hint.p: The integral defines the quantity. Finding a closed form, inventing a special function, or approximating numerically are three ways of reading that quantity, not three different meanings.

introduction.p: Numerical methods approximate integrals, derivatives, and roots when exact calculations are unavailable or inconvenient. We will derive the methods, state the smoothness conditions behind their error estimates, and examine how step size, stopping rules, and rounding affect the results.

Numerical integration approximates a definite integral using sampled function values. It is useful when the function is given by data, has no accessible antiderivative, or requires a numerical answer. An approximation should be accompanied by an error bound or a clearly identified error estimate.

subsection.title: Data instead of formulas
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem says that if we know an antiderivative F of f, then
But a laboratory instrument may not give us a formula. It may only give measurements.
Suppose a small cart is pulled along a track. A sensor records the force at several positions.
The work done by the force is
The units confirm the meaning:
But the table does not give a formula for F(x). There is no antiderivative to find. Still, the work is a real physical quantity. The cart moved. The force did work.
We have to estimate the integral from the data.
The simplest idea is familiar from the first chapters on integration: on each short interval, pretend the force is nearly constant. Then
Adding these small pieces gives an approximate total work.

note.title: Data form of the integral problem
note.p: A table can give enough information to estimate an integral, even when it does not give enough information to find an exact antiderivative.

subsection.p: This happens constantly: velocity from GPS samples, temperature from a probe, force from a sensor, power usage from a meter, rainfall from a weather station, and density from measurements along a rod.
The integral still means accumulation. Only the method of computation changes.

exercise.title: Why can a table still define an integral problem?

statement.p: A force sensor may give only a table of values, not a formula for F(x). In your own words, why is the work \int_a^b F(x)\,dx still a real quantity, and what information does the table give that an antiderivative formula would have given?

hint.p: The integral still means accumulation. A table supplies samples of the integrand, not an elementary antiderivative.

subsection.title: Non-elementary antiderivatives
subsection.p: Sometimes we do have a formula, but the formula has no antiderivative built from the elementary functions of this course.
A standard example is
The integrand
is continuous, positive, and easy to evaluate. So the definite integral exists. It is a real number: the area under the curve from 0 to 1.

figure.caption: The area \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx exists, even though the antiderivative is not elementary.

description.p: The area \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx exists, even though the antiderivative is not elementary.

subsection.p: The difficulty is not the integral. The difficulty is the antiderivative. There is no elementary function F such that

Proving that fact belongs to a later course. For us, the practical consequence is enough: the Fundamental Theorem cannot turn this integral into a simple endpoint calculation using familiar functions.
But the integral still has a decimal value. In fact,
A numerical method should be able to recover this number, and should tell us how much confidence to place in the digits.

note.title: Important distinction
note.p: A function can be easy to evaluate but hard to antidifferentiate.
Numerical integration uses values of the function directly. It does not require an elementary antiderivative.

exercise.title: Why can a function be easy to evaluate but hard to antidifferentiate?

statement.p: The integrand e^{-x^2} is continuous and easy to compute, yet \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx cannot be finished by the Fundamental Theorem with elementary functions. In your own words, what distinction does that example make, and why does numerical integration still make sense?

hint.p: Existence of a definite integral is about the integrand, not about whether an antiderivative is elementary. Numerical rules use values of f directly.

subsection.title: Speed versus accuracy
subsection.p: The original definition of the integral used Riemann sums:
If n is large and the function is well behaved, these sums can approximate the integral well. But a large n means many function evaluations.
There is a practical tradeoff:

p.em: more samples \Longrightarrow usually better accuracy, but more computation.

subsection.p: The word “usually” matters. More samples help when they are used intelligently and when the function is well behaved on the interval. They do not automatically fix every problem.

For example, if the integrand has a sharp spike, a coarse grid may miss it. If the integral is improper, applying a rule directly at an infinite endpoint or a vertical asymptote may make no sense. If a computer subtracts nearly equal numbers many times, roundoff error may accumulate.
So numerical integration has two parts:
and
A fast approximation without an error estimate is only a guess with arithmetic attached.

exercise.title: Why is more sampling not automatically better?

statement.p: Riemann sums suggest that a larger n should improve an approximation. In your own words, why is that only usually true, and what can go wrong even if you take many samples?

hint.p: A missed narrow peak, an improper endpoint, or subtractive rounding can invalidate an approximation. The algorithm must supply an applicable error bound or an explicitly qualified estimate.

Sometimes we care about the size of the error relative to the size of the true answer. If I\neq0, the relative error is

subsection.p: There are two common ways to judge an approximation.
First, if we know enough about the function, we can use an error bound. An error bound gives a guaranteed maximum possible error.

Second, if we compute several approximations using smaller and smaller step sizes, we can watch the values stabilize. This gives evidence, and often very good evidence, but it is not the same as a proof unless it is supported by a theorem.

exercise.title: What extra sentence makes a numerical answer useful?

statement.p: Suppose a computation reports \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx A. In your own words, why is that incomplete, and what is the difference between watching approximations stabilize and having an error bound?

hint.p: Absolute error is |I-A|. Stabilization is evidence. A bound is a guarantee, provided the hypotheses of the theorem hold.

The next section builds two rules whose geometry is easy to see and whose errors can be controlled: the midpoint rule and the trapezoidal rule.

introduction.p: The midpoint rule uses a rectangle whose height is the function value at the midpoint. The trapezoidal rule joins the endpoint values by a line. Applying either rule on many subintervals approximates an integral. We will derive their error bounds under bounds on the second derivative.

subsection.p: Why use the midpoint instead of an endpoint? The midpoint balances the interval. If the function is increasing, a left rectangle underestimates and a right rectangle overestimates. The midpoint often cancels part of those errors.
For a line, the cancellation is perfect.

statement.p: On one interval, the midpoint rule uses height f\bigl((a+b)/2\bigr). In your own words, why does that choice often cancel part of the error of endpoint rectangles, and why is the rule exact for every line?

hint.p: If a function is increasing, a left rectangle underestimates and a right rectangle overestimates. The midpoint height of a line is exactly its average height.

example.title: midpoint rule is exact for a line
example.p: So the midpoint rule gives the exact answer.
This happens for every linear function on every interval. The midpoint height of a line is exactly the average height of the line.

This straddling is useful, but it is not guaranteed for every function. To understand when an approximation is above or below the true value, we need to look at concavity.

subsection.title: Error patterns from concavity
subsection.p: The trapezoidal rule replaces the graph by a secant line. The midpoint rule replaces the graph by a horizontal line at the midpoint height.
Concavity tells us which approximation lies above or below the true area.
If
on an interval, the graph is concave up. It bends upward. The secant line lies above the graph, so the trapezoid overestimates the integral.
For the same concave-up graph, the midpoint rectangle underestimates the integral. The curve spends more area above the midpoint height than below it.

paragraphs.title: Warning: changing concavity
paragraphs.p: If the function changes concavity on the interval, these simple over-under rules may not apply to the whole interval.
So on [0,1], the graph is concave down at first and concave up later. We should not expect one global concavity picture to explain all of the error.
In that case, use error bounds.

exercise.title: How does concavity decide overestimate versus underestimate?

statement.p: Suppose f'' does not change sign on [a,b]. In your own words, why does a concave-up graph make the trapezoidal rule overestimate and the midpoint rule underestimate, and why can that pattern fail if concavity changes?

hint.p: A secant lies above a concave-up graph. The midpoint rectangle sits at a height that, for the same shape, leaves more area above it than below. Changing concavity mixes the two pictures.

subsection.title: Error bounds
subsection.p: An error pattern tells us the direction of the error. An error bound tells us how large the error can be.

The size of the error is controlled by curvature. If the graph is nearly linear on each small interval, the midpoint and trapezoidal rules are accurate. The second derivative measures how far the graph is from being linear.

The midpoint bound is half the trapezoidal bound when the same K, a, b, and n are used. This does not mean the midpoint rule is always exactly twice as accurate, but it explains why midpoint approximations often perform very well.

paragraphs.p: On a subinterval [c,d], let L be the line through the endpoint values. For an interior point x, choose C so that f(t)-L(t)-C(t-c)(t-d) vanishes at c,x,d. Applying Rolle’s Theorem twice gives C=f''(\xi)/2. Hence |f(x)-L(x)|\le K(x-c)(d-x)/2. Integrating this bound, with \Delta x=d-c, shows that the one-interval trapezoid error is at most

The formula for the guarantee is what fails, not necessarily the approximation itself.

paragraphs.p: This warning matters in applications. Before using an error bound, check the interval, the continuity of the derivatives, and whether the integral is proper.
The midpoint and trapezoidal rules approximate a curve by flat or straight pieces. The next rule asks a natural question:

statement.p: The midpoint and trapezoidal bounds shrink like 1/n^2 and are controlled by a bound on |f''|. In your own words, why is a bound not a prediction of the exact error, and why can the rules still be used on \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx even though those particular bounds do not apply?

hint.p: Curvature measures how far the graph is from linear. If f'' is unbounded, the guarantee fails. The approximation itself may still produce useful numbers.

introduction.p: Simpson's rule integrates a quadratic interpolant through two endpoints and their midpoint. Its composite form uses an even number of equal subintervals. When the fourth derivative is bounded, the error is bounded by a constant times the fourth power of the mesh width.

example.p: So Simpson’s Rule is exact in this example.
That should not be surprising. Simpson’s Rule integrates the quadratic interpolating polynomial. If the original function is already quadratic, the approximation is the function itself.

subsection.p: One parabola over a wide interval may not be enough. As before, we divide the interval into smaller pieces.

subsection.p: A compact way to remember the formula is:

p.me: S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3} \left[ f(x_0)+f(x_n) + 4\sum_{\substack{i=1\\i\text{ odd}}}^{n-1} f(x_i) + 2\sum_{\substack{i=2\\i\text{ even}}}^{n-2} f(x_i) \right].

subsection.p: The odd interior points get weight 4. The even interior points get weight 2.

paragraphs.title: Warning: n must be even
paragraphs.p: Composite Simpson’s Rule pairs neighboring subintervals. If n is odd, one subinterval is left unpaired.

For example, n=5 gives five subintervals. Simpson’s Rule can cover four of them in two pairs, but one remains. In that situation, either change n to an even number or combine Simpson’s Rule with another rule on the leftover interval.
For this course, when using Simpson’s Rule, choose n even.

exercise.title: Why is Simpson’s Rule exact for cubics, not only quadratics?

statement.p: Simpson’s Rule is built by integrating a quadratic interpolant, yet it also integrates every cubic exactly. In your own words, why is that possible, and how does writing Simpson as the weighted average \frac13 T+\frac23 M help explain the improvement?

hint.p: On a symmetric interval, the odd cubic term integrates to zero in both the true integral and Simpson’s formula. The leading curvature errors of the trapezoid and midpoint have opposite signs.

subsection.title: Simpson error bound
subsection.p: The midpoint and trapezoidal error bounds were controlled by f'', because lines fail when curvature is present.
Simpson’s Rule is exact for cubics. So its first possible error comes from behavior beyond cubic. That is why the fourth derivative appears.

note.title: A bound is a guarantee, not a prediction
note.p: An error bound tells us the approximation cannot be worse than a certain amount. It does not usually tell us the actual error exactly.

paragraphs.title: Why the hypotheses matter
paragraphs.p: The Simpson error bound assumes that f^{(4)} exists, is continuous, and is bounded on the interval.
is continuous on [0,1], and the integral
exists. But the derivatives of f become singular near x=0. In particular, the fourth derivative is unbounded near 0.
Simpson’s Rule may still produce useful approximations, but the standard Simpson error bound does not apply on [0,1].

p.me: \text{The numerical rule can still be used. The guarantee is what fails.}

paragraphs.p: That warning is important in computation. A formula can return a number even when the theorem that estimates its error does not apply.
Numerical integration approximates accumulation. But the other half of calculus can also be approximated. If we know values of a function from data, can we estimate its derivative?
That question leads to numerical differentiation.

exercise.title: Why does Simpson’s error bound involve the fourth derivative?

statement.p: Midpoint and trapezoidal errors are controlled by f''. Simpson’s bound is controlled by f^{(4)} and shrinks like 1/n^4. In your own words, why does exactness through cubics push the first possible error to the next derivative, and why is a bound still only a guarantee?

hint.p: A rule that is exact for polynomials up through degree 3 first feels the failure of a degree-4 term. Doubling n divides the bound by 16, but the actual error may be smaller.

exercise.title: What fails when the fourth derivative is unbounded?

statement.p: Simpson’s Rule can still be applied to \int_0^1\sqrt{x}\,dx, even though f^{(4)} blows up at x=0. In your own words, what exactly fails in that situation, and what does that teach about trusting a formula that still returns a number?

hint.p: The numerical rule can still be used. The theorem that estimates its error is what no longer applies.

introduction.p: Finite differences estimate derivatives from sampled values. Their truncation error decreases as the step shrinks under suitable smoothness assumptions, but subtracting nearby values and dividing by a small step can amplify measurement and rounding errors. We will examine this tradeoff.

There are three basic finite-difference formulas.

subsection.p: Geometrically, all three are slopes of secant lines.

subsection.title: Truncation error
subsection.p: A finite-difference formula replaces a limit by a finite step. The error from doing that is called truncation error.
The word means: we stopped a limiting process early.
Assume f''' is continuous near a, with |f'''|\le K. Repeated use of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives the finite identity
The orientation of the integral makes the identity valid for negative s too. In either direction, |R_3(s)|\le K|s|^3/6. Therefore
Each remainder quotient has absolute value at most Kh^2/6. The one-sided errors generally have opposite leading terms proportional to h. Averaging the quotients cancels those terms:
Continuity of f''' also gives R_3(s)/s^3\to f'''(a)/6: subtract f'''(a) in the integral and bound the difference by its maximum near a. Consequently
The leading centered error is usually proportional to h^2. These are finite remainder estimates; Taylor polynomials will be developed in Chapter 16.

subsection.title: Roundoff error
subsection.p: Truncation error suggests a simple strategy:
But computation has another error source.
A computer does not usually store real numbers exactly. It stores rounded approximations. When two nearly equal rounded numbers are subtracted, the small difference may lose important digits.
That is exactly what finite differences do.

p.me: \text{Small \(h\) reduces truncation error but can increase roundoff error.}

subsection.p: This is the central tension in numerical differentiation.

note.title: Practical lesson
note.p: For numerical derivatives, do not blindly make h extremely small.
Use a moderately small h, compare several step sizes, and prefer centered differences when the data allow them.

exercise.title: Why is smaller h not always better?

statement.p: Making h smaller reduces truncation error, yet a computer experiment can show the error decreasing and then increasing. In your own words, what competing error is growing, and why is numerical differentiation more delicate than numerical integration?

hint.p: Finite differences subtract nearby values and divide by a small number. Roundoff (or measurement noise) is magnified by division by h. Integration averages; differentiation magnifies.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A finite-difference formula can return a number even when the derivative does not exist.
Numerical evidence must be interpreted with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses in mind.

subsection.p: This warning is especially important with noisy data. If the measurements contain small errors, dividing by a small h can turn small measurement errors into large derivative errors.
Differentiation magnifies noise. Integration averages noise.
That is one reason numerical differentiation is usually more delicate than numerical integration.

exercise.title: Why can a difference quotient return a number even when the derivative does not exist?

statement.p: For f(x)=|x| at x=0, the three finite-difference formulas give 1, -1, and 0. In your own words, why none of those numbers means that f'(0) exists, and what extra evidence should accompany a numerical derivative?

hint.p: A formula can compute a quotient even when left and right slopes disagree. Interpret the number with the graph, the data, and the hypotheses.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: Numerical integration and numerical differentiation replace limiting definitions by finite calculations. Both require analysis of truncation and rounding errors.
For integration, smaller subintervals usually improve the approximation, and the error bounds can be very strong for smooth functions.
For differentiation, smaller steps reduce truncation error but may increase roundoff error. The best computation is a compromise.
The next natural place where approximation, derivatives, and error meet is Newton’s method. We already used Newton’s method to find roots. Now we can ask sharper computational questions:

p.me: \text{How close is the current guess to the root?}
\text{What happens when the derivative is small or the root is repeated?}

subsection.p: Those questions bring Newton’s method back, this time as a numerical algorithm rather than only a tangent-line idea.

introduction.p: Newton's iteration for a root of f is

when the denominator is nonzero. This section examines convergence near a root, error and residual estimates, multiple roots, and stopping rules. It also shows how a poor starting value or a small derivative can cause failure.

subsection.title: Stopping criteria
subsection.p: A computer almost never lands on the exact root. It produces a sequence
and we must decide when the sequence is good enough.
There are two numbers we can easily monitor.
First, we can monitor the residual:
This tells us how close the function value is to 0.
Second, we can monitor the step size:
This tells us how much the iterates are still moving.
Both are useful. Neither is perfect by itself.

example.title: square root of 2
example.p: By n=3, the residual is tiny and the step is small enough for a moderate decimal tolerance. The required precision determines whether another step is needed.

note.title: A practical stopping rule
note.p: Choose tolerances \varepsilon_{\text{res}}>0 and \varepsilon_{\text{step}}>0. Stop when
and
Also choose a maximum number of iterations, so the method cannot run forever.

subsection.p: A typical algorithm therefore asks for three pieces of numerical judgment:
The maximum iteration count is not mathematical decoration. It protects us from cycles, divergence, and programming mistakes.

paragraphs.title: Why residual alone can mislead
paragraphs.p: A small residual does not always mean a small error in x. The reason is slope.
If the graph is very flat near the axis, then the function value can be small even when the input is not very close to the root.
If a careless stopping rule accepts every residual less than 0.02, then x=0 would be accepted even though it is one million units away from the root.
The residual must be interpreted together with the scale of the function and the slope near the root.

p.me: \text{Small \(f(x_n)\) is strongest evidence when \(f'\) is not small near the root.}

paragraphs.title: Why step size alone can mislead
paragraphs.p: A small step size can also be misleading. An iteration may stop moving because of roundoff error, because the derivative is badly scaled, or because the method is trapped near a point that is not a root.
So a step-size test should usually be paired with a residual test. We want the iterates to stop moving and the function value to be close to zero.

exercise.title: Why is neither residual nor step size enough by itself?

statement.p: A Newton iteration can monitor |f(x_n)| and |x_n-x_{n-1}|. In your own words, why can a small residual occur far from a root, and why can a small step occur even when the current point is not a trustworthy root?

hint.p: A flat graph can have a small function value far from the axis. An iteration can also stall from roundoff, a tiny derivative, or a trap that is not a root. Pair the two tests.

subsection.title: Error estimates
subsection.p: A residual is easy to compute. The actual error
is usually not easy to compute, because the root r is the thing we are trying to find.
Still, we can sometimes bound the error.

exercise.title: How can a residual bound the unknown error |x_n-r|?

statement.p: The root r is what we are trying to find, so the true error is not directly available. In your own words, why does a lower bound on |f'| near the root convert a small residual into a bound on |x_n-r|?

hint.p: The Mean Value Theorem says |f(x_n)|=|f'(c)|\,|x_n-r|. If the slope cannot be too small, a small function value forces a small input error.

subsection.title: The Newton step as an error estimate
subsection.p: The Newton step is
Near a simple root, the tangent line predicts that the root is approximately
So
is often a rough estimate of the current error |x_n-r|.

This is why the step size is useful as a stopping test. If the next tangent correction is tiny, then the current approximation is probably close to a root, provided the residual is also tiny and the derivative is not causing trouble.
But there is something even better near a simple root.
Earlier, the quadratic remainder argument using Rolle’s Theorem gave the Newton error relation
for some point c_n between x_n and r. So near a simple root,
This is quadratic convergence.
If the current error is about 10^{-3}, the next error may be about 10^{-6}. If the current error is about 10^{-6}, the next error may be about 10^{-12}.
That is why Newton’s method can suddenly gain many digits.

note.title: Practical lesson
note.p: When Newton’s method is converging well to a simple root, the number of correct digits often roughly doubles from one step to the next.
When it is not converging well, no stopping rule should pretend that it is.

subsection.title: Multiple roots
subsection.p: Newton’s method is fastest near a simple root. A simple root is a root r for which
If
then the graph meets the axis with zero slope; it may touch the axis or cross it flatly. Newton’s method may still converge, but the convergence often becomes much slower.

exercise.title: Why does a multiple root slow Newton’s method?

statement.p: Near a simple root, Newton’s method often doubles the number of correct digits. Near a double root, the error may merely be cut in half each step. In your own words, what geometric difference between a simple crossing and a flat touch explains the change?

hint.p: Quadratic convergence near a simple root uses a nonzero derivative there. At a root of finite multiplicity m>1, ordinary Newton iteration usually has only linear convergence, with leading error factor (m-1)/m. Such a root can touch or cross the axis.

example.p: and it is a double root. More generally, a root has multiplicity m if, near the root, f(x)=(x-r)^m g(x), where m is a positive integer and g is continuous with g(r)\ne0. For the differentiations below we also assume g is sufficiently differentiable. Here m=2 and g=1. Since
Starting from x_0=2, the iterates are:
The error is cut in half each time. That is convergence, but it is not quadratic convergence. It is only linear convergence.

description.p: At a double root, the graph is tangent to the x-axis. Newton’s method still moves toward the root, but much more slowly.

example.p: The same pattern appears for higher multiplicity. If

For a double root, this factor is 1/2. For a triple root, it is 2/3. The larger the multiplicity, the slower the basic Newton iteration becomes.

warning.title: Multiple-root warning
warning.p: If Newton’s method converges only linearly, one possible reason is that the root is multiple.
Repeatedly small residuals with slow-moving iterates may indicate a flat crossing or a flat touch near the axis.

subsection.p: If the multiplicity m is known, a modified Newton step can help:
For
this modified method reaches the root in one step. For more general functions with a root of multiplicity m, it can restore much faster convergence near the root.
But the multiplicity is not always known. That is why observing the behavior of the iteration matters.

subsection.title: A first glimpse of chaotic iteration
subsection.p: Newton’s method is an iteration:
where
So Newton’s method is not only a root-finding formula. It is also a dynamical system: a rule that sends each point to a next point.
Under the local convergence hypotheses, a simple root attracts Newton iterates started sufficiently close to it.
Far from a root, the dynamics can be complicated.

hint.p: The method can jump to another root, cycle, divide by zero, or behave unpredictably. Record residual and step size, and restart or switch methods if the residual does not drop.

example.p: This example is not here because we need to solve x^2+1=0 over the real numbers. We already know there is no real solution.
This example shows that a simple iteration rule can produce complicated behavior.

warning.title: Computational warning
warning.p: Newton’s method can be extremely fast near a good root. Far from a good root, it can move to a different root, enter a cycle, become undefined, or behave unpredictably.
Always monitor the iterates.

subsection.p: Practical use of Newton's method requires checks on convergence, residuals, and the computed iterates.

subsection.title: A safe Newton workflow
subsection.p: When using Newton’s method as a numerical algorithm, follow a disciplined workflow.

li.p: Choose a function f whose root solves the original problem.
Choose a starting value x_0 from a graph, table, physical estimate, or bracket.
Compute
only when f'(x_n)\neq0.
At each step, record x_n, f(x_n), and x_n-x_{n-1}.
Stop only when the residual and step size are both small enough.
If the method leaves the physical domain, cycles, or fails to reduce the residual, restart with a better initial guess or use a safer method such as bisection.

subsection.p: Newton’s method is a perfect example of this chapter’s theme. Calculus gives the idea: follow the tangent line. Computation adds the discipline: check whether the idea is working.
The same discipline belongs to numerical integration. We have formulas, but formulas become understanding only when we test them.

Compute the first part exactly, and approximate the second part numerically. Does this improve the result?

paragraphs.p: This experiment is a counterexample to a lazy belief:

p.me: \text{``A higher-order rule always achieves its stated convergence order.''}

paragraphs.p: The rule’s error theorem has hypotheses. The function must meet them.

exercise.title: Why is a small change between successive approximations not a proof?

statement.p: One experiment keeps doubling n until two successive approximations differ by less than a tolerance. In your own words, why is that difference useful evidence, and why is it still not the same thing as an error bound?

hint.p: Two close wrong answers can agree with each other. Stabilization supports confidence; a theorem or independent estimate supplies a guarantee.

subsection.title: Experiment 4: build a small numerical-integration program
subsection.p: A numerical method becomes clearer when you implement it yourself.
The goal is not to build a professional scientific library. The goal is to translate the formulas into an algorithm and test the algorithm on examples where you know what should happen.

note.title: What the project tests
note.p: A numerical answer should not arrive alone. It should come with checks:

p.me: \text{Does the algorithm reproduce simple exact cases?}
\text{Do the observed errors match the smoothness of the function?}
\text{Does the code enforce the hypotheses of the rule?}

exercise.title: Why should a numerical program reproduce simple exact cases?

statement.p: Before trusting a homemade integrator on a hard integral, we test it on cases whose exact values we know. In your own words, why is that a mathematical check and not just a programming convenience?

hint.p: If the code cannot recover a line, a quadratic, or another exact case the rule should get right, later decimals have no authority.

subsection.title: A final computational habit
subsection.p: Numerical computation is not button pressing. It is mathematical experimentation with responsibility.
For every numerical answer, ask:

li.p: What exact quantity is being approximated?
Which rule or algorithm produced the approximation?
What hypotheses does the rule need?
What error estimate or stability evidence supports the answer?
What simple test case confirms that the implementation is working?

subsection.p: This chapter began with numerical integration: approximating accumulated quantities. It then returned to numerical root-finding: approximating solutions of equations.
Both examples illustrate the need to test a stopping criterion against a known reference.

p.me: \text{An approximation is useful only when we understand its error.}

subsection.p: The next chapter carries this lesson into a new setting. A differential equation gives a law for a derivative, but the unknown function may not have a formula we can write down. Then we must do for functions what we have done for numbers and integrals: build approximations step by step, and ask how much to trust them.

exercise.title: What five questions should travel with every numerical answer?

statement.p: The section ends with a computational habit: name the exact quantity, the rule, the hypotheses, the error evidence, and a test case. In your own words, why would omitting any one of those five leave the answer incomplete?

hint.p: A decimal without a method, a method without hypotheses, or a result without a check is still only a number with arithmetic attached.

subsection.p: For further numerical methods, the optional sections and derive extrapolation and provide a complete adaptive algorithm with a stopping rule and explicit failure conditions.

introduction.p: These problems compare numerical integration rules, finite-difference derivatives, and Newton iteration. For each approximation, identify the exact quantity, the algorithm, its hypotheses, and the available error evidence.

subsection.p: The error estimates have hypotheses. Those hypotheses are not decoration. The midpoint and trapezoidal bounds need a bounded second derivative. Simpson’s bound needs a bounded fourth derivative. Newton’s fast convergence needs a simple root and a good starting point. Numerical differentiation is sensitive to roundoff because it subtracts nearly equal numbers.
A method can still produce a number when its hypotheses fail. The guarantee is what may fail.

exercise.title: What common idea unites the chapter’s methods?

statement.p: Midpoint, trapezoid, Simpson, finite differences, and Newton’s method all replace a difficult object by a simpler local picture. In your own words, what is that common idea, and why is controlling the error as important as producing the approximation?

hint.p: Local information can produce global understanding only if we know how large the replacement error might be.

exercise.title: Why is numerical integration usually more forgiving than numerical differentiation?

statement.p: Integration averages values over an interval. Differentiation subtracts nearby values and divides by a small step. In your own words, why do those two personalities lead to different computational warnings?

hint.p: Averaging can reduce noise. Subtracting nearly equal values and dividing by a small step magnifies roundoff and measurement noise. For a sufficiently smooth function, shrinking the step reduces truncation error, so these competing errors require a balance.

note.title: End-of-chapter habit
note.p: For every numerical answer, ask four questions:

p.me: \text{What evidence or theorem supports the claimed accuracy?}

subsection.p: The next section turns this habit toward a new kind of problem. So far, numerical methods have mostly produced numbers: values of integrals, derivatives, and roots. But many laws of science ask for more than one number. They ask for a whole unknown function.

section.title: Additional topics: Richardson and Romberg methods

introduction.p: When an approximation has a known leading error term in the step size, two mesh sizes can be combined to cancel that term. This optional section derives Richardson extrapolation and applies it repeatedly to the trapezoidal rule to obtain Romberg integration. The improved orders require the stated error expansion and sufficient smoothness.

subsection.title: Cancel a leading error term
subsection.p: Suppose an approximation to I has the expansion

where the same coefficient c applies at h and h/2. Here O(h^s) means an absolute value bounded by a fixed constant times h^s for all sufficiently small positive h. Then A(h/2)=I+c h^p/2^p+O(h^{p+r}). Multiplying the finer value by 2^p and subtracting cancels the leading error:
This is Richardson extrapolation. In the same regime,
The difference gives an error estimate only while the assumed expansion describes the actual calculation. Cancellation, insufficient smoothness, or rounding can invalidate this interpretation.

example.title: Improve a numerical derivative
example.p: If f has five continuous derivatives near x, finite Taylor expansions give
Thus (4D(h/2)-D(h))/3 approximates f'(x) with error O(h^4). This does not remove the division by a small number: at very small h, subtracting nearly equal function values can make rounding dominate.

subsection.title: Repeated extrapolation of trapezoidal rules
subsection.p: For a sufficiently smooth function on [a,b], the composite trapezoidal rule has an expansion in even powers of its uniform mesh width:

One sufficient condition for this expansion through the displayed order is that f have 2m+2 continuous derivatives on the interval. It comes from Taylor expansion on the panels and summing their endpoint contributions. The first coefficient is c_2=(f'(b)-f'(a))/12; symmetry removes the odd powers. This expansion is stronger information than the trapezoidal error bound alone.
Let h_k=(b-a)/2^k. Set R_{k,0}=T(h_k) and form the triangular Romberg table by

Column j cancels the leading error of order h^{2j} from the preceding column. For fixed j and sufficient smoothness, its error is O(h_k^{2j+2}) as the mesh shrinks. Finite-precision diagonal entries need not improve at every refinement.
Each refinement reuses previous function values:
Only the newly inserted midpoints are evaluated. The first extrapolated column is exactly the composite Simpson rule on that grid: R_{k,1}=(4T(h_k)-T(2h_k))/3.

example.title: An exactly checkable table
example.p: For f(x)=x^4 on [0,1], I=1/5 and direct finite summation gives T(h)=1/5+h^2/3-h^4/30.
The second extrapolation cancels the h^4 term, leaving the exact integral in exact arithmetic.

paragraphs.title: A practical stopping policy
paragraphs.p: Choose a tolerance \tau=\tau_{\rm abs}+\tau_{\rm rel}|R_{k,k}| with \tau_{\rm abs}>0, \tau_{\rm rel}\ge0. One policy requires at least three refinements and two consecutive diagonal changes below the current tolerance. Also impose a maximum refinement level and function-evaluation budget, reject nonfinite values, and stop with a failure report if the mesh cannot be represented or the changes cease decreasing while the tolerance is unmet. Report the latest diagonal change as an estimate, not a certified bound. A known derivative bound or other rigorous remainder estimate is needed for a certified stopping decision.

warning.title: The expansion has hypotheses
warning.p: For f(x)=\sqrt{x} on [0,1], derivatives blow up at zero and the usual even-power expansion is unavailable. Applying the Romberg recurrence is still possible, but the advertised orders no longer follow. Increasing the table depth cannot repair an unjustified error model.

exercise.title: Derive and test an extrapolation

statement.p: If A(h)=I+ch^3+O(h^4), find the Richardson combination. Build the first three Romberg rows for \int_0^1x^2\,dx. Which column first gives the exact result, and why?

hint.p: Use (8A(h/2)-A(h))/7. For the quadratic, T(h)=1/3+h^2/6, so the first extrapolated column is exact.

section.title: Additional topics: a complete adaptive quadrature algorithm

introduction.p: The computing experiments refined a uniform grid. Adaptive quadrature instead subdivides individual intervals where an error indicator is large. This optional section supplies a complete adaptive Simpson algorithm, an absolute-tolerance stopping rule, and explicit failure safeguards. Its Richardson estimate uses .

subsection.title: Compare one panel with two
subsection.p: On [a,b], put m=(a+b)/2 and
Compare S_1=S(a,b) with S_2=S(a,m)+S(m,b). In the smooth asymptotic regime, halving the mesh reduces the leading Simpson error by a factor of 16. Therefore

The difference divided by 15 estimates the error of S_2; the correction Q cancels its leading term. With a smooth enough integrand, Q has a higher order than S_2. We retain the more conservative indicator E for accepting the interval.

Give the whole interval an absolute error budget \tau>0. When an interval is split, give each child half its parent's budget. Accept a leaf when its indicator is at most its budget. The leaf budgets sum to \tau, so the sum of the accepted indicators is at most \tau. This is an accounting guarantee for the indicators, not a theorem that every possible integrand has that actual error.

subsection.title: An implementation with explicit outcomes
subsection.p: The following Python implementation assumes a finite-valued integrand throughout a finite interval a<b. It returns the approximation, the summed error indicator, the number of function evaluations, and the accepted intervals. It uses a stack rather than unbounded recursion, reuses parent samples, and performs at least two subdivision levels by default to reduce premature acceptance. Exhausting the depth or evaluation budget, encountering a nonfinite value, or losing representable midpoints raises a failure instead of reporting success. The roundoff indicator 50\epsilon_{\rm mach}(|S_L|+|S_R|) is a practical scale check, where \epsilon_{\rm mach} is the spacing from one to the next larger floating-point number. It is not a bound on all floating-point errors.
subsection.pre:
"""Executable numerical examples accompanying the selected PreTeXt additions.""" from math import isfinite, fsum from sys import float_info
def adaptive_simpson(f, a, b, tol, max_depth=20, max_evals=100000, min_depth=2): """Return (value, estimated_error, evaluations, accepted_intervals).
Error is an estimator, not a rigorous bound for arbitrary functions. Fail explicitly on invalid inputs or exhausted safeguards. """ if not all(isfinite(v) for v in (a, b, tol, b-a)): raise ValueError("Require finite endpoints, width, and tolerance") if not a < b or not tol > 0: raise ValueError("Require a < b and tol > 0") if (type(min_depth) is not int or type(max_depth) is not int or not 0 <= min_depth <= max_depth or type(max_evals) is not int or max_evals < 3): raise ValueError("Invalid depth or evaluation budget") evaluations = 0
def sample(x): nonlocal evaluations if evaluations >= max_evals: raise ArithmeticError("Evaluation budget exhausted") evaluations += 1 value = f(x) if not isfinite(value): raise ArithmeticError("Nonfinite function value") return value
def midpoint(left, right): mid = left + (right-left)/2 if not left < mid < right: raise ArithmeticError("No representable midpoint") return mid
def simpson(left, right, fl, fm, fr): value = ((right-left)/6)*fsum((fl, 4*fm, fr)) if not isfinite(value): raise ArithmeticError("Nonfinite quadrature value") return value
m = midpoint(a, b) fa, fm, fb = sample(a), sample(m), sample(b) coarse = simpson(a, b, fa, fm, fb) stack = [(a, b, fa, fm, fb, coarse, tol, 0)] values, errors, intervals = [], [], [] while stack: left, right, fl, fm, fr, old, budget, depth = stack.pop() mid = midpoint(left, right) lm, rm = midpoint(left, mid), midpoint(mid, right) f_lm, f_rm = sample(lm), sample(rm) sl = simpson(left, mid, fl, f_lm, fm) sr = simpson(mid, right, fm, f_rm, fr) fine = fsum((sl, sr)) delta = fine-old floor = 50*float_info.epsilon*(abs(sl)+abs(sr)) estimate = max(abs(delta)/15, floor) corrected = fine+delta/15 if not all(isfinite(v) for v in (fine, estimate, corrected)): raise ArithmeticError("Nonfinite refinement result") if depth >= min_depth and estimate <= budget: values.append(corrected) errors.append(estimate) intervals.append((left, right)) continue if depth >= max_depth: raise ArithmeticError("Maximum subdivision depth reached") if depth >= min_depth and budget < floor: raise ArithmeticError("Tolerance below roundoff indicator") half_budget = budget/2 if half_budget == 0: raise ArithmeticError("Tolerance budget underflow") # Right child first: the left child is processed next. stack.append((mid, right, fm, f_rm, fr, sr, half_budget, depth+1)) stack.append((left, mid, fl, f_lm, fm, sl, half_budget, depth+1)) value, error = fsum(values), fsum(errors) if not isfinite(value) or not isfinite(error) or error > tol: raise ArithmeticError("Final accumulation failed") return value, error, evaluations, intervals
subsection.p: The stopping rule is implemented in the acceptance branch and checked again after accumulation. The minimum depth does not override the maximum depth, and all resource limits have explicit outcomes. If the routine fails, increase resources only after examining the reason; a singularity or unattainable tolerance may require a change of variables or an analytic treatment.

subsection.title: Test cases and the limits of sampling

example.title: A known integral
example.p: Calling adaptive_simpson(lambda x: 4/(1+x*x), 0, 1, 1e-8) approximates \pi. Compare the returned value with \pi and record the indicator and evaluation count. For a more localized problem, try f(x)=e^{-2500(x-0.37)^2} on [0,1] and plot the accepted interval widths. Small intervals should cluster near the peak. Compare with a high-accuracy reference calculation; do not infer accuracy from the indicator alone.

warning.title: A small indicator cannot certify an arbitrary function
warning.p: On [0,1], the nonnegative polynomial

vanishes at every point sampled before the default minimum-depth acceptance decisions. The algorithm can return zero with zero indicator, although the integral is positive. This is sampling aliasing: the data miss the behavior between samples. More initial panels, independent shifted samples, and known breakpoints reduce the risk; no finite sampling scheme alone certifies all continuous functions.

paragraphs.title: How a derivative bound changes the guarantee
paragraphs.p: If a valid bound |f^{(4)}|\le K is known on a leaf of width w, the two-panel Simpson value S_2 has the rigorous exact-arithmetic bound

Each half-panel contributes at most K(w/2)^5/2880, and adding the two bounds gives this constant. A certified variant accepts leaves using this derivative bound and returns the uncorrected S_2, summing the valid leaf bounds. It must also account for floating-point evaluation and accumulation errors. The corrected value Q requires its own error analysis; the bound for S_2 cannot simply be attached to it.

exercise.title: Test success and failure paths

statement.p: Check the routine on 1,x,x^2,x^3,x^4 over [0,1]. Force separate failures with an evaluation budget of three, maximum depth zero, a nonfinite function value, and adjacent floating-point endpoints. Use \int_0^1x^k\,dx=1/(k+1) as the reference. Explain why the aliasing example is a more demanding test than the cubic examples.

hint.p: For the depth test set min_depth=0 and use a noncubic integrand with a small tolerance. Cubics are exactly integrated by Simpson's rule in exact arithmetic. The aliasing polynomial has positive area but supplies zeros at all sampled points, so exact sample arithmetic would still miss it.

chapter.title: Differential Equations: Laws Written as Derivatives

introduction.p: A differential equation specifies a relation involving an unknown function and its derivatives. Initial conditions specify the starting values. We will formulate rate models, solve several important equation types, and use direction fields and numerical methods when an explicit solution is unavailable.

To model a changing quantity with a differential equation, express its rate in terms of time, the current state, or other changing quantities. The unknown is the function that satisfies that rate equation and the given initial conditions.

subsection.title: A law that gives a rate
subsection.p: A hot cup of coffee cools quickly when it is much hotter than the room. Later, when it is only a little warmer than the room, it cools slowly.
That observation is the heart of Newton’s law of cooling:

p.me: \text{rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference}.

note.title: A differential equation
note.p: A differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives.
The equation
is a first-order differential equation because it involves the first derivative T', but not higher derivatives such as T''.

subsection.p: The equation does not yet tell us the temperature at every time. It tells us how the temperature should be changing once the temperature is known.
That is the new kind of problem.

exercise.title: What does it mean to write a law as a derivative?

statement.p: A differential equation specifies y' rather than y itself. In your own words, why is that a natural way to write a scientific law, and what extra information is needed before a unique solution is determined?

hint.p: Many laws say how a quantity is changing, not what its current value is. An initial condition picks one graph from a family.

subsection.title: Solution as an unknown function
subsection.p: A solution of a differential equation is a function that makes the equation true.
Start with a simpler equation:
This says that the rate of change of y depends on the current value of y.
If y is below 1, then 1-y>0, so the solution should rise.
If y is above 1, then 1-y<0, so the solution should fall.
If y=1, then 1-y=0, so the solution should stay flat.
Before solving the equation by a method, we can check proposed functions.

example.p: The same differential equation has many solutions. That should not be surprising. An antiderivative also comes with a constant C. A differential equation often gives a whole family of possible functions.

note.title: Solution of a differential equation
note.p: A function y(t) is a solution of a differential equation on an interval I if y is differentiable on I and the equation is true for every t in I.

subsection.p: The interval matters. A formula may solve an equation on one interval but fail to make sense on another. This is the same domain discipline we used for logarithms, square roots, inverse trigonometric functions, and improper integrals.

paragraphs.p: These are not equal for all t. They agree only when
A differential equation must hold on an interval, not just at one point. Therefore

exercise.title: What does it mean for a function to solve a differential equation?

statement.p: The same equation y'=1-y is solved both by 1-e^{-t} and by 1+2e^{-t}, while y=1+t is not a solution. In your own words, what must be true on an interval for a proposed function to count as a solution, and why is agreement at a single point not enough?

hint.p: Substitute the function and its derivative into the equation. The identity must hold for every t in an interval, not just at one instant.

note.p: An initial value problem combines a differential equation with a starting value. For example,
The differential equation gives the law of change. The initial condition tells which solution curve we are on.

exercise.title: Why does an initial condition select one history from a family?

statement.p: The functions y=1+Ce^{-t} all solve y'=1-y. In your own words, what does the differential equation determine, what does y(0)=y_0 determine, and why should that pair be called an initial value problem?

hint.p: The equation gives the law of change. The starting value tells which solution curve we are on.

subsection.title: Checking a proposed solution
subsection.p: Checking a solution is often easier than finding one. It is also one of the best ways to understand what the equation means.

note.title: How to check a proposed solution
note.p: To check a proposed solution of a differential equation:

li.p: State the interval where the function is being considered.
Differentiate the proposed function.
Substitute the function and its derivative into the differential equation.
Check that the equation is true for every point of the interval.
If there is an initial condition, check it separately.

example.title: checking a cooling model
example.p: Suppose the room temperature is 20^\circ\text{C}, and the proposed coffee temperature is

paragraphs.title: What the formula says
paragraphs.p: The number 20 is the equilibrium temperature. The term
is the remaining temperature difference above the room. It decays toward 0, so
The coffee approaches room temperature. It does not pass below it in this model.

note.title: A model check
note.p: A solution should satisfy the differential equation, the initial condition, and the behavior of the situation. Algebra alone is not enough if the model’s interpretation has been forgotten.

paragraphs.p: Many differential equations cannot be solved by guessing a familiar formula. But even without a formula, the equation still gives information. Since
tells the slope a solution must have at each point (t,y), we can draw those slopes. That picture is the next step.

exercise.title: Why is checking a proposed solution part of understanding the model?

statement.p: Checking a formula is often easier than finding one. In your own words, what should a complete check include besides differentiation and substitution, and why is algebra alone not enough if the interpretation has been forgotten?

hint.p: State the interval, check the differential equation, check any initial condition, and ask whether the long-term behavior matches the situation.

subsection.p: The little segments are not solution curves. They are instructions for solution curves. A true solution curve must pass through the field by matching the local direction at each point.

note.title: Direction field
note.p: For a differential equation
a direction field or slope field is a plot of small line segments, where the segment at (t,y) has slope F(t,y).

subsection.p: The direction field is especially helpful when the equation is hard to solve exactly. It can show whether solutions rise or fall, whether they approach a stable value, and how different initial conditions change the behavior.

exercise.title: What is a direction field a picture of?

statement.p: The equation y'=F(t,y) assigns a slope to each point (t,y). In your own words, why are the little segments not themselves solution curves, and what instruction do they give to any true solution that passes through a point?

hint.p: Each segment is a local direction, not a whole history. A solution curve must match the prescribed slope at every point it visits.

subsection.p: Some solutions do not move at all.

For an autonomous equation, all points with the same y-value have the same slope. That is why the direction field in looks the same across each horizontal row.

exercise.title: What is an equilibrium solution?

statement.p: For y'=1-y, the constant function y=1 is a solution. In your own words, why does a constant solution correspond to a place where the right-hand side is zero, and what extra feature does an autonomous equation y'=f(y) give the picture?

hint.p: If y never changes, then y'=0, so F(t,c)=0. In an autonomous equation, every point at the same height has the same slope.

subsection.title: Qualitative behavior
subsection.p: A direction field can tell us how solutions behave without giving exact formulas.
For
the sign of y' depends on whether y is below, equal to, or above 1.
So the line
acts like an attracting level. Solutions below it rise toward it. Solutions above it fall toward it.
We can read this from the equation, from the sign table, or from the direction field. The three views agree.

exercise.title: What can you read from a direction field without a formula?

statement.p: A sign chart or a field can say whether solutions rise, fall, or approach a level. In your own words, what kind of question is that qualitative information answering, and what kind of question does it deliberately not answer?

hint.p: Long-term trend and shape often come from the sign of y'. Exact values at a specific time usually require a formula or a numerical method.

subsection.title: Reading long-term behavior from the field
subsection.p: A direction field can answer questions that do not require an exact formula.
For
the field shows that solutions approach
as t increases. The field also shows that the approach slows down, because slopes near y=1 are small.
For
the sign chart shows:
and
These conclusions are qualitative. They tell the shape and long-term trend, not the exact value at a specific time.
That is often enough for a first understanding of a model. Before computing, we should know what kind of behavior to expect.

paragraphs.title: Warning: the physical domain matters
paragraphs.p: may be used for a normalized population. In that interpretation,
does not make physical sense. The equation still has mathematical behavior there, but the model should not be interpreted as a population model for negative y.
A differential equation is not the world. It is a model of selected features of the world.

paragraphs.title: Warning: a direction field is not a uniqueness proof
paragraphs.p: A direction field can suggest that one solution curve passes through each point. For many equations in this chapter, that is true. But it is not automatic.
For t<0, both sides are 0. At t=0, the derivative is also 0. So this piecewise function solves the same initial value problem.
Two different solution curves pass through the same initial point.

warning.title: What the warning teaches
warning.p: A direction field is a powerful picture, but it is still a picture. Clean uniqueness requires hypotheses on the function F(t,y). In this chapter, our examples will be well behaved, but we should remember that the warning exists.

paragraphs.p: The direction field gives the geometry of a differential equation. The next question is computational. If the field tells us the slope at every point, can we follow those slopes one small step at a time and build an approximate solution curve?
That step-by-step method is Euler’s method.

exercise.title: Why is a direction field not a uniqueness proof?

statement.p: A field may look as if one curve passes through each point, yet y'=\sqrt{|y|} with y(0)=0 has more than one solution. In your own words, what does the picture fail to guarantee, and why does the physical domain of a model matter even when the mathematics continues?

hint.p: Clean uniqueness needs hypotheses on F(t,y). A model of population, for example, should not be interpreted for negative values even if the equation still has behavior there.

introduction.p: Euler's method approximates a solution of y\prime=F(t,y) by repeated tangent-line steps. With step size h, it uses y_{n+1}=y_n+hF(t_n,y_n). We will compute these steps and examine how the step size affects accuracy.

subsection.p: Euler’s method is simple because it uses only the slope at the beginning of each step. That simplicity is also its weakness.

exercise.title: What local idea is Euler’s method repeating?

statement.p: The derivative gives y(x+h)\approx y(x)+y'(x)h. In your own words, why does substituting the differential equation y'=F(x,y) turn that approximation into a step-by-step method, and why is using only the slope at the beginning of each step both a strength and a weakness?

hint.p: The new value is the old value plus slope times step. The method is simple because it uses one slope; it is crude because that slope may change during the step.

subsection.title: Step size and accumulated error
subsection.p: Euler’s method makes a small error at each step. Then it uses the approximate point from that step to compute the next slope. So errors do not merely appear; they can accumulate.
For the same problem,
we can approximate y(2) with several step sizes.
The smaller step sizes give better approximations here. This is what we hope for: more, shorter tangent-line steps should trace the solution curve more faithfully.
But there is a cost. Smaller steps require more computation.
while
The tradeoff is familiar from numerical integration:

p.em: smaller step size \Longrightarrow usually smaller error, but more work.

subsection.p: Accuracy improves under the convergence hypotheses as the step shrinks. A large step can instead produce behavior inconsistent with the exact solution.

paragraphs.title: A large-step warning
paragraphs.p: It stays positive and decays toward 0.
They alternate signs and grow in size. That is the opposite of the true solution.
The differential equation describes stable decay. The numerical method, with a large step, creates fake instability.

warning.title: Numerical warning
warning.p: A differential equation and a numerical method are different objects. The equation may have one behavior, while a poor step size in the method can produce another.

paragraphs.p: Choose the step size using accuracy and stability considerations, and compare the numerical behavior with the direction field.

exercise.title: Why can a large Euler step invent false behavior?

statement.p: For y\prime=-4y, a large Euler step can produce growing oscillations although the exact solution decays. Explain how the numerical update produces this discrepancy.

hint.p: Each Euler value is approximate, and the next slope is evaluated at that value. A large step may therefore lead to behavior inconsistent with the direction field.

subsection.p: This method is also called Heun’s method. It is not the most powerful numerical method for differential equations, but it fixes one clear defect of Euler’s method: it does not rely only on the starting slope.

exercise.title: What extra information does improved Euler use?

statement.p: Improved Euler averages a beginning slope with an estimated ending slope. In your own words, why should that be a better representative of the whole step, and what computational price does the improvement pay?

hint.p: If the slope changes during the interval, the starting slope alone is biased. Averaging uses two evaluations of F per step instead of one.

The price is also clear. Ordinary Euler evaluates F once per step. Improved Euler evaluates F twice per step. Better information usually costs more computation.

This distinction matters.

note.title: What Euler’s method teaches
note.p: A differential equation gives local instructions. Euler’s method turns those instructions into a path by repeating one simple idea:

subsection.p: This is enough when no exact formula is available. But sometimes the equation itself contains a hidden integral. In those cases, we can do better than following short tangent steps. We can solve the equation exactly.
The first such equations are separable.

exercise.title: Why is an Euler table an approximate function, not only a number?

statement.p: Euler’s method produces a list of points rather than a formula such as y=1-e^{-x}. In your own words, why should a report of y(2)\approx0.9375 name the method and the step size, and what object is being approximated besides a single value?

hint.p: Connecting the points gives a piecewise linear path. The output is an approximate solution curve, so the method, step size, and interval belong in the answer.

introduction.p: A separable differential equation has the form y\prime=g(t)h(y). On intervals where h(y)\ne0, divide by h(y) and integrate to obtain an implicit relation between t and y. Check the zeros of h separately, since they may give equilibrium solutions lost by division.

note.p: When you divide by an expression involving y, separately check the values of y that make that expression zero. They often give equilibrium solutions.

note.title: Implicit solution
note.p: An implicit solution of a differential equation is an equation involving x and y whose differentiable branches satisfy the differential equation.
An explicit solution gives y directly as a function of x. An implicit solution may leave x and y tied together.

example.title: a family of hyperbolas
example.p: This implicit equation has two branches:
The initial condition y(0)=2 selects the upper branch:

paragraphs.title: Domains still matter
paragraphs.p: Solving a differential equation is not just manipulating symbols until a formula appears. A solution must live on an interval where the function is differentiable and the equation makes sense.
A formula without a domain is not yet a complete solution.

note.title: What separable equations give us
note.p: Separation turns some differential equations into integral problems. It connects this chapter back to the Fundamental Theorem:

p.em: a law for a derivative \Longrightarrow an integral relation \Longrightarrow a solution curve.

paragraphs.p: The next separable model has two equilibrium solutions instead of one. It grows almost exponentially at first, slows as it approaches a limit, and has a characteristic slow--fast--slow shape.
That model is the logistic equation.

exercise.title: When is an implicit equation a legitimate solution?

statement.p: Separation may produce a relation such as y+y^3/3=x^2/2 instead of a formula y=f(x). In your own words, why can that still be a solution, and why is a formula without a domain still incomplete?

hint.p: Differentiating the implicit relation can recover the differential equation. A solution must live on an interval where the function is differentiable and the original equation makes sense.

introduction.p: For an autonomous equation y\prime=f(y), zeros of f give equilibria and its sign determines whether solutions increase or decrease. A phase line organizes this information without requiring an explicit formula. We will apply it to logistic and threshold population models.

subsection.title: Carrying capacity
subsection.p: Pure exponential growth says
The rate is proportional to the current population. That can describe early growth, when resources are plentiful. It cannot describe growth forever.
A population in a fixed environment has limited food, space, or available hosts. The model should slow down as the population approaches a maximum sustainable size.

exercise.title: Why does logistic growth slow as it approaches a carrying capacity?

statement.p: Explain the roles of rP and 1-P/K in the logistic equation. Why does the exponential model approximate early growth when P\ll K but fail to model a fixed carrying capacity?

hint.p: When P is much smaller than K, the slowing factor is near 1. When P=K, growth stops because remaining capacity is gone.

note.title: Phase line
note.p: For an autonomous equation
a phase line marks the equilibrium values f(y)=0 and uses arrows to show where y'>0 and where y'<0.

subsection.p: A phase line is a compressed direction field. Since the slope depends only on y, the whole plane can be summarized on one vertical axis.

paragraphs.title: A threshold model
paragraphs.p: The logistic equation says that any small positive population grows. Some populations do not behave that way. If the population is too small, individuals may have trouble finding mates, protecting each other, or maintaining enough genetic variety. Below a threshold, the population may decline.

figure.caption: In a threshold model, the population must start above A to move toward the carrying capacity K.

description.p: In a threshold model, the population must start above A to move toward the carrying capacity K.

paragraphs.p: The threshold model has different equilibria and sign intervals from the logistic model.
The value A is a tipping threshold. Starting just above it and starting just below it lead to opposite long-term outcomes.

exercise.title: What information is compressed into a phase line?

statement.p: For an autonomous equation y'=f(y), a phase line marks equilibria and uses arrows to show rise or fall. In your own words, why can one vertical axis summarize the whole direction field, and what does that picture tell you before any formula is found?

hint.p: If the slope depends only on y, every horizontal row of the plane looks the same. The arrows already predict long-term approach or departure.

subsection.title: Stable and unstable equilibria
subsection.p: An equilibrium solution is a constant solution. But not all equilibria behave the same way.
For
an equilibrium y=c occurs when
The arrows near c decide whether nearby solutions move toward c or away from it.

note.title: Stable and unstable equilibrium
note.p: An equilibrium y=c is stable if solutions starting sufficiently close to c stay as close as desired for all forward time. It is asymptotically stable if it is stable and all sufficiently nearby solutions also converge to c. The attracting equilibria below are asymptotically stable.
It is unstable if it fails the stability condition: some arbitrarily nearby starting values leave a fixed neighborhood in forward time.

subsection.p: For the logistic equation,
the equilibrium P=K is stable. Solutions below K move upward, and solutions above K move downward.
The equilibrium P=0 is unstable. A solution that starts exactly at 0 stays there, but a solution that starts slightly above 0 moves away from 0.
For the threshold model,
the equilibrium P=A is unstable. A tiny change in the initial condition can change the long-term outcome.
while
The threshold A is not a resting place that attracts the population. It is a dividing line.

note.title: What stability means in a model
note.p: A stable equilibrium is forgiving: small errors in the starting value still lead back to it.
An unstable equilibrium is delicate: small errors in the starting value move the solution away from it.

subsection.p: This matters in applications. A population near a stable carrying capacity can recover from small disturbances. A population near an unstable threshold may not.

exercise.title: What is the difference between a stable equilibrium and a threshold?

statement.p: In the logistic model, P=K attracts nearby solutions, while P=0 does not. In a threshold model, starting just above or just below A leads to opposite futures. In your own words, what does stability mean for a model, and why is an unstable threshold a dividing line rather than a resting place?

hint.p: A stable equilibrium is forgiving of small errors in the starting value. An unstable one is delicate: nearby solutions move away, so the long-term outcome can flip.

subsection.title: Harvesting and tipping points
subsection.p: A fish population may grow logistically, but people may also remove fish by harvesting. A simple constant-harvest model is
where
The term
is natural growth. The term h is removal.
Equilibria occur when
So the equilibrium populations are intersection points between the logistic growth curve and the horizontal harvest line.
The growth curve
is a parabola. Its maximum occurs at
The maximum value is
This number is the largest sustainable constant harvest in the model.

figure.caption: A constant harvest is sustainable only if the harvest line meets the natural growth curve.

description.p: A constant harvest is sustainable only if the harvest line meets the natural growth curve.

example.title: Example
example.p: Move all terms to one side:
To determine stability, examine the sign of
When P<200, the harvest is larger than natural growth, so
When 200<P<800, natural growth is larger than harvest, so
When P>800, natural growth is again smaller than harvest, so
Thus P=200 is unstable, and P=800 is stable.
The lower equilibrium is a threshold. If the population falls below 200, the model predicts decline toward extinction. If the population stays above 200, it can recover toward 800.

paragraphs.title: Three harvesting regimes
paragraphs.p: The middle case is delicate. If
For K=1000 and r=0.6, this becomes
for every P, and equality occurs only at P=500. A population starting above 500 decreases toward 500. A population starting below 500 decreases away from 500 toward extinction.

warning.title: Model warning
warning.p: The equation
continues mathematically below P=0, but the population model does not.
If the population reaches extinction, harvesting cannot continue at the same constant rate. The physical domain P\ge0 is part of the model.

paragraphs.p: The logistic and threshold models show why a differential equation is more than a formula to solve. It is a field of tendencies. It tells what the system tries to do from each starting value.

The next class of equations has a different structure. It may include an outside input, such as salt entering a tank or money deposited into an account. The equation is not always separable, but the product rule gives it a way forward.

exercise.title: Why can a constant harvest create a tipping point?

statement.p: For P\prime=rP(1-P/K)-h, equilibria occur where logistic growth equals the harvest rate. Explain why the maximum of the growth term gives the largest sustainable constant harvest and what happens when h exceeds it.

hint.p: The growth parabola has a maximum. If the harvest line misses that curve, there is no positive equilibrium, and harvesting exceeds natural growth. The model also stops making sense at extinction.

introduction.p: A first-order linear equation has the form y\prime+p(t)y=q(t), where p and q are known functions. Such equations model a current amount affected by an outside input, as in mixing tanks, deposits with interest, or cooling in a changing environment. An integrating factor reduces the equation to a product derivative.

subsection.title: Mixing and finance examples
subsection.p: Linear equations appear whenever there is a current amount and an outside input.

paragraphs.title: Why the interval matters
paragraphs.p: The formula assumes that p(t) and q(t) are continuous on the interval where we solve the equation. If a coefficient breaks, the solution may have to be handled on separate intervals.

warning.title: Coefficient warning
warning.p: A solution of a differential equation lives on an interval where the equation makes sense. Singular coefficients split the real line into separate problems.

paragraphs.p: First-order equations already show several personalities. Some are separable. Some are linear. Some are best understood by a phase line. Some require numerical methods.
But many laws of motion do not stop at the first derivative. A spring, a pendulum in a small-angle approximation, and a vibrating string involve acceleration. Their laws begin with
That is the next door: differential equations where the unknown function is governed by its second derivative.

exercise.title: Why can a singular coefficient split one equation into separate problems?

statement.p: The equation y'+(1/t)y=1 is linear, but 1/t is undefined at t=0. In your own words, why must a solution live on an interval where the equation makes sense, and why does a formula such as y=t/2+C/t require special attention at zero even when C=0?

hint.p: Continuous coefficients are part of the hypotheses. A singularity of p(t) or q(t) is a wall between intervals, not a point to be crossed casually.

introduction.p: Newton's second law relates force to acceleration, so motion models often involve the second derivative of position. For a mass attached to a spring, the restoring force gives a second-order equation. We will solve constant-coefficient examples and relate their solutions to oscillation and damping.

statement.p: Hooke’s law gives a force F=-ky, and Newton’s second law converts force into acceleration. In your own words, why does that produce y''+\omega^2 y=0, and what sentence about acceleration and displacement is the heart of simple harmonic motion?

paragraphs.title: Energy check
paragraphs.p: The undamped spring keeps oscillating because no energy is lost.
The first term is kinetic energy. The second is spring potential energy.
The energy moves back and forth between motion and spring stretch. It does not disappear.

exercise.title: Why does a second-order equation need two starting values?

statement.p: The general solution y=C_1\cos(\omega t)+C_2\sin(\omega t) has two constants. In your own words, why is position alone not enough to determine the future of a spring, and what second piece of initial data is required?

hint.p: Motion needs both where the mass is and how fast it is moving. A mass at equilibrium may stay there or pass through with high speed.

subsection.title: Damping
subsection.p: Real vibrations usually die down. A guitar string grows quiet. A shock absorber settles after a bump. A swinging door stops swinging.
The missing ingredient is damping.
Damping is a force that opposes velocity. A simple model is
The spring force is still

The mass m resists acceleration, the damping coefficient c resists velocity, and the spring constant k resists displacement.

subsection.p: For light damping, the motion still oscillates, but the oscillations shrink. One common form of such a solution is

paragraphs.title: Energy with damping
paragraphs.p: Energy decreases, except at instants when y'=0. The damping term drains energy from the motion.

exercise.title: How does damping change the energy?

statement.p: Without friction, energy moves back and forth between motion and spring stretch. With a damping term -cy', oscillations typically shrink. In your own words, why does a force that opposes velocity drain energy, and what role does the decaying exponential envelope play?

hint.p: Damping resists velocity, so it does negative work. The factor e^{-\beta t} shrinks the oscillating amplitude.

subsection.p: A system can also be forced from outside. A child on a swing is pushed. A bridge is hit by periodic wind. A guitar string is driven by a vibrating body.

note.title: Resonance, first view
note.p: A system resonates when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency. The forcing then reinforces the natural motion instead of fighting it.
