subsection.p: Real systems have damping, so the amplitude does not grow forever. But the warning survives: forcing near the natural frequency can create a much larger response than forcing far from it.

warning.title: Model warning
warning.p: The equation
predicts unbounded growth at resonance because it ignores damping and structural limits. It is a warning model, not a complete physical description.

subsection.p: Second-order equations already show that the state of a system may need more than one number. A spring is not determined by position alone. To know what happens next, we also need velocity.
That idea leads naturally to systems of differential equations.

exercise.title: What does it mean for a driven oscillator to resonate?

statement.p: When the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency, the undamped response amplitude can become large. In your own words, why does that happen, and why is the unbounded-growth model a warning rather than a complete physical description?

hint.p: Forcing then reinforces the natural motion instead of fighting it. Real systems have damping and structural limits, so amplitude does not grow forever.

introduction.p: When the state has several components, their rates form a system of differential equations. A spring can be described by position and velocity; interacting populations require one variable for each population. The equations couple those components through their rates of change.

subsection.title: Two populations
subsection.p: A single population model may look like
That can describe a species living alone with plentiful resources. But species do not usually live alone. They compete, cooperate, eat, flee, and depend on one another.
Let
and
The rabbits are prey. The wolves are predators.
If there were no wolves, the rabbits might grow approximately exponentially:
If there were no rabbits, the wolves might decline:
But when both are present, they meet. The number of encounters should increase when there are more rabbits and also when there are more wolves. A simple model makes the encounter term proportional to
Predation decreases the rabbit population and increases the wolf population. One model is
The first equation says that rabbits reproduce, but are eaten. The second says that wolves decline without food, but benefit from encounters with rabbits.
This is not one equation. It is a system.

note.title: System of differential equations
note.p: A system of differential equations is a set of differential equations for several unknown functions.
A solution of
is a pair of functions
that satisfies both equations on the same time interval.

subsection.p: The equations are coupled. The derivative R' depends on W, and the derivative W' depends on R. We cannot solve one equation first and then the other. The two populations move together.

paragraphs.title: Equilibria
paragraphs.p: An equilibrium occurs when both derivatives are zero:
Thus there are two biologically meaningful equilibria:
means no rabbits and no wolves. The equilibrium
means the two populations balance each other in the model.

exercise.title: Why do two interacting populations require a system?

statement.p: A single equation P'=rP uses one number as the state. Rabbits and wolves need two. In your own words, why are the equations coupled, and why can you not solve one population first and then the other?

hint.p: Each derivative depends on both unknowns. The two populations move together, so a solution is a pair of functions on the same time interval.

subsection.title: Predator-prey equations as a picture
subsection.p: For one autonomous equation,
a phase line summarized the motion. For two autonomous equations,
the state is a point in the (R,W)-plane. The differential equation assigns a velocity vector to each point:
So the phase line becomes a phase plane.
For the predator-prey model,

description.p: A predator-prey system is read in the phase plane. The point (R(t),W(t)) moves according to the vector (R',W'). The plotted orbit is a numerical trajectory from (80,20). Its asymmetric shape comes from the stated equations.

subsection.p: The picture suggests a cycle.
When wolves are few, rabbits increase. Then the abundance of rabbits lets wolves increase. More wolves reduce the rabbits. With fewer rabbits, wolves decline. Then the rabbits can recover.
The equations do not describe one population rising or falling by itself. They describe a moving point in the plane.

paragraphs.title: A numerical glimpse
paragraphs.p: Both populations are increasing, but rabbits are increasing faster. In the phase plane, the point initially moves mostly to the right and slightly upward.
Both populations are decreasing. The point moves left and down.
This is the system version of a direction field. Instead of little line segments with a slope, we draw little arrows with two components.

note.title: Phase plane
note.p: For a system
the phase plane is the (x,y)-plane together with direction arrows
A solution traces a curve in this plane as time passes.

paragraphs.p: The phase plane does not usually give exact formulas for R(t) and W(t). It gives the shape of the interaction.
That is often the first thing we need.

exercise.title: What does a phase plane show that a pair of time graphs does not?

statement.p: For a system, the state is a point (x,y), and the right-hand side supplies an arrow at each point. In your own words, why is a solution a moving point in that plane, and what information is missing from the phase-plane picture?

hint.p: Time is the parameter that traces the curve; it need not appear as an axis. The picture shows the shape of the interaction more than exact formulas for x(t) and y(t).

note.title: The bridge
note.p: A solution of a system is a moving point:
So differential equations lead naturally to parametrized curves, vector fields, and functions of several variables.

subsection.p: This is where single-variable calculus begins to lean toward the next subject. The derivative of one function was enough for motion on a line. Motion in a plane needs two coordinate functions. Interactions need functions of several variables. The geometry of change begins to expand.

Before leaving differential equations, we should collect the warnings that protect the methods we have used: solutions can be lost by division, numerical methods can invent false behavior, and the same differential equation can describe many different histories until an initial condition chooses one.

exercise.title: Why do systems lead naturally to multivariable calculus?

statement.p: Even the oscillator y''+\omega^2 y=0 can be rewritten as a first-order system for (y,v). In your own words, why does that change the meaning of state from one number to a point, and what new kind of function then appears on the right-hand side?

hint.p: The right-hand side is built from functions of several variables. Parametrized curves and vector fields are the geometry of that moving point.

note.title: Division rule for separable equations
note.p: When separating variables, if you divide by an expression involving y, first ask:

subsection.p: This is not only a technical warning. In models, equilibrium solutions often carry the main interpretation. Extinction, carrying capacity, room temperature, and chemical balance all appear as constant solutions.
Discarding these solutions would omit the model's equilibria.

exercise.title: Why can algebra lose the most important solutions?

hint.p: Extinction, carrying capacity, and room temperature appear as constant solutions. Check those candidates before dividing them away.

warning.p: A numerical method has its own behavior. It is not the same object as the differential equation.
Before trusting a numerical solution, check whether it agrees with the qualitative behavior of the equation.

hint.p: The method has its own dynamics. Before trusting a table of values, ask whether they agree with the qualitative arrows of the field.

A second-order motion needs position and velocity.

note.title: Initial data rule
note.p: A differential equation gives the rule of motion. Initial conditions give the starting state.
A first-order equation usually needs one starting value. A second-order equation usually needs two: position and velocity.

subsection.p: This is why a spring cannot be described by its position alone. If the mass is at equilibrium, it may stay there, or it may be passing through with high speed. The position is the same. The future is not.

exercise.title: Why is a differential equation incomplete without enough starting information?

statement.p: The same first-order equation can describe many histories, and a second-order spring needs both position and velocity. In your own words, what does the differential equation determine, what do initial conditions determine, and why can two masses at the same place have different futures?

hint.p: The equation is the rule of motion. Initial data choose the starting state. A first-order law usually needs one starting value; a second-order law usually needs two.

subsection.title: The three warnings together
subsection.p: The warnings can be remembered as three questions.

cell.p: Did we divide by an expression that might be zero?
We may have lost equilibrium solutions.
Is a numerical step size too large?
Euler’s method may create false oscillation or false growth.
Have we supplied enough initial information?
The differential equation may describe a family, not one solution.

subsection.p: Differential equations are powerful because they describe change locally. That same local nature makes them sensitive to algebraic assumptions, numerical choices, and initial data.
The chapter ends by gathering the main methods and putting them back to work in applications.

introduction.p: The review problems ask you to formulate differential equations, use direction fields and phase lines, apply Euler's method, and solve separable, linear, second-order, and coupled equations. State initial conditions and check any solutions excluded by algebraic steps.

subsection.title: Skills: solve and interpret first-order equations
subsection.p: The first task in a differential equation is not to solve. It is to recognize what kind of equation is in front of us and what kind of answer is reasonable.

subsection.title: A final map of the chapter
subsection.p: The main ideas of the chapter can be summarized in one picture of dependencies.

subsection.p: No one route is the whole subject. Often the best solution uses several at once.

For example, in a logistic model, the phase line tells us that a positive solution should approach K. The exact formula tells us when it reaches K/2. Euler’s method can approximate values when parameters are changing or when the equation becomes too complicated to solve exactly. The model interpretation tells us which values of P make physical sense.

note.title: What differential equations add to calculus
note.p: Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. Differential equations use those ideas to describe laws.

exercise.title: What do differential equations add to calculus?

statement.p: Earlier, calculus measured change and accumulated change. In your own words, how do differential equations change the role of the derivative, and why does that turn an unknown function into the object we seek?

hint.p: The derivative becomes something we are given by a law, not only something we compute from a known formula.

introduction.p: Euler's method advances with one slope at the start of a step. Runge–Kutta methods sample additional slopes to approximate the change more accurately. This optional section compares explicit Euler, improved Euler (Heun), midpoint, and classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta methods. It assumes an initial value problem with a smooth solution on the interval being computed.

subsection.title: Two slopes and four slopes
subsection.p: For y'=F(t,y), use a step from (t_n,y_n) to t_n+h. Explicit Euler is y_{n+1}=y_n+hF(t_n,y_n). Heun's method predicts with Euler and averages the initial and predicted final slopes:
The explicit midpoint method uses the initial slope to predict the midpoint, then uses its slope for the whole step:
Both are second-order methods, but they need not give the same value on a nonlinear equation. Here the k_i are slopes; the factor h is applied when forming changes.

The two midpoint slopes are evaluated at different predicted values of y. Replacing one by the other changes the method. For a system, apply the same formulas to vector values, evaluating all components of each stage together.

subsection.title: Local error and accumulated error
subsection.p: The one-step local error is the difference between an exact solution value at the end of a step and one numerical step started from the exact value at its beginning. A method has order p when this error is O(h^{p+1}) and its accumulated, or global, error over a fixed finite interval is O(h^p). Here O(h^r) means a magnitude bounded by a constant times h^r for all sufficiently small positive h, with the constant independent of the step size. Some texts divide the local error by h; here we do not.

For the following orders, assume F and its partial derivatives through order four are continuous and bounded in a neighborhood containing the exact and numerical trajectories, and one constant L\ge0 satisfies |F(t,u)-F(t,v)|\le L|u-v| there. This is the Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable. A partial derivative in t or y means varying that input while holding the other fixed. The initial value is exact, the interval length is fixed, and the stated orders describe exact arithmetic as h\to0.

To see the second-order match, write F_t,F_y for the two derivatives at the starting point. Along an exact solution, y''=F_t+F_yF. Expanding the final slope in Heun's method gives k_2=F+h(F_t+F_yF)+O(h^2); its averaged update is y+hF+\tfrac12h^2(F_t+F_yF)+O(h^3), matching the exact Taylor expansion through degree two. The midpoint calculation gives the same degree-two match.

For RK4, Taylor expansion of all four stages matches the exact solution through degree four. One compact way to state this calculation is to define DG=G_t+FG_y for any smooth function G(t,y). The exact change and the RK4 change both have the expansion
with all terms evaluated at the start. Here D^2F=D(DF) and D^3F=D(D^2F). The weights alone are not a quadrature proof: the predicted stage values must also produce this Taylor match.

The loss of one power in global error comes from accumulating about 1/h steps. More precisely, smoothness gives a one-step perturbation bound 1+Ch for some fixed C\ge0. If the local error is at most Kh^{p+1}, then the global errors satisfy e_{n+1}\le(1+Ch)e_n+Kh^{p+1}. Iterating this inequality over nh\le T gives e_n\le KTh^p e^{CT} when e_0=0. This explains why local accuracy needs both smoothness and control of error propagation.

example.title: A reproducible accuracy comparison
example.p: For y'=y, y(0)=1, the exact endpoint is y(1)=e. With h=1/n, the one-step multipliers are 1+h for Euler, 1+h+h^2/2 for Heun and midpoint, and 1+h+h^2/2+h^3/6+h^4/24 for RK4. Raise each multiplier to the n-th power to reproduce these endpoint absolute errors:

Halving the step eventually divides the error by roughly 2, 4, and 16, respectively. At equal slope-evaluation cost, compare Euler with 4n steps, Heun with 2n steps, and RK4 with n steps; equal step counts alone do not give equal work.

warning.title: Higher order does not remove stability restrictions
warning.p: For y'=\lambda y, RK4 advances with multiplier P(z)=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24, where z=h\lambda. On y'=-4y, choosing h=1 gives P(-4)=5, so the numerical values grow although the exact solution decays. A higher-order explicit method still needs a suitable step. Nonsmooth laws, long time intervals, rapidly decaying components, and roundoff require separate attention.

exercise.title: Compare accuracy at equal cost

statement.p: Approximate y(1) for y'=t+y, y(0)=1, using Euler with 16 steps, Heun with 8, and RK4 with 4. Each uses 16 slope evaluations. Compare with y(t)=2e^t-t-1. Repeat with twice as many evaluations. Also verify the RK4 multiplier on the test equation.

hint.p: Use the correct time in every stage. Expected error ratios approach 2,4,16 as the step shrinks. Successive substitutions in the four stages give the degree-four polynomial multiplier.

chapter.title: Parametric Curves, Polar Coordinates, and Conics

introduction.p: A plane curve need not be the graph of a single function y=f(x). Parametric equations describe both coordinates using one parameter, and polar coordinates describe position using a radius and angle. This chapter develops calculus in these coordinates, studies conic sections and planetary motion, and introduces complex numbers in polar form.

A parametric curve is described by coordinate functions x(t) and y(t) on a specified parameter interval. The parameter may represent time, but it need not. The description records how the curve is traced, including its direction and possible repeated traversal.

subsection.title: A curve as a moving point
subsection.p: Imagine a point moving around the unit circle. At time t, put

figure.caption: The parameter t tells how the point moves around the circle.

description.p: The parameter t tells how the point moves around the circle.

subsection.p: The curve itself is the circle. The parametrization tells more: it tells where the point is at each time, the direction of travel, and how fast the point moves.
This extra information is often useful. A road map shows the road. A schedule tells how the traveler moves along it. A parametric curve contains both.

note.title: Parametrization of a plane curve
note.p: A parametrization of a plane curve is a pair of functions
defined for t in an interval I. The moving point
traces the curve as t runs through I.
The variable t is called a parameter. It is often time, but it does not have to be.

But

The coordinate formulas must be accompanied by a parameter interval to specify which part of the curve is traced and how often.

hint.p: A road map shows the road. A schedule tells where the traveler is, in what order, and how fast. A parametrization contains both.

subsection.p: Sometimes a parametric curve can be translated into an ordinary Cartesian equation by removing the parameter.

This equation tells the geometric shape. It does not tell the direction of motion or the speed. Those belong to the parametrization.

subsection.p: Eliminating the parameter can be helpful, but it forgets information.

exercise.title: What does eliminating the parameter forget?

statement.p: Three different parametrizations can satisfy the same equation x^2+y^2=1 while tracing the circle once, twice, or clockwise. In your own words, what information is lost in the Cartesian equation, and why can ignoring the parameter interval accidentally enlarge the curve?

hint.p: Elimination remembers the set of points, not orientation, speed, starting point, ending point, or repeated tracing. The domain of t is part of the description.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A Cartesian equation describes the set of points on the curve. A parametrization also describes the motion along the curve.
When you eliminate the parameter, you may lose:

p.em: orientation, speed, starting point, ending point, repeated tracing.

subsection.p: There is another warning. Eliminating the parameter can accidentally enlarge the curve if the parameter interval is ignored.

subsection.title: Different parametrizations of the same curve
subsection.p: A single geometric curve can have many parametrizations. This is not a nuisance. It is a choice of schedule.
The line segment from A=(1,2) to B=(5,4) can be described by
At t=0, the point is A. At t=1, the point is B.

For the first parametrization,
The components of motion are constant.
For the second parametrization,
At s=0, both derivatives are 0. The point starts from rest, then speeds up.
The road is the same. The trip is different.

paragraphs.p: The segment from A=(1,2) to B=(5,4) can also be traced backward:
Now the starting point is B, and the ending point is A.

note.title: Parametrization as schedule
note.p: A geometric curve tells where the point can be.
A parametrization tells where the point is, in what order, and at what rate.

paragraphs.p: This distinction will matter when we compute slopes, lengths, and areas. The geometry may be unchanged, but the parameter controls the calculations.

The next section asks how to do calculus on such curves. A tangent slope is no longer found from y=f(x). Instead, both x and y are changing, and the slope must be built from their rates.

The point on the wheel momentarily stops when it touches the ground. The curve has cusps there. This is exactly the kind of behavior that parametric equations handle naturally: the formulas describe not only the curve, but also the motion that creates it.

The next coordinate system also comes from motion, but of a different kind. Instead of following horizontal and vertical coordinates, we measure a point by how far it is from the origin and which direction it lies.

introduction.p: A polar curve r=f(\theta) has the parametric description x=f(\theta)\cos\theta, y=f(\theta)\sin\theta. We will use these coordinate formulas to find tangents and lengths, and use circular sectors to derive the polar area formula. The parameter interval determines which parts of the curve are traced and how often.

note.title: Polar checklist before computing area or length
note.p: Before using a polar formula, ask:

li.p: What interval of \theta traces the desired curve?
Is the curve traced once or more than once?
Does r become negative, creating points on the opposite ray?
Does the curve pass through the origin?
If two curves intersect, are there intersections reached at different angles?

paragraphs.p: Polar coordinates are powerful because they match circular and radial geometry. But the price is that the same point may have many names.

The next family of curves makes especially good use of polar coordinates. It includes parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas. These curves can be described by distance from a fixed point and a fixed line, and in polar form they appear in one equation.

exercise.title: What should you ask before computing polar area or length?

statement.p: The section ends with a checklist: interval, repeated tracing, negative r, the origin, and hidden intersections. In your own words, why does skipping those questions turn a correct formula into a wrong geometric count?

hint.p: The formula integrates the parametrization you feed it. If the tracing is wrong, the integral is faithfully wrong.

introduction.p: Circles, parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas look like different curves. But they belong to one family.
One way to discover them is to slice a cone. A horizontal slice gives a circle. A slanted slice may give an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola.
There is another way, better suited to calculus and polar coordinates: compare distances.
A conic is controlled by a fixed point and a fixed line.
The curve consists of all points whose distance to the focus has a constant ratio to their distance to the directrix.
That ratio is called the eccentricity.

subsection.p: The polar form
makes eccentricity visible. The single number e decides whether the orbit closes, opens into a parabola, or splits into hyperbola branches.

That fact is more than geometry. It is one of the reasons polar coordinates are central in astronomy and mechanics. Planetary orbits are conics with the sun at a focus. The same polar equation that classifies conics will become an orbit equation.
The next optional project follows that thread. It asks why an ellipse is the natural curve for a planet, and why equal areas swept out by the radius vector correspond to equal times.

exercise.title: When is a Cartesian standard equation the better language?

statement.p: Standard equations such as x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1 put a center at the origin, while polar form puts a focus at the pole. In your own words, why might you choose one description or the other?

hint.p: Cartesian form is convenient for axes of symmetry and translations of the center. Polar form is convenient when the important point is a focus, as in an orbit.

introduction.p: The last section brought conics into one family. A parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola can be described by one polar equation:
The number e decides the type of curve. When 0<e<1, the curve is an ellipse.
This is not only a classification trick. It is the equation that appears in one of the great discoveries of science: planets move on ellipses with the sun at a focus.

That sentence is Kepler’s first law. We use the ideal two-body model: the central body is fixed, the force is inverse-square attraction, and other bodies and drag are neglected. It belongs naturally here because the focus of a polar conic sits at the pole.

subsection.p: Kepler’s first law says that a planet moves on an ellipse with the sun at one focus.
Kepler’s second law says something about the speed of the motion.

subsection.p: This is an area statement, so it should remind us of the polar area formula:

Equivalently,
This equation has a simple geometric meaning. When the planet is close to the sun, r is small. To keep
constant, the angular speed \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} must be larger. When the planet is far from the sun, r is large, so the angular speed is smaller.

p.me: \text{Planets move faster near the sun and slower far from the sun.}

subsection.p: The equal-area law directly controls angular speed. To check the ordinary speed along this elliptical orbit, write h=r^2\theta'>0. From r=p/(1+e\cos\theta), differentiation gives r'=he\sin\theta/p. Hence v^2=(r')^2+(r\theta')^2=(h/p)^2(1+e^2+2e\cos\theta)=(h/p)^2(e^2-1+2p/r). This increases as the distance r decreases, so the speed is also larger nearer the sun.

hint.p: If \frac12 r^2\theta' is constant, a smaller r forces a larger angular speed. The same ellipse is traced at different speeds.

The key idea is that gravity is a central force. It points along the line from the planet to the sun.
Gravity pulls the planet inward along the radial direction; it has no sideways force component.
This sideways fact is what produces equal areas in equal times.

subsection.p: The bridge is already visible. A planet is a moving point, like the parametric curves at the start of this chapter. Its coordinates change with time. Its velocity and acceleration are pairs of derivatives. Its force has a direction.
So the chapter’s first idea returns in a richer form:

introduction.p: A complex number x+iy represents a point in the plane. Its polar form records its distance from the origin and its angle. Multiplication multiplies the distances and adds the angles, so complex numbers provide formulas for scaling and rotation.

subsection.p: This optional connection will be developed later using infinite series.

Parametric curves taught us to let time move a point in the plane. Polar coordinates taught us to measure that point by radius and angle. Complex numbers show that the same plane can be treated as a number system, where multiplication rotates.
The proof of Euler’s formula still waits. To prove it, we need a new kind of infinite process: not an infinite area, but an infinite sum of functions.

exercise.title: Why are complex exponentials useful for oscillation?

statement.p: The equation x''+\omega^2 x=0 has sine and cosine solutions, which complex notation packages as e^{i\omega t}. In your own words, what computational convenience does that packaging provide, and why is this a bridge rather than a new requirement for the chapter?

hint.p: Differentiation becomes multiplication by i\omega. The same plane is being treated as a number system whose multiplication rotates.

introduction.p: Parametric and polar formulas depend on how a curve is traced. Repeated traversal can multiply a length or area integral, a zero coordinate derivative can invalidate a slope quotient, and signed radii affect the interpretation of polar coordinates. Check the parameter interval before applying a formula.

exercise.title: Why does a 0/0 slope formula fail to decide the tangent?

statement.p: When both parametric derivatives vanish, the slope quotient is undefined. The same issue occurs for polar curves. Describe the different tangent behaviors that can occur and the limits or expansions that can distinguish them.

hint.p: A cusp, a smooth pause, or a retracing may all produce vanishing derivatives. Nearby slopes, elimination of the parameter, or a local picture can tell them apart.

subsection.title: The chapter’s main cautions
subsection.p: The formulas in this chapter are reliable when their hypotheses match the tracing.

cell.p: Is dx/dt\neq0? If both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish, study nearby motion.
Does the parametrization retrace the curve? The length integral counts distance traveled.
Is the curve traced once? What is the orientation?
What interval of \theta sweeps the region exactly once? Does r become negative?
Did the curves meet at the origin or with different polar names?
First rewrite the denominator so the constant term is 1, then read eccentricity.
Remember that arguments are not unique: \theta and \theta+2\pi k describe the same direction.

subsection.p: A formula is a tool, not a substitute for the picture.

exercise.title: What habit protects every formula in this chapter?

statement.p: Parametric, polar, and complex languages all carry more information than a plain Cartesian equation. In your own words, why is ask how the curve is being traced the safest habit before using a length, area, or tangent formula?

hint.p: Extra information about direction, speed, and repeated tracing is useful only if you remember that the formula follows the tracing, not just the set of points.

introduction.p: These problems compare Cartesian, parametric, polar, and complex descriptions of plane curves. Choose coordinates appropriate to the geometry, calculate slopes, lengths, and areas, and check the direction and multiplicity of tracing.

Scaling, rotation, circular motion, oscillation, and the preview of Euler’s formula.

subsection.p: No coordinate system is universally best. The skill is knowing which one makes the structure visible.

part.title: Infinite Processes and Approximation by Polynomials

introduction.p: A sequence is an indexed list of numbers, and a series is defined by the limit of its finite partial sums. This chapter develops convergence criteria, tests for positive and signed series, and the distinction between absolute and conditional convergence. These results will justify the function series and approximations in the next chapter.

A sequence assigns a value to each integer index in its domain. Decimal approximations, Newton iterates, and successive integral approximations are examples. We will define convergence, prove criteria that establish a limit, and examine recursive sequences.

subsection.title: The Cauchy criterion: convergence without knowing the limit
subsection.p: Sometimes an approximation has no known target value. We can still ask whether all sufficiently late terms are close to one another. A real sequence (a_n) is Cauchy if, for every \varepsilon>0, there is an integer N such that

statement.p: A sequence of real numbers converges to a real number if and only if it is Cauchy.

proof.p: If a_n\to L, choose N so that |a_n-L|<\varepsilon/2 for all n\ge N. The triangle inequality proves the Cauchy condition.
Conversely, a Cauchy sequence is bounded: take an eventual distance bound of 1 from one fixed term and then include the finitely many earlier terms. Define the tail bounds

Here \inf means greatest lower bound and \sup means least upper bound; completeness of the real line ensures both exist. The sequence \ell_N increases and u_N decreases, and both are bounded. The Monotone Convergence Theorem gives their limits. The Cauchy condition implies u_N-\ell_N\to0: if every pair of tail terms has distance less than \varepsilon, the tail's supremum minus its infimum is at most \varepsilon. Their limits are therefore the same number L. Since \ell_N\le a_N\le u_N, squeezing gives a_N\to L.

example.title: Controlling all later steps
example.p: If |a_{n+1}-a_n|\le2^{-n} for n\ge0, then for m>n the finite geometric sum gives
This tends to zero independently of m, so the sequence converges. We have proved existence of a limit before identifying it.

warning.title: Adjacent terms are not enough
warning.p: The condition |a_{n+1}-a_n|\to0 is weaker. For a_n=\ln n, adjacent differences \ln(1+1/n) tend to zero, but |a_{2n}-a_n|=\ln2. This sequence is not Cauchy.
The criterion depends on the number system being complete. Rational decimal truncations of \sqrt2 are Cauchy, yet they have no rational limit. They do have a real limit.

note.p: For a recursive sequence, the equation

subsection.p: The next section uses sequences in a new way. Instead of studying a list of terms directly, we build a new sequence by adding the first n terms. If those partial sums settle toward a limit, we will call the result an infinite sum.

introduction.p: An infinite series is defined as the limit of its partial sums. We add the first n terms and ask whether those finite totals converge as n\to\infty. Geometric and telescoping series provide cases where the partial sums can be calculated explicitly.

subsection.title: What series add to calculus
subsection.p: A finite sum is arithmetic. An infinite series is calculus because it is a limit:
The preceding examples have explicit formulas for their partial sums.
For many series there is no useful explicit formula for S_n. Convergence tests determine whether the partial sums converge without such a formula.
The first warning is close at hand.
For a series to converge, its terms must get small. But small terms are not enough.
The next section begins with the series
Its terms tend to zero, but its partial sums grow without bound.

exercise.title: Why is an infinite series calculus rather than arithmetic?

section.title: The harmonic series and first warnings

introduction.p: Convergence of \sum a_n requires a_n\to0, but this condition is not sufficient. The harmonic series demonstrates the distinction: its terms tend to zero while its partial sums grow without bound. We will prove that divergence and use it as a comparison.

subsection.title: Terms can go to zero while the series diverges
subsection.p: Look at the series
Its terms are
These terms approach zero:
So each individual term becomes tiny. But the accumulated sum is another question. The first few partial sums are
The partial sums keep increasing. That alone does not prove divergence. They might increase toward a horizontal ceiling, as the geometric partial sums did.
The partial sums are unbounded.
The series
is called the harmonic series. It diverges, even though its terms approach zero.
This is the first essential warning in infinite series:
A term is one small contribution. A series is the accumulated effect of infinitely many contributions. Small pieces can still have an infinite total.

exercise.title: Why can terms go to zero while the series diverges?

statement.p: The harmonic series has terms 1/k\to 0, yet it diverges. In your own words, why is a term only one small contribution, and why can infinitely many shrinking contributions still have an infinite total?

hint.p: Convergence is about accumulated running totals, not about one term becoming tiny. Small pieces can still pile up without a ceiling.

statement.p: If a series converges, then a_k\to 0. Equivalently, if the terms do not approach zero, the series diverges. In your own words, why does that implication run in only one direction, and what has been learned if the terms do go to zero?

hint.p: A necessary condition can rule a series out, but it cannot rule a series in. Passing the first obstacle is not the same as arriving.

example.p: the terms do not approach zero. Therefore the series diverges.
There is no need to study the partial sums. The individual terms are already too large to allow convergence.

example.p: The terms do not approach zero. Therefore the series diverges.

The partial sums oscillate instead of approaching a number.

example.p: The term test gives no conclusion. It does not say the harmonic series converges. It only says that the first obstacle to convergence has been passed.

subsection.title: The harmonic series
subsection.p: The harmonic series is
It is the simplest series whose terms go to zero but whose sum still diverges.
The partial sums grow slowly:
Slow growth can look like convergence if we only compute a few terms. This is a common trap in numerical work. A long plateau is not the same as a limit.
The right proof groups the terms.

subsection.p: This proof is more than a trick. It shows a new habit. When we cannot compute partial sums exactly, we compare them with something simpler.
That is the main idea behind the next tests.

exercise.title: Why does grouping doubled blocks prove harmonic divergence?

statement.p: Grouping the harmonic series into blocks whose lengths double shows that each new block contributes at least 1/2. In your own words, why does that force the partial sums to be unbounded, and what new habit does the argument teach for later tests?

hint.p: Infinitely many blocks of size at least 1/2 cannot have a finite total. When exact partial sums are unavailable, comparison with something simpler becomes the method.

paragraphs.title: Why the hypotheses matter
paragraphs.p: The integral test is not a rule for every function. It requires f to be continuous, positive, and decreasing.
The positivity matters because the proof uses increasing partial sums and area comparison. If signs change, cancellation can change the behavior.
The decreasing condition matters because the rectangles must consistently sit above or below the curve. If the function jumps up and down, the rectangle comparison can fail.

p.em: Do not use the integral test until positivity and decreasing behavior have been checked.

exercise.title: Why can an improper integral decide a positive series?

statement.p: The Integral Test compares rectangle sums with the area under a positive decreasing curve. In your own words, why do the series and the improper integral stand or fall together, and why must positivity and decreasing behavior be checked first?

hint.p: If the area is infinite, the rectangles sitting above the curve are infinite too. If the area is finite, the increasing partial sums are bounded above. Without a consistent above-or-below comparison, the picture fails.

statement.p: For a convergent positive series, the Integral Test also bounds the remainder after a partial sum. In your own words, why is the leftover infinite tail comparable to leftover area, and why does that give a stopping rule rather than just a yes-or-no verdict?

subsection.title: Direct comparison
subsection.p: The harmonic series and the series \sum 1/k^2 now become measuring sticks.
If a positive series is smaller than a known convergent positive series, it must converge. If it is larger than a known divergent positive series, it must diverge.

subsection.p: The phrase “for all sufficiently large k” means that finitely many early terms do not matter. Changing, adding, or deleting finitely many terms can change the value of a convergent series, but it cannot change whether the series converges.

paragraphs.title: Why the test works
paragraphs.p: For positive series, partial sums increase. If every term of a_k is eventually no larger than the corresponding term of b_k, then the partial sums of a_k are eventually controlled by the partial sums of b_k, plus a finite starting amount.
A finite starting amount cannot cause divergence. The infinite tail decides.

exercise.title: Why do nonnegative terms leave only two possibilities?

statement.p: For a series with a_k\ge 0, the partial sums are increasing. In your own words, why does that force the series either to converge or to diverge to infinity, and why is there no room for oscillation?

hint.p: An increasing sequence either is trapped by a ceiling or keeps rising. Cancellation is what would have allowed bouncing, and there is none.

statement.p: Direct comparison uses an inequality. Limit comparison uses a finite positive ratio of leading behaviors. In your own words, why can a known convergent series pull a smaller positive series along with it, and why do two series that look alike for large k share the same fate?

subsection.p: Positive series are now under partial control. But many important series alternate signs:
The positive series diverges. The next section shows how alternating signs change its convergence behavior.

introduction.p: Alternating signs can make a series converge even when the corresponding series of absolute values diverges. The alternating harmonic series is an example. The alternating-series test gives a convergence criterion and a remainder bound when term magnitudes decrease to zero.

statement.p: The Alternating Series Test needs decreasing term sizes and terms approaching zero. In your own words, why do alternating signs alone fail, and why can terms going to zero still fail if the sizes are not decreasing in an organized way?

subsection.title: Conditional convergence
subsection.p: The alternating harmonic series converges:
converges.
But the positive series made from the absolute values is the harmonic series:
and this diverges.
So the convergence of the alternating harmonic series depends on cancellation. If we remove the signs, it falls apart.

note.title: Conditional convergence
note.p: A series
is conditionally convergent if
converges, but

subsection.p: Thus
Conditional convergence is useful, but delicate. It depends on a balance between positive and negative terms.
This delicacy is one reason we next study absolute convergence, which is safer. If a series converges even after all signs are made positive, then it does not need cancellation to survive.

exercise.title: Why is conditional convergence delicate?

statement.p: A series converges conditionally if it converges, but the series of absolute values diverges. In your own words, why does that mean the convergence depends on cancellation, and why is a safer kind of convergence waiting in the next section?

hint.p: Remove the signs and the harmonic series reappears. Survival that requires a balance of plus and minus is useful, but it is not the same as having finite total size.

introduction.p: A series converges absolutely when the sum of its term magnitudes is finite. Absolute convergence implies convergence, regardless of the signs. This section develops the ratio and root tests for absolute convergence and Dirichlet's and Abel's tests for controlled cancellation.

statement.p: Absolute convergence means \sum |a_k| converges. Conditional convergence means the signed series converges while the absolute series diverges. In your own words, why does finite total size force ordinary convergence, and why is cancellation a weaker, more fragile reason to converge?

hint.p: If the total size is finite, the positive and negative parts are each finite, so their difference is finite. Conditional convergence keeps an infinite supply of both signs and balances them by order.

exercise.title: Why does the Ratio Test compare a series with a geometric series?

statement.p: The Ratio Test looks at \lim |a_{k+1}/a_k|. In your own words, why does a limit strictly less than 1 make the terms eventually shrink like a geometric series, and why is the test especially natural for factorials and exponentials?

hint.p: If consecutive terms are eventually no larger than a fixed fraction r<1 of the previous term, comparison with \sum r^k takes over. Factorials and exponentials change by a clean multiplicative factor from one term to the next.

subsection.p: The Ratio Test compares consecutive terms. The Root Test measures the average exponential size of one term.

exercise.title: When is the Root Test the natural test?

statement.p: The Root Test looks at \lim \sqrt[k]{|a_k|}. In your own words, why does a k-th power in the term invite a k-th root, and why is a limit strictly less than 1 again a geometric comparison?

hint.p: Taking the k-th root undoes a k-th power. If the roots settle below 1, then eventually |a_k|\le r^k for some r<1.

subsection.title: Dirichlet's and Abel's tests: controlled cancellation
subsection.p: The alternating-series test is one way to control cancellation. A more general method separates a series into a factor with bounded accumulated sums and a factor whose size changes monotonically.

paragraphs.title: Summation by parts
paragraphs.p: For integers q\ge p, put A_{p,k}=\sum_{j=p}^k a_j and A_{p,p-1}=0. Since a_k=A_{p,k}-A_{p,k-1}, expanding and shifting the finite sums gives
This is the discrete version of integration by parts. It uses only finite sums, so no convergence is assumed in the identity.

statement.p: Suppose the partial sums A_n=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k are bounded in absolute value, and b_n\ge0 decreases to zero. Then \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_nb_n converges.

proof.p: If |A_n|\le M, with A_0=0, then |A_{p,k}|=|A_k-A_{p-1}|\le2M. Summation by parts gives
The bound tends to zero independently of q. The Cauchy criterion for series proves convergence.

subsection.p: More generally, a monotone real sequence tending to zero has one sign (or is identically zero); reversing its sign if necessary reduces it to the stated version. Taking a_n=(-1)^{n-1} recovers the alternating-series test.

example.title: Cancellation without alternating every term
example.p: follows by telescoping 2\sin(\theta/2)\sin(n\theta)=\cos((n-1/2)\theta)-\cos((n+1/2)\theta). Its magnitude is at most 1/|\sin(\theta/2)|. Thus \sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n\theta)/n converges by Dirichlet. If \theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z, all terms are zero, so convergence holds there too. For \theta=\pi/2, the absolute-value series is 1+1/3+1/5+\cdots, which diverges by comparison with half the harmonic series. This instance is conditionally convergent.

statement.p: If \sum a_n converges and (b_n) is a bounded monotone real sequence, then \sum a_nb_n converges.

proof.p: By monotone convergence, b_n\to b for some real b. Put c_n=b_n-b. The sequence c_n is monotone and tends to zero. The partial sums of a_n are bounded because they converge. Dirichlet's test, with a sign reversal if needed, proves convergence of \sum a_nc_n. Since \sum a_nb_n=b\sum a_n+\sum a_nc_n at the level of partial sums, Abel's test follows.

example.title: A factor need not tend to zero
example.p: The alternating harmonic series converges, and b_n=2+1/n is bounded and decreasing. Abel's test therefore proves convergence of \sum(-1)^{n-1}(2+1/n)/n. Dirichlet's test with the product split in this particular way would not apply, because b_n\to2, rather than zero.

warning.title: Keep the hypotheses attached
warning.p: Bounded partial sums alone do not imply that \sum a_n converges. Also, replacing monotonicity by boundedness is invalid: \sum(-1)^n/n converges and b_n=(-1)^n is bounded, but their product is the divergent harmonic series. Abel's test here is a test for numerical series; a theorem about limits of power series at endpoints is a different result.

exercise.title: Select the cancellation test

statement.p: Prove that \sum_{n=1}^\infty\cos(n\pi/2)/\sqrt n converges conditionally. Then use Abel's test to show that \sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^{n-1}(3-1/n)/n converges.

hint.p: The cosine partial sums are bounded; the nonzero absolute terms are 1/\sqrt{2k}, whose sum diverges. For the second series, multiply the convergent alternating harmonic series by the bounded increasing sequence 3-1/n.

subsection.p: By now the list of tests is long enough that the main difficulty is choosing.
A series usually carries clues in its shape. The table below is not a rigid algorithm, but it gives a practical order of attack.

subsection.p: We now know how to test many numerical series:

section.title: Rearrangement and the danger of infinity

introduction.p: Rearranging finitely many terms preserves their sum. For an infinite series, this remains true under absolute convergence. A conditionally convergent series can change its sum or diverge after rearrangement. We will explain the difference through its positive and negative terms.

subsection.title: Finite sums can be rearranged freely
subsection.p: A finite sum does not care about order:
Both sides use exactly the same four numbers. Addition is commutative and associative, so rearranging finitely many terms does not change the answer.
This is one of the habits we bring from algebra.
But an infinite sum is not completed all at once. It is a limit of partial sums:
So the order matters because the order controls the path taken by the partial sums.
A finite sum has a last term. An infinite sum does not.

p.me: \text{Infinite addition is not just finite addition with more terms.}

exercise.title: Why can order matter for an infinite sum but not a finite one?

statement.p: Finite addition is commutative: rearranging finitely many terms cannot change the answer. In your own words, why is an infinite sum not just finite addition with more terms, and why does order control the path taken by the partial sums?

hint.p: A finite sum has a last term, so the whole collection is added at once. An infinite sum is a limit of running totals, and a different order is a different sequence of running totals.

Since L>0, this is a different sum.

exercise.title: How can the same terms produce a different sum?

statement.p: A rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series can converge to \frac32 of the original sum. In your own words, why does using the same terms in a different order change the accumulated limit, and what does that warn about conditional convergence?

hint.p: Putting two positive terms before each negative term changes how the running totals climb and drop. The terms are the same; the path of partial sums is not.

subsection.title: Why conditional convergence is fragile
subsection.p: For a conditionally convergent series, the positive terms and negative terms each have infinite total size.
That sentence is worth unpacking.
Suppose
converges conditionally. Define the positive and negative parts:
Then
and
Since the original series converges but the absolute-value series diverges, the positive and negative parts cannot both have finite total size. If they did, then
would converge.
They also cannot have only one infinite side. If
then the original partial sums would drift to +\infty. If
then the original partial sums would drift to -\infty.
So for conditional convergence we must have
There is infinite positive supply and infinite negative supply. The original order balances them just enough to converge.
A rearrangement can disturb that balance.

subsection.title: The Riemann rearrangement idea
subsection.p: The last observation leads to a striking theorem.

statement.p: If a series converges conditionally, then its terms can be rearranged to converge to any real number chosen in advance.

subsection.p: A full proof belongs in a later analysis course, but the idea is accessible.

Suppose the target number is T. Take unused positive terms in their original order, and do the same for negative terms. If the running sum already exceeds T, begin with the negative block. Insert any zero terms in their original order, one between successive blocks. Thus every original term is eventually used exactly once.
Start adding positive terms until the partial sum rises above T. This is always possible because the positive terms have infinite total sum.
Then add negative terms until the partial sum falls below T. This is always possible because the negative terms have infinite total size.
Then add positive terms again until the partial sum rises above T. Then negative terms until it falls below T. Continue forever.
The overshoots get smaller because the individual terms of any convergent series must approach 0. So the rearranged partial sums are forced closer and closer to T.

figure.caption: The Riemann rearrangement idea: alternate above and below a target, with shrinking overshoots.

description.p: The Riemann rearrangement idea: alternate above and below a target, with shrinking overshoots.

subsection.p: This theorem is one of the clearest signs that infinity changes the rules. A finite sum cannot be rearranged to become a different number. A conditionally convergent infinite sum can.

exercise.title: Why can a conditionally convergent series be steered to any target?

statement.p: The Riemann rearrangement theorem says that the terms of a conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any chosen real number. In your own words, why does infinite positive supply and infinite negative supply make that possible, and why do the overshoots still shrink?

hint.p: You can always add enough unused positive terms to rise above the target, then enough unused negative terms to fall below it. Individual terms of a convergent series go to zero, so the overshoots become small.

subsection.title: Why absolute convergence is safer
subsection.p: Absolute convergence prevents this danger.

note.title: Rearrangements of absolutely convergent series

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: Given an error tolerance \varepsilon>0, choose N so large that the absolute tail is small:
Now take any rearrangement of the series. Go far enough in the rearranged partial sums so that all of the first N original terms
After that point, the only possible difference between the rearranged partial sum and the full sum S comes from terms in the tail
The total absolute size of that tail is less than \varepsilon. Therefore the rearranged partial sums must stay within \varepsilon of S.
Since \varepsilon was arbitrary, the rearranged series converges to S.
This is why absolute convergence is stronger than ordinary convergence. It says the series has finite total size, not merely a lucky cancellation pattern.
The next section collects the main traps in this chapter. Each trap comes from using a test after forgetting one of its hypotheses.

exercise.title: Why does absolute convergence make order irrelevant?

statement.p: If \sum |a_k| converges, every rearrangement converges to the same sum. In your own words, why does a small absolute tail lock the sum in place no matter which later terms appear next?

hint.p: Once the first N original terms have all appeared, any remaining difference comes from the tail. Finite total size makes that tail smaller than any chosen tolerance, independently of order.

section.title: Additional topics: contraction and fixed-point iteration

introduction.p: A fixed-point equation can identify a possible limit, but the examples in showed that this is not enough to prove convergence. A contraction supplies the missing control. This optional section uses the Cauchy criterion to prove existence, uniqueness, and usable error estimates.

subsection.title: Distance, completeness, and contraction
subsection.p: On a closed interval D=[a,b], measure distance by d(x,y)=|x-y|. A map T:D\to D is a contraction if there is a constant q, with 0\le q<1, such that

The requirement T(D)\subseteq D keeps every iterate inside the set where the estimate holds. By the Mean Value Theorem, a differentiable map on the interval is a contraction if |T'(x)|\le q<1 throughout it.

The same argument works for other kinds of objects. A metric space is a set D equipped with a distance d that is nonnegative, is zero exactly when its inputs are equal, satisfies d(x,y)=d(y,x), and obeys the triangle inequality d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z). A sequence is Cauchy when d(x_m,x_n) becomes arbitrarily small for all sufficiently large m,n. The space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges to an element of D. Closed real intervals are complete by and the preservation of inequalities under limits.

subsection.title: The contraction theorem and its error estimates

statement.p: Let D be a nonempty complete metric space and let T:D\to D be a contraction with constant q<1. There is exactly one fixed point x_*\in D. For every starting point x_0\in D, the iteration x_{n+1}=T(x_n) converges to x_*. For n\ge1,

proof.p: Repeated contraction gives d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le q^k d(x_1,x_0). For m>n, the triangle inequality and the finite geometric sum give

Thus the iterates are Cauchy and have a limit x_*\in D. The contraction inequality implies continuity of T, so taking the limit in x_{n+1}=T(x_n) gives x_*=T(x_*). Two fixed points would satisfy d(x_*,y_*)\le qd(x_*,y_*), forcing their distance to be zero.
Letting m\to\infty in the finite-tail bound proves the first estimate. Starting the same geometric bound at the most recent step proves the second. For any x\in D,
Rearranging proves the residual estimate, including the third bound. If q=0, the map is constant and one step already reaches its fixed point.

subsection.p: The first bound is an a priori estimate: it can predict an iteration count from the initial step. The second is an a posteriori estimate: it uses the step just computed. In exact arithmetic, stop with an error at most \varepsilon when q|x_n-x_{n-1}|/(1-q)\le\varepsilon. A small step alone is not the bound; the factor q/(1-q) matters, especially when q is near one.
If an implementation produces approximate steps \widetilde x_{n+1} with d(\widetilde x_{n+1},T\widetilde x_n)\le\delta, while keeping them in D, then
This follows by iterating e_{n+1}\le qe_n+\delta. It explains the error floor caused by inaccurate function evaluations or rounding. A certified residual bound must include those evaluation errors.

example.title: Solving x=\cos x
example.p: The map T(x)=\cos x sends [0,1] into itself. On that interval, |T'(x)|=\sin x\le\sin1<0.85, so take q=0.85. Starting at x_0=1 gives x_1\approx0.540302, x_2\approx0.857553, and eventually x_*\approx0.739085. The theorem proves convergence for every start in the interval, even though the iterates need not be monotone. The residual estimate bounds the distance to the root by |x-\cos x|/0.15.

warning.title: Why the set and the constant matter
warning.p: The contraction T(x)=x/2 on the open interval (0,1) has no fixed point there: its iterates tend to zero outside the set. Completeness prevents this escape. On [0,1], the map T(x)=1-x has a fixed point but contraction constant only 1; most iterates oscillate. Neither hypothesis can simply be discarded.

exercise.title: Prove convergence and choose a stopping rule

statement.p: For T(x)=(x+2)/3 on [0,2], prove the self-map and contraction properties, identify the fixed point, and find an a priori iteration count guaranteeing error at most 10^{-6} when x_0=0. Express an a posteriori stopping test.

hint.p: Use q=1/3, x_*=1, and |x_1-x_0|=2/3. The first bound is 3^{-n}, so n=13 suffices. Stop when |x_n-x_{n-1}|/2\le10^{-6}.

chapter.title: Power Series, Taylor Polynomials, and Taylor Series

introduction.p: A power series is a series whose terms are powers of the input multiplied by fixed coefficients. We will determine where it converges and justify operations on it inside that interval. Taylor polynomials match derivatives at a chosen point; remainder estimates determine whether they approximate the function and whether its Taylor series represents it.

For each fixed x, a power series is a numerical series. Its convergence can change with x; for example, \sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n converges exactly when |x|<1. This section determines the radius and interval of convergence and tests the endpoints separately.

subsection.p: Start with

The same expression

A finite polynomial does not have this issue. For example,

subsection.p: The word “power” comes from the powers
For each fixed x, the power series becomes the numerical series
It may converge or diverge. The set of all x-values where it converges is called the interval of convergence.

exercise.title: Why does an infinite polynomial need a domain?

statement.p: A finite polynomial such as 1+x+x^2+x^3 is defined for every real x. The infinite expression 1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots is not. In your own words, why does a power series become a numerical series at each input, and why can the same formula converge at one x and diverge at another?

hint.p: There is no last term to add. At each fixed x, you must ask whether the partial sums settle. Geometric series already show that the answer depends on the size of x.

subsection.title: Center of a power series
subsection.p: Power series do not have to be centered at 0. They can be centered at any real number a.
For example,

The center is always included in the interval of convergence.

subsection.title: Radius and interval of convergence
subsection.p: The examples suggest a pattern. A power series converges in a symmetric region around its center. The endpoints need separate attention.

subsection.p: The interval of convergence is the full set of x-values where the series converges. It depends on the radius and on what happens at the endpoints.

paragraphs.title: Why the convergence set is an interval

converges. So the original power series converges absolutely at every point closer to the center.
This explains the shape: once a power series converges at one point, it converges at all points closer to the center.

The opposite statement follows by the same logic. If the series diverges at some point, it must diverge at every point farther from the center. Otherwise convergence farther out would force convergence closer in.
That is why the convergence set is an interval centered at a, with possible choices about the two endpoints.

exercise.title: Why is the convergence set always an interval?

statement.p: A power series converges in an interval of some radius R around its center, with endpoints left to be tested. In your own words, why can the set of convergent inputs not be a scattered collection of points, and what do the three possibilities R=0, R=\infty, and 0<R<\infty mean?

hint.p: If the series converges at some point, it converges absolutely at every closer point. That forces a solid interval around the center, possibly degenerating to a single point or expanding to the whole line.

subsection.title: Endpoint testing
subsection.p: The radius tells us what happens inside and outside. It does not tell us what happens at the endpoints.
The reason is simple: the Ratio Test often gives the limiting value 1 at the endpoints, and the Ratio Test is silent when the limit is 1.

exercise.title: Why must endpoints be tested separately?

statement.p: The radius determines the open interval of absolute convergence. Explain why the two endpoints must be tested separately and how equal radii can give different convergence intervals.

hint.p: At an endpoint the geometric safety margin disappears, and you are back to a numerical series. That series may converge, diverge, or converge only conditionally, independently of the interior.

subsection.p: The next section shows why power series are worth this work. Inside their interval of convergence, they can be handled almost like polynomials.

introduction.p: Inside their radii of convergence, power series can be added, multiplied, differentiated, and integrated under the conditions given below. Work on a common interval where the required series converge. At the endpoints, test convergence and justify the operation separately.

exercise.title: When may power series be added like polynomials?

statement.p: Power series with the same center can be added coefficient by coefficient on a common interval of absolute convergence. Explain why this does not automatically justify endpoint operations.

hint.p: Absolute convergence lets you rearrange and combine tails with finite total size. Endpoints can depend on cancellation, so they are not inherited automatically.

hint.p: Differentiation is a limit operation on an infinite sum, so it needs control. The interior has a geometric safety margin; an endpoint does not, so the differentiated series must be tested there again.

subsection.title: Why power series behave better than arbitrary series
subsection.p: Term-by-term differentiation and integration are not gifts we receive for every infinite sum of functions. They are special properties of power series inside their radius of convergence.
The reason is that power series have a geometric safety margin.

The series converges absolutely at distance \rho from the center:

For every x with |x-a|\le r,
The numerical series
converges by comparison with the convergent series at distance \rho. So the power series is controlled on the whole smaller interval, not just point by point.
That uniform control is what lets us safely pass limits through sums, derivatives, and integrals. A later optional section will give this idea a name: uniform convergence.
For now, the practical rule is enough.

hint.p: On a smaller closed interval around the center, the terms are dominated by a single convergent numerical series independent of x. At an endpoint that dominating geometric bound is lost.

note.title: Computational lesson
note.p: A series representation is not only a formula. It is also an algorithm. Its usefulness depends on how fast its terms shrink.

subsection.p: The geometric series gave us logarithms and inverse tangents. But the functions
do not obviously come from the geometric series. To reach them, we need a new question:

p.em: Can the derivatives of a function tell us which polynomial should approximate it?

subsection.p: That question leads to Taylor polynomials.

exercise.title: Why can a slowly convergent series still be the right idea?

statement.p: The Leibniz series for \pi/4 is beautiful but slow, while arctangent at smaller inputs is faster. In your own words, why does a series representation become a computational tool, and why does using the same series closer to its center change the efficiency?

hint.p: A series is useful only where its remainder is controllable. Smaller inputs make powers shrink faster, so the same identity can be a poor calculator or a good one depending on where it is evaluated.

introduction.p: The Taylor polynomial at a matches a function's value and derivatives through a chosen order. Its first-degree case is the tangent-line approximation f(a)+f\prime(a)(x-a). Higher degrees incorporate higher derivatives. The next section will bound the remainder.

exercise.title: Why does a Taylor polynomial match derivatives at a center?

statement.p: The tangent line matches value and slope. A Taylor polynomial continues the matching through higher derivatives. In your own words, why is that the right way to build a local polynomial, and what local information is each extra coefficient recording?

hint.p: Near a point, the first things a smooth function reveals are its value, its rate of change, its bending, and so on. Matching those derivatives makes the polynomial share the function’s local shape.

exercise.title: What is each Taylor term doing?

statement.p: For \sqrt{1+x} near 0, the linear term follows the tangent, the quadratic term corrects for concavity, and the cubic term corrects the correction. In your own words, why is a Taylor polynomial not just a formula, and why do later terms matter less when you stay close to the center?

hint.p: Each coefficient is derivative data at one point. Close to the center, higher powers of x-a are small, so the first few matched derivatives dominate the picture.

These are still finite polynomials. We have not yet proved that the corresponding infinite series equal the functions. That distinction matters.

paragraphs.title: A necessary warning
paragraphs.p: Taylor polynomials require derivatives at the center.
is continuous at 0, but it is not differentiable at 0. The left slope is -1, and the right slope is 1. There is no single number f'(0).
So there is no first-degree Taylor polynomial for |x| centered at 0 that matches the derivative. The needed local data does not exist.

note.title: Moral
note.p: A Taylor polynomial is built from derivatives at a center. If those derivatives do not exist, the polynomial cannot be built in the usual way.

paragraphs.p: There is another warning. Even when the polynomial exists, it is only a local approximation until we understand its error.
approximates the function near zero under the relevant remainder estimate. Matching derivatives at one point alone gives no accuracy bound far from that point.

p.me: \text{How far is \(f(x)\) from its Taylor polynomial?}

paragraphs.p: The answer is the remainder term. Without it, approximation has no scale.

exercise.title: What does a Taylor polynomial match at its center?

statement.p: Taylor polynomials require derivatives at the center, and even when they exist they are not automatically accurate far away. In your own words, why can |x| have no first-degree Taylor polynomial at 0, and why is matching at a point not yet a statement about error on an interval?

hint.p: Without a derivative, there is no slope to match. With a derivative, contact at a point still says nothing about how large the leftover gap becomes as you move away. That gap is the remainder.

introduction.p: The remainder R_n(x)=f(x)-T_n(x) is the error in the Taylor polynomial. Taylor's theorem expresses or bounds that error under differentiability assumptions. Those bounds determine where the approximation is accurate and whether the remainder tends to zero as the degree increases.

exercise.title: Why is approximation without a remainder only a hope?

statement.p: A Taylor polynomial gives a computable piece of a function. The remainder is the part not yet captured. In your own words, why is the approximation looks reasonable not yet a mathematical statement, and what question does the remainder force you to answer?

hint.p: Looking nearby is not a bound. The remainder asks how large the gap can be, which is the only way an approximation gets a scale.

The problem is not the function. The function is defined at x=2. The problem is that the power series centered at 0 has radius 1. A Taylor polynomial is built from local information. It should not be trusted far from its center without an error estimate.

exercise.title: What controls the size of a Taylor error?

statement.p: The Lagrange remainder bound involves a bound M on the next derivative, the distance |x-a|^{n+1}, and a factorial (n+1)!. In your own words, why do those three ingredients explain both why Taylor polynomials are local and why higher degree can still help?

hint.p: Far from the center, the power of distance grows. Close to the center, that power is small, and dividing by a factorial makes higher-degree leftovers even smaller if the next derivative is not too wild.

subsection.title: Solving differential equations by series
subsection.p: A differential equation gives a law for an unknown function. Sometimes the solution is one of the familiar functions. Sometimes it is not.
Power series give a way to build a solution from its coefficients.

hint.p: A differential equation is a law for derivatives. A power series stores those derivatives as coefficients. The resulting algorithm is trustworthy only when the leftover terms are controlled.

paragraphs.p: Taylor series turn functions into algorithms. But the algorithms work because their errors can be bounded. The next section explains, in a preview form, why power series allow such safe term-by-term work inside their radius of convergence.

introduction.p: Pointwise convergence allows the index needed for a given accuracy to depend on the input. Uniform convergence requires one index to work for every input in the set. This section defines that distinction, shows how uniform convergence preserves continuity and integrals, and applies it to power series on smaller closed intervals inside their radii.

exercise.title: Why is pointwise convergence not enough for integrals?

statement.p: A sequence of tall, thin spikes can go to zero at every point while each spike still has area 1. In your own words, why does that show that limits and integrals cannot always be interchanged, and what kind of control would prevent the spike from hiding?

hint.p: Each fixed x is eventually outside the spike, so the pointwise limit is zero. Area is an interval-wide quantity, so it needs interval-wide error control, which is what uniform convergence supplies.

note.title: The safety-margin rule
note.p: Power series may be manipulated like polynomials on intervals that stay strictly inside their radius of convergence.

subsection.p: This is the hidden reason the earlier sections worked. When we integrated

Uniform convergence explains the good behavior of power series inside the radius. The next section shows what can go wrong when we forget the warnings: Taylor series may have surprising endpoint behavior, term-by-term operations may fail for arbitrary function series, and a Taylor series may even converge without converging to the function that produced it.

exercise.title: Why are power series trustworthy inside their radius?

statement.p: A power series converges uniformly on every closed interval strictly inside its radius. In your own words, why does that geometric safety margin justify term-by-term integration and differentiation there, and why does the same justification stop at the endpoints?

hint.p: Inside a smaller radius, the terms are dominated by a convergent numerical series independent of x. That one bound controls the whole interval. At an endpoint the dominating geometric comparison is gone.

introduction.p: A Taylor series may fail to represent its defining function, and convergence inside an interval does not decide endpoint behavior. Also, term-by-term differentiation and integration require hypotheses on convergence. The examples below distinguish these failures.

note.title: Moral
note.p: The Taylor series is built from derivative data at one point. That data can be insufficient. To prove that a Taylor series equals a function, we need the remainder to satisfy

subsection.p: This is why Taylor’s theorem was not optional bookkeeping. The remainder is the bridge between the Taylor polynomials and the function.

exercise.title: Why can a Taylor series converge without equaling the function?

statement.p: The flat function that is e^{-1/x^2} away from 0 has every derivative zero at the origin, so its Taylor series is identically zero. In your own words, why does that show that derivative data at one point can be insufficient, and what extra statement is needed before the series is the function?

hint.p: The Taylor series records only the derivatives at the center. If those derivatives cannot see the function, the series cannot either. The remainder must tend to zero.

subsection.title: Endpoint behavior differs from interior behavior
subsection.p: Inside the radius of convergence, power series behave predictably. They converge absolutely. They can be differentiated and integrated term by term.
At the endpoints, that safety margin disappears.
Several power series have the same radius but different endpoint behavior:

and when
It does not decide what happens at
Those endpoints become ordinary numerical series, and ordinary series tests must be used.

paragraphs.title: Differentiation can lose endpoints
paragraphs.p: So the original series converged at x=-1, but the differentiated series does not.

paragraphs.title: Integration can gain endpoints
paragraphs.p: The original geometric series diverges at both endpoints. The integrated series converges at x=-1 by the Alternating Series Test, but diverges at x=1 as the harmonic series.
So the integrated series has interval
The radius stayed the same. The endpoint behavior changed.

note.title: Endpoint rule
note.p: Differentiation and integration preserve the radius of convergence, but they do not preserve endpoint behavior.
After any term-by-term operation, test endpoints again.

exercise.title: Why is endpoint behavior not decided by the interior?

statement.p: Differentiation and integration preserve radius but not endpoint behavior. In your own words, why can the interior be completely safe while an endpoint still requires a fresh numerical test, and why should every term-by-term operation be followed by that test?

hint.p: Inside the radius there is a geometric margin. An endpoint sits exactly where that margin vanishes, so a new series may gain or lose an endpoint even though R is unchanged.

subsection.title: Termwise operations can fail for arbitrary function series
subsection.p: Power series behave well inside their radius because they have geometric control. Arbitrary infinite sums of functions may have no such control.
Here is a concrete failure for integration.
