paragraphs.title: Differentiation has its own warning
paragraphs.p: Even uniform convergence of functions is not enough to justify differentiating limits.

So differentiating the approximating functions did not guarantee differentiability of the limit. To pass derivatives through a limit or an infinite sum, we need extra control, usually control of the derivative series itself.

note.title: Moral
note.p: Pointwise convergence is usually too weak for term-by-term operations.
Power series are special because they converge uniformly on every closed interval strictly inside their radius of convergence.

exercise.title: Why do term-by-term operations need hypotheses?

statement.p: Arbitrary series of functions can fail to pass integrals or derivatives through the limit, even when each approximant is well behaved. In your own words, why is pointwise convergence usually too weak, and why are power series special inside their radius?

hint.p: Passing an integral or a derivative through a limit is an interval-wide claim. Power series earn that claim by uniform geometric control on compact subintervals of the open interval of convergence.

subsection.title: A good local approximation can become bad far away
subsection.p: Taylor polynomials are local approximations. They are built from derivative information at one center. A polynomial that is excellent near the center can be useless far away.
The geometric series gives the clearest example:
The degree N partial sum is
For |x|<1,
At x=\frac12,
So the approximation becomes excellent quickly.
But at x=2, the function is perfectly defined:
The partial sums are
These values grow without bound. They do not approach -1.

The problem is not that 1/(1-x) is undefined at 2. It is defined there. The problem is that the power series centered at 0 has radius 1. The singularity at x=1 blocks the series before it can reach x=2.

figure.caption: The Maclaurin series for \frac1{1-x} has radius 1. It cannot pass the singularity at x=1, even though the function is defined again at x=2.

description.p: The Maclaurin series for \frac1{1-x} has radius 1. It cannot pass the singularity at x=1, even though the function is defined again at x=2.

warning.title: Local approximation warning
warning.p: A Taylor polynomial may be excellent near its center and poor far away.
A Taylor series may represent a function only on part of the function’s domain.

subsection.p: A power-series calculation needs a specified domain, convergence justification, and an applicable remainder estimate. Without these, formal manipulations may not establish an identity or an accurate approximation.

exercise.title: Why can a good local approximation become useless far away?

statement.p: The geometric partial sums approach 1/(1-x) for |x|<1, but at x=2 they explode while the function is perfectly defined. In your own words, why is a Taylor polynomial a local object, and why does existence of the function at a far point not license using the series there?

hint.p: A Taylor polynomial is built from data at one center, but being a polynomial it is defined everywhere. Its accuracy away from that center needs a remainder estimate. The associated infinite Taylor series has its own convergence radius and need not represent the function beyond it.

introduction.p: These problems determine convergence intervals, construct Taylor polynomials and series, bound remainders, and justify operations on function series. Distinguish a convergent formal series from a series that actually represents the given function.

statement.p: The series for e^x, \sin x, and \cos x are now in hand, and they will produce Euler’s formula. In your own words, why is it plausible that those three series belong to one rotating picture rather than three unrelated identities?

hint.p: Cosine and sine are respectively the even and odd parts of the exponential series after the imaginary substitution that cycles the signs. The next chapter turns that cycle into rotation in the plane.

introduction.p: In , a single bound independent of x controlled a whole interval. The M-test extends that idea from power series to arbitrary series of functions. This optional section uses the Cauchy criterion from .

subsection.title: A numerical majorant controls a function series
subsection.p: For functions f_n:D\to\mathbb R, the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) converges uniformly to F on D when its partial sums S_N(x) satisfy: for every \varepsilon>0, there is one N_0 such that |F(x)-S_N(x)|<\varepsilon for all N\ge N_0 and every x\in D.

statement.p: Suppose |f_n(x)|\le M_n for every x\in D, where M_n\ge0 and \sum M_n converges. Then \sum f_n(x) converges absolutely at every point and uniformly on D. Its remainder satisfies

proof.p: Absolute convergence at each point follows by numerical comparison. For every q\ge p,

The Cauchy criterion makes the right side arbitrarily small for sufficiently large p, independently of q and x. Letting q\to\infty yields the remainder bound. The tails of the convergent majorant series tend to zero, so this same bound proves uniform convergence.

subsection.p: If each f_n is continuous, the uniform-limit theorem makes F continuous. On a finite closed interval, the integration theorem in then gives \int_a^b F=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\int_a^b f_n. To differentiate term by term, one needs additional control of the derivative series; the M-test for the original terms alone is insufficient.

subsection.title: Examples, error bounds, and limitations

example.title: A uniformly convergent trigonometric series
example.p: For every real x, |\sin(nx)/n^2|\le1/n^2. Since \sum1/n^2 converges, the function

is continuous, and the integral-test tail bound gives |F(x)-S_N(x)|\le1/N for every real x. On any [0,b], term-by-term integration is valid and yields \int_0^bF(x)\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^\infty(1-\cos(nb))/n^3. This conclusion uses no Fourier-series theorem.

example.title: The power-series safety margin revisited
example.p: If \sum c_n(x-a)^n has radius R>0, fix 0<r<R. On |x-a|\le r, take M_n=|c_n|r^n. This numerical series converges because r lies inside the radius. The M-test proves uniform convergence on that smaller interval. An endpoint at distance R requires its own analysis.

warning.title: Uniform convergence does not control every operation
warning.p: The series \sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(n^2x)/n^2 passes the M-test on \mathbb R. But its formally differentiated series is \sum\cos(n^2x), which diverges at x=0 because its terms equal 1. The original M-test does not justify that differentiation.

subsection.p: The M-test is sufficient, not necessary. A function series with constant terms f_n(x)=(-1)^{n-1}/n converges uniformly on any set, because the alternating-series remainder is at most 1/(N+1) independently of x. But any nonnegative majorant M_n must be at least 1/n, so no convergent majorant exists.

exercise.title: Find the domain-wide bound

statement.p: Prove uniform convergence of \sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n^2 on [-1,1] and give a remainder bound. Then show that \sum_{n=0}^\infty(1-x)x^n converges pointwise on [0,1] but not uniformly.

hint.p: Use M_n=1/n^2 and remainder at most 1/N. The second sum equals 1 for x<1 and 0 at x=1. Its continuous partial sums cannot converge uniformly to this discontinuous limit; alternatively, their error for x<1 is x^{N+1}, whose supremum is 1.

chapter.title: Complex Numbers, Fourier Ideas, and the Road Ahead
chapter.shorttitle: Complex Numbers and the Road Ahead

introduction.p: Complex exponentials express rotation through Euler's formula e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta. This chapter uses that relation to study oscillation and introduces Fourier series, boundary identities, conservation laws, and stationary-action calculations. The final optional section proves a local differential-equation existence and uniqueness theorem using the convergence results from earlier chapters.
Complex numbers extend the real numbers by a number i satisfying i^2=-1. We will use their algebra and polar form to define the complex exponential and prove Euler's formula.

exercise.title: Why is e^{it} the natural language of oscillation?

statement.p: As t changes, e^{it} moves around the unit circle, with velocity a quarter-turn of position and acceleration pointing back to the origin. In your own words, why does that make sine and cosine shadows of one rotation, rather than two unrelated waves?

hint.p: The real part is cosine and the imaginary part is sine. Differentiating multiplies by i, which rotates the velocity onto the tangent. Differentiating again multiplies by -1, which is the geometry of circular motion.

introduction.p: The equation y^{\prime\prime}+\omega^2y=0 has sine and cosine solutions. Complex exponentials combine these oscillations in e^{i\omega t}, whose real and imaginary parts are \cos(\omega t) and \sin(\omega t). We will use this representation for constant-coefficient second-order equations.

subsection.p: The equation says

A second-order equation needs two initial conditions. To know how the mass will move, we need both its initial position and its initial velocity:
Position alone is not enough. If the mass is at y=1, it could be moving right, moving left, or momentarily stopped. Those motions have different futures.

exercise.title: Why are sine and cosine shadows of a rotation?

statement.p: The complex motion e^{i\omega t} satisfies the spring equation, and its real and imaginary parts are \cos(\omega t) and \sin(\omega t). In your own words, why does oscillation appear as the shadow of rotation, and why is the general real solution a linear combination of those two shadows?

hint.p: A rotating point in the plane projects onto two back-and-forth motions. Linearity lets you mix those two real solutions, which is enough to match any initial position and velocity.

exercise.title: What does it mean that energy is conserved?

statement.p: For the undamped spring, the quantity E=\frac12 m(y')^2+\frac12 k y^2 has derivative zero. In your own words, why is a conserved quantity a quantity whose derivative vanishes, and how does that explain the exchange between kinetic energy and spring potential?

hint.p: If E'=0, then E cannot change. At a turning point the mass is stopped and all the energy is potential; at equilibrium the spring is unstretched and all the energy is kinetic.

exercise.title: Why does damping drain energy?

statement.p: A damping force opposing velocity produces E'=-c(y')^2\le 0. In your own words, why does that term make oscillation fade, and what role do complex characteristic roots play in describing the faded motion?

hint.p: Negative derivative of energy means the energy is decreasing whenever the mass is moving. Light damping gives complex roots whose real part produces exponential decay multiplying the oscillation.

introduction.p: A Fourier series represents a periodic function using a constant and sine and cosine terms at integer multiples of a basic frequency. Integrals determine the coefficients by measuring these components. This section derives those formulas and works through examples; full convergence theory requires further results.

Still, the guiding picture is simple:

p.em: complicated periodic motion can often be approximated by adding simple waves.

subsection.p: This is why Fourier series belong after vibrations. One oscillator gives one wave. Many oscillators, or one complicated periodic signal, give a mixture.

exercise.title: Why do Fourier series use waves instead of powers?

statement.p: Taylor series build functions from powers near a center. Fourier series build periodic functions from sines and cosines over a cycle. In your own words, why is that a different question, and why does the symbol \sim warn that having a Fourier series is not automatically the same as equaling it everywhere?

hint.p: Fourier coefficients describe frequency components rather than derivatives at a point. Convergence of the resulting series requires separate conditions, particularly at discontinuities.

subsection.title: Orthogonality of sine and cosine, geometrically
subsection.p: To find the coefficients in a Fourier series, we need a way to measure how much one function points in the direction of another.
For ordinary vectors, the dot product measures alignment. Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero.
For functions on [-\pi,\pi], the analogous dot product is an integral:
If
we say the functions are orthogonal on [-\pi,\pi].
This language is geometric. The functions are being treated like vectors, but with infinitely many coordinates.

exercise.title: Why do integrals measure how much of each wave is present?

statement.p: On [-\pi,\pi], the inner product of two functions is an integral, and distinct sine and cosine waves are orthogonal. In your own words, why is that the analogue of a dot product, and why does orthogonality let you extract one coefficient without the others interfering?

hint.p: Perpendicular vectors have dot product zero, so projection onto one direction ignores the others. Integrating a function against one wave is the same idea: the other waves contribute signed area zero over a full period.

subsection.p: Fourier’s idea becomes surprising when the target function has corners or jumps.

figure.caption: Fourier partial sums approximate a square wave by adding sine waves. Near each jump, ripples remain.

description.p: Fourier partial sums approximate a square wave by adding sine waves. Near each jump, ripples remain.

subsection.p: The approximation improves away from the jumps. But near a jump, something strange happens. The partial sums overshoot the top level and undershoot the bottom level.
As we add more terms, the ripples get narrower. But the first overshoot near the jump does not simply disappear. It approaches a persistent limiting size.
This is called the Gibbs phenomenon.

note.title: Gibbs phenomenon
note.p: Fourier partial sums of a function with a jump often overshoot near the jump. Adding more terms makes the overshoot region narrower, but the overshoot height approaches a persistent limiting size.

subsection.p: There is also a convergence warning at the jump itself. The square wave jumps from -1 to 1 at t=0. The Fourier series does not choose the left value or the right value. It converges to the midpoint:
More generally, for a sufficiently well-behaved periodic function, the Fourier series converges at a jump to the average of the left-hand and right-hand limits.
The Fourier partial sums overshoot near a jump even as their values converge away from it. This behavior must be distinguished from pointwise convergence.

exercise.title: What does Gibbs phenomenon admit about jumps?

statement.p: For the square-wave example, Fourier partial sums overshoot near a jump and converge at the jump to the average of the two sides. Explain why this prevents uniform convergence and how it differs from Taylor representation.

hint.p: The jump is still visible in the approximation; the series does not pretend the function is continuous. Taylor series need local derivatives at a center, while Fourier coefficients are averages over a whole period.

subsection.title: Why Fourier series belong after Taylor series
subsection.p: Taylor series and Fourier series are cousins. Both try to build complicated functions from simple functions.
But they have different personalities.

table.title: Why Fourier series belong after Taylor series

cell.p: local behavior near a center a
periodic behavior over a whole cycle

subsection.p: A Taylor series asks:

p.me: \text{How does the function behave near one point?}

subsection.p: A Fourier series asks:

p.me: \text{What frequencies make up this repeating shape?}

subsection.p: Taylor coefficients come from derivatives at one point:
Fourier coefficients come from integrals over a whole period:
So Taylor series are local. Fourier series are global over a period.

This also explains why Fourier series can handle jumps better than Taylor series. A Taylor series is tied to local differentiability at a center. A Fourier series is built from waves and measures average alignment over an interval. It can still make sense when the function has corners or jumps.
Euler’s formula compresses the real waves into complex exponentials:
So a Fourier series can also be written in the compact complex form
The corresponding coefficients are
This form belongs more naturally to a later course, but the meaning is already visible:

p.me: \text{complex exponentials are rotating waves, and Fourier series add rotating waves.}

subsection.p: The chapter began with a rotating exponential, reached vibrating springs, and then combined many waves. One more bridge remains. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus was the hinge of single-variable calculus. It also has a second life: it is the first example of a boundary theorem.

exercise.title: Why do Fourier series belong after Taylor series?

statement.p: Taylor coefficients come from derivatives at one point. Fourier coefficients come from integrals over a period. In your own words, why is one viewpoint local and the other global over a cycle, and how does Euler’s formula compress the real waves into complex exponentials?

hint.p: Local matching is the Taylor personality. Measuring frequencies over a whole loop is the Fourier personality. Since e^{int}=\cos(nt)+i\sin(nt), the two real families become one complex family.

statement.p: The oriented interval from a to b has boundary \{b\}-\{a\}. In your own words, why does direction matter, and why do those opposite signs make split intervals add correctly?

hint.p: Traveling from a to b arrives at b and leaves a. If you split at an interior point, the extra interior endpoint is counted plus and then minus, so it cancels.

paragraphs.title: Warning: jumps are not ordinary derivatives
paragraphs.p: The theorem requires F to be differentiable on the interval. If F jumps, the ordinary derivative does not capture the jump.
But H is not differentiable at 0. Away from 0, it is constant, so its derivative is 0 where the derivative exists.
If we tried to integrate the ordinary derivative away from the jump, we would get
The missing change is concentrated at the jump. Ordinary single-variable calculus does not represent that jump as an ordinary derivative. This is why the differentiability hypothesis matters.
\int_a^b F\prime=F(b)-F(a) requires the theorem's differentiability and integrability conditions. A jump in F is not included in an ordinary derivative integral.

exercise.title: Why is the Fundamental Theorem a boundary theorem?

statement.p: The identity \int_a^b F'(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a) says that what accumulates inside is measured by the signed boundary. In your own words, why is that a geometric reading rather than only an antiderivative rule, and why do hidden jumps refuse to be ordinary derivatives?

hint.p: The interior contributions telescope, leaving only the ending value minus the starting value. A jump is not produced by a continuous derivative, so the theorem’s hypotheses are part of the geometry.

paragraphs.p: When an integrand is exact, its integral depends only on the boundary:
This is exactly what an antiderivative does. Finding an antiderivative is finding a function F whose differential is the integrand.

exercise.title: What does it mean for an integrand to be exact?

statement.p: An exact differential has the form dF=F\prime(x)\,dx. Explain why its integral reduces to a signed endpoint difference and how finding an antiderivative identifies such a differential.

hint.p: If every small piece is a change in F, adding the pieces is telescoping. Only the two ends survive, which is exactly what an antiderivative computes.

subsection.p: Single-variable calculus has carried this pattern all along:
The next bridge uses the same boundary idea for conservation. If a quantity inside an interval changes, then something must be created inside or must cross the boundary.

exercise.title: Why does dx carry direction?

statement.p: Reversing limits changes the sign of an integral, and substitution replaces dx by g'(u)\,du. In your own words, why is f(x)\,dx already the simplest differential form, and how does that habit prepare line integrals in the plane?

hint.p: The symbol dx is an oriented measuring stick, not mere decoration. Along a plane curve the same idea produces P\,dx+Q\,dy, with each coordinate contributing its own directed step.

introduction.p: A conservation law balances the change of a quantity in a region against inflow, outflow, and production within it. In one dimension, the region is an interval and fluxes enter or leave through its endpoints. We will derive integral and differential forms of that balance.

subsection.p: Imagine a straight road. Cars move along it. At position x and time t, let

For motion we need another quantity. Let

exercise.title: Why are density and flux different quantities?

statement.p: Density \rho measures how much is present per unit length. Flux q measures how fast stuff crosses a point. In your own words, why can a traffic jam have high density and small flux, and why do you need both quantities to write a conservation law?

hint.p: Being crowded is not the same as moving. Conservation tracks how the amount inside changes, which requires both how much is there and how much is crossing the ends.

subsection.p: In multivariable calculus, the flux becomes a vector field. Instead of moving only left or right, material can flow in many directions. The derivative q_x becomes divergence:

There is one final bridge. Calculus has optimized numbers: shortest distance, largest area, greatest profit. But physics and geometry often ask for the best path. That means optimizing a whole function.

exercise.title: Why does an interval law become a local law?

statement.p: If the conservation identity holds on every interval, the integrand \rho_t+q_x must vanish. In your own words, why does that local equation deserve the name divergence, and what does it say about how interior change is produced by nearby flux imbalance?

hint.p: A continuous integrand whose integral vanishes on every interval must be zero: a nonzero value would retain its sign on a small interval. The term q_x measures how flux changes along the line, the one-dimensional divergence.

section.title: Least action and the shape of a path

introduction.p: Some optimization problems vary an entire path rather than a single number. A path determines an integral, called a functional, and small changes in the path change that integral. We will use differentiation and integration by parts to find a condition for a stationary value. Stationary does not necessarily mean minimal.

exercise.title: Why is optimizing a path different from optimizing a number?

statement.p: Ordinary optimization chooses a number that makes a function extreme. A path problem chooses a whole function. In your own words, why is arc length a functional rather than an ordinary function, and why does testing a path require wiggling it?

hint.p: The input is now a curve, and the output is one number such as length or time. A nearby competitor is the original path plus a small wiggle that keeps the endpoints fixed.

subsection.title: The brachistochrone problem
subsection.p: One of the most famous path problems asks for the fastest slide.
Place a bead at a point A. Let it slide without friction under gravity to a lower point B. We may choose the shape of the wire connecting A to B.
Which wire gives the shortest travel time?
The shortest path is a straight line. But the fastest path is not a straight line. A path that drops steeply at first lets the bead gain speed quickly, and that speed can help later.
This is the brachistochrone problem. The word comes from Greek roots meaning “shortest time.”
Let y measure vertical distance downward from the starting height. Then y>0 means the bead has fallen. If the bead starts from rest, conservation of energy gives
So the speed is
A small piece of arc length is
Since
the small time is
Thus the total travel time is the functional
The problem is to find the function y(x) that makes this integral as small as possible, with fixed endpoints.
That is not an ordinary optimization problem. The input is the whole curve.
The answer is beautiful: the fastest curve is an arc of a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling circle.
One convenient cycloid parametrization is
where y is measured downward.

figure.caption: The brachistochrone is not the shortest path. It is the path of shortest time.

description.p: The brachistochrone is not the shortest path. It is the path of shortest time.

note.title: Lesson of the brachistochrone
note.p: The best path depends on what is being optimized.
Shortest distance and shortest time are different questions.

subsection.p: The full proof that the cycloid is the fastest curve belongs to the calculus of variations. But the setup already shows the new kind of calculus: an integral depends on a path, and we seek the path that makes the integral extreme.

exercise.title: Why is the fastest path not the shortest path?

statement.p: The brachistochrone is a cycloid, not a straight line. In your own words, why can dropping steeply at first produce a shorter travel time even though the path is longer, and what does that say about the quantity being optimized?

hint.p: Time is distance over speed, and speed is gained by falling. A path that gathers speed early can win on time while losing on length. The best path depends on what the integral is measuring.

subsection.p: The brachistochrone is famous but technically demanding. The easiest variational problem is the shortest path between two points.
We know the answer geometrically: the shortest path is a straight line. Let us see how calculus finds that answer.

note.title: What the calculation did
note.p: We did not vary a number. We varied a whole path:
Then we required the first-order change to vanish for every endpoint-fixed wiggle \eta.

subsection.p: The boundary condition on \eta matters. If the endpoints were not fixed, the boundary term from integration by parts would not disappear. Once again, boundary terms carry real information.

exercise.title: Why is a first variation the analogue of a derivative being zero?

statement.p: If a path is shortest, every allowed wiggle should give a critical value at wiggle size zero. In your own words, why does \mathcal{L}'(0)=0 for every endpoint-fixing wiggle play the role of f'(c)=0, and why do the boundary terms from integration by parts disappear?

hint.p: The unknown is the whole path, so the test must work against every small deformation. Fixed endpoints force the wiggle to vanish at the ends, which kills the boundary term and leaves an interior condition on the path.

subsection.title: Why this is beyond ordinary single-variable calculus
subsection.p: A functional often has the form

Here \partial L/\partial y means differentiate with respect to the second argument while holding the other arguments fixed; \partial L/\partial y\prime means differentiate with respect to the third argument, the slope. Assume L is twice continuously differentiable on the relevant domain. The function L is called a Lagrangian. It tells how the path and its slope contribute to the accumulated quantity.
The first variation calculation leads to the Euler--Lagrange equation:
This formula belongs to the calculus of variations. It is a cousin of the ordinary condition
but it applies when the unknown is a function.
For the shortest path problem,
Since L does not depend directly on y,
The Euler--Lagrange equation becomes

paragraphs.title: Least action
paragraphs.p: Physics uses the same idea in time.
Suppose a particle moves along a line, with position x(t). Its kinetic energy is

The principle of least action says, historically, that the physical path makes this quantity “least.” The more accurate statement is that the physical path makes the first variation of the action equal to zero. It makes the action stationary.
where the wiggle fixes the endpoints:
Differentiate the action with respect to \varepsilon at \varepsilon=0:
Use integration by parts on the first term:
The boundary term vanishes because the endpoints are fixed. Therefore
For this to be zero for every allowed wiggle \eta, we need
That is Newton’s second law for a force
A law of motion has emerged from a stationary-action principle.

note.title: Stationary does not always mean minimum
note.p: The historical phrase is “least action,” but the safest calculus statement is
This is like ordinary calculus: f'(c)=0 may indicate a minimum, a maximum, or neither. More work is needed to decide which.

paragraphs.p: This is why the subject goes beyond the ordinary single-variable course. We need to make sense of spaces of functions, allowed variations, endpoint conditions, existence of minimizers, and the difference between minimum and stationary.
But the seed is already here:

p.em: differentiate an accumulated quantity, watch the boundary terms, and set the first variation to zero.

paragraphs.p: That sentence connects much of the road ahead. In multivariable calculus, the boundary of an interval becomes the boundary of a region. Flux through endpoints becomes flux through curves and surfaces. The Fundamental Theorem becomes Green’s theorem, the Divergence Theorem, and Stokes’ theorem.
The book began with distance and velocity. It ends by pointing to the same pattern in larger geometry:

p.me: \text{change inside is measured by derivatives and boundaries.}

exercise.title: Why does least action live beyond single-variable calculus?

statement.p: The Euler–Lagrange equation is a stationarity condition for a functional whose input is a path. Explain how integrating kinetic minus potential energy defines the action and why this optimization differs from varying a single real number.

hint.p: You are no longer choosing one number; you are choosing a motion x(t). Stationary action is the condition that this motion not change the integral to first order under wiggles, which recovers the laws of mechanics as a variational statement.

introduction.p: These projects combine derivatives, integrals, differential equations, approximations, and geometric descriptions. Each may be completed individually or in a small group. Present the assumptions, calculations, useful graphs, error estimates where appropriate, and an explanation of the results.

subsection.title: Model, solve, and test a cooling law
subsection.p: Newton’s law of cooling was one of our first differential equation models:
It says that the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the object and its surroundings.
This project asks you to build the model from data, solve it, and then test whether it deserves to be trusted.

note.p: A cup of coffee is placed in a room whose temperature is
The coffee temperature is recorded every 5 minutes.
Does Newton’s law of cooling give a reasonable model for this data?

paragraphs.p: For each recorded time t_j, compute the model prediction
Record your results in a table.
Plot the residuals. A good model should not show a strong pattern in the residuals. If the residuals are all positive early and all negative later, the model is missing something systematic.

paragraphs.p: Write a short conclusion answering these questions.

What physical effects might make the model imperfect?

paragraphs.p: A model is not good because it has a formula. A model is good when it explains the data well enough for the question being asked.

exercise.title: Why must a model be solved and then tested?

statement.p: The cooling project asks for a solution, a parameter estimate, and a comparison with data. Explain why solving the equation does not establish the model's accuracy and how mismatches should affect its assumptions.

hint.p: A solved formula is only as good as the law and the measurements that produced it. Testing asks whether the local rule actually shapes the observed global behavior.

exercise.title: Why is an approximation incomplete without an error bound?

statement.p: The integral and Taylor-calculator projects compare several numerical methods and insist on a stopping rule. In your own words, why can three different approximations of the same integral still be unfinished work until their errors are controlled?

hint.p: Additional computed digits do not establish accuracy. An applicable error bound quantifies the possible difference from the exact value.

subsection.title: Build a Taylor-series calculator
subsection.p: A calculator evaluates functions so quickly that it is easy to forget the question:

p.me: \text{How does the calculator know the value?}

subsection.p: For many functions, one answer is Taylor series. The calculator does not store every value of \sin x, e^x, or \cos x. It uses algorithms, and Taylor polynomials are one of the first algorithms we can understand.

note.title: Project question

Use a similar recurrence for your chosen series.

paragraphs.title: Warning: small terms are not always enough
paragraphs.p: A common mistake is to stop when the next term is small, without knowing whether the tail is controlled. For alternating series with decreasing terms, that is justified. For other series, it may not be.
A numerical implementation needs both efficient evaluation and documented accuracy.

subsection.p: Parametric equations describe a moving point:
Real motion data often comes as sampled positions, not exact formulas. This project asks you to recover velocity, speed, distance traveled, and qualitative shape from a table.

paragraphs.p: Motion data turns the derivative from a formula into a measurement problem.

subsection.title: Explain the FTC as the first boundary theorem
subsection.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says
For most of the book, this was the theorem that connected antiderivatives and definite integrals. In , we gave it a second meaning:
The derivative is accumulated over the interval. The original function is evaluated on the boundary.

note.title: Project question
note.p: Write a short explanation of the Fundamental Theorem as the one-dimensional version of a boundary theorem.

paragraphs.title: Part A: start with finite differences
Part B: pass from finite differences to the integral
paragraphs.p: to explain why the telescoping sum becomes
You do not need to give a fully rigorous proof. The goal is to explain the idea clearly.

paragraphs.title: Part C: explain orientation
paragraphs.p: Draw an oriented interval from a to b. Label the left endpoint with a minus sign and the right endpoint with a plus sign.
Also explain why reversing the interval reverses the sign:

paragraphs.title: Part D: include examples
paragraphs.p: Your explanation should include at least two ordinary calculus examples.
Also include an example with a trigonometric function, such as

paragraphs.title: Part E: connect to the road ahead
paragraphs.p: End your report by explaining at least one of the following bridges.

li.p: In line integrals, the interval becomes a curve, but the boundary is still the two endpoints.
In Green’s theorem, a region in the plane has a boundary curve.
In the Divergence Theorem, a solid has a boundary surface.
In conservation laws, the amount inside changes because something crosses the boundary or is created inside.

paragraphs.p: The exact higher-dimensional theorems belong to multivariable calculus. But the pattern already appears in one dimension:

p.em: integral of a derivative over a region = integral of the original quantity over the boundary.

exercise.title: Why is the Fundamental Theorem the first boundary theorem?

statement.p: One project asks you to explain the FTC as a telescoping finite-difference statement that becomes an integral of a derivative. In your own words, why do interior cancellations leave only the boundary, and why does that viewpoint point toward Green, Stokes, and the Divergence Theorem?

hint.p: Adding consecutive changes cancels everything except the last value minus the first. In higher dimensions the same pattern remains: what happens inside is measured by what happens on the oriented boundary.

subsection.title: Closing note: what calculus has taught us
subsection.p: This book has followed one thread through many forms.
A derivative began as a velocity:
Then it became a tangent slope, a local linear approximation, a sensitivity, an optimizer, and a law of change.
An integral began as accumulated distance:
Then it became area, mass, work, probability, numerical approximation, and a boundary principle.
A Taylor polynomial began as a local approximation:
Then it became a gateway to infinite series, Euler’s formula, and waves.
The same ideas now point outward.

table.title: Closing note: what calculus has taught us

cell.p: double integrals, triple integrals, line integrals, surface integrals
Green’s theorem, Stokes’ theorem, Divergence Theorem
approximation theory, numerical methods, complex analysis
waves, signal processing, heat flow, quantum mechanics

subsection.p: The subject is larger than this book. But the central pattern is already here:

p.em: calculus measures change, accumulates change, and explains how local rules shape global behavior.

subsection.p: That pattern is worth carrying forward.

exercise.title: What pattern has calculus been teaching all along?

statement.p: The book began with a speedometer and an odometer and ended with series, waves, conservation, and paths. In your own words, why are derivatives, integrals, remainders, and boundary terms one language rather than four subjects, and what does it mean that local rules shape global behavior?

hint.p: Instantaneous change and accumulated change undo each other. Approximations become trustworthy through error. Models and conservation laws turn a local derivative statement into a global picture. That is the pattern to carry forward.

section.title: Additional topics: local existence and uniqueness

introduction.p: used initial conditions to select solutions, but this selection requires hypotheses on the slope law. We can now give a precise theorem and prove it using completeness, uniform convergence, and the contraction theorem. This optional section can be read independently of the complex-number and Fourier material in this chapter.

subsection.title: A Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable
subsection.p: Consider y'=F(t,y), y(t_0)=y_0. Fix positive a,b and the rectangle
The law is Lipschitz in y on R if one constant L\ge0 satisfies

whenever (t,u),(t,v)\in R. The same L must work for every time in the rectangle. A bound |\partial F/\partial y|\le L suffices: this derivative means differentiating with respect to y while holding t fixed, and the one-variable Mean Value Theorem applies. Lipschitz continuity does not require that derivative to exist; F(t,y)=|y| is Lipschitz with L=1.

theorem.title: A local existence and uniqueness theorem

statement.p: Suppose F is continuous on R, satisfies the Lipschitz condition above, and |F(t,y)|\le M on R. Choose h>0 so that

Then there is a continuously differentiable solution on I=[t_0-h,t_0+h] with y(t_0)=y_0 and |y(t)-y_0|\le b. It is unique among solutions on I whose graphs stay in R. In particular, the initial value problem has a unique local solution near t_0.

subsection.p: The stated bounds M and L determine a positive interval length. There is always a positive admissible h; for example, h=\min\{a,b/(M+1),1/(2(L+1))\} works, including when M=0 or L=0. The theorem provides a guaranteed local interval, which need not be the largest possible interval.

subsection.title: Proof by successive approximations
subsection.p: Integrating the differential equation gives the equivalent integral equation
Let D consist of continuous functions u:I\to\mathbb R satisfying |u(t)-y_0|\le b. Measure distance by the uniform distance

This is a metric, and D is complete. Indeed, a Cauchy sequence in this metric is Cauchy at each point, hence has a pointwise real limit by . Taking the limit in the uniform Cauchy bound shows uniform convergence to that function. The uniform-limit theorem preserves continuity, and taking pointwise limits preserves |u(t)-y_0|\le b. Thus the limit belongs to D.
Define the Picard map
Continuity of F and u makes Tu continuous, and
So T maps D into itself. Moreover,

The contraction constant is q=Lh<1. By , T has a unique fixed point y in D. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows that this fixed point is continuously differentiable and solves the differential equation. Conversely, every solution with graph in R satisfies the integral equation, so uniqueness of the fixed point proves the stated uniqueness. Any other local solution is close to y_0 by continuity and hence stays in R on a sufficiently small interval; the same contraction argument on that interval shows that the two local solutions agree there.
Starting with u_0(t)=y_0, successive approximations u_{n+1}=Tu_n converge uniformly, with the explicit bound

example.title: Picard iterates for exponential growth
example.p: For y'=y, y(0)=1, take a=1, b=1, M=2, L=1, and h=1/2. The iterates are u_0=1, u_1=1+t, u_2=1+t+t^2/2, and in general u_n=\sum_{k=0}^n t^k/k!. Their uniform limit is e^t. Picard iteration integrates an entire previous function; Euler and Runge–Kutta methods instead advance numerical values along a grid.

subsection.title: What the hypotheses do and do not guarantee

example.title: Continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness
example.p: The law F(t,y)=2\sqrt{|y|} is continuous but not Lipschitz near y=0, since |F(t,u)-F(t,0)|/|u|=2/\sqrt u for u>0. For the initial data y(0)=0, the zero solution and every function
solve the equation. At t=c, both one-sided derivatives are zero, so these are actual differentiable solutions. The solution may wait and then depart. Initial data alone do not force uniqueness.

figure.caption: Three solutions of y'=2\sqrt{|y|} pass through (0,0): immediate departure, departure after time one, and the zero solution.

description.p: On the interval from minus one to two, a parabola beginning at time zero, a parabola beginning at time one, and the zero solution all coincide initially on the horizontal axis.

example.title: Without continuity, existence can fail
example.p: Define F(y)=1 if y=0 and F(y)=0 otherwise. There is no differentiable solution of y'=F(y) with y(0)=0 on a neighborhood of zero. A solution would have y'(0)=1, hence y(t)>0 for all sufficiently small positive t. There its derivative would be zero, forcing it to be constant by the Mean Value Theorem. Continuity at zero would make that constant zero, a contradiction.

subsection.p: Lipschitz continuity is sufficient for uniqueness, but not necessary. For y'=-\sqrt[3]{y}, y(0)=0, the law is not Lipschitz at zero, yet the zero solution is the only forward solution. Along any differentiable solution, (y^2)'=-2|y|^{4/3}\le0. Starting from y^2=0, nonnegativity forces y=0 for future times. This statement concerns forward uniqueness; backward departure is possible.

warning.title: Local does not mean global
warning.p: The smooth law y'=y^2, y(0)=1, has the unique solution y=1/(1-t) near zero, but the solution becomes unbounded at time one. Local existence and uniqueness do not imply that a solution continues for all time.

exercise.title: Find a guaranteed interval

statement.p: Apply the theorem to y'=t+y^2, y(0)=1, on |t|\le1, |y-1|\le1. Find valid M,L,h. Then verify the waiting solutions in the nonuniqueness example at the joining point.

hint.p: Here 0\le y\le2, so M=5 and L=4 work. Choose h=1/5: hM=1 and hL=4/5<1. At the joining point, y_c'=0=2\sqrt{|y_c|}.

introduction.p: This appendix reviews factoring, completing the square, rational expressions, powers, inequalities, and finite sums. These algebraic tools are used to simplify calculus expressions, determine domains, and prove error bounds.

Factoring expresses a polynomial as a product. It reveals zeros and signs and can expose common factors for cancellation. Completing the square gives a form useful for recognizing graphs and evaluating integrals.

introduction.p: This appendix reviews the unit-circle definitions, identities, addition formulas, inverse functions, and equations used in calculus. Angles are measured in radians unless degrees are explicitly stated. The derivative formulas for sine and cosine depend on that convention.
Right triangles are a good beginning. The unit circle is the calculus definition.
A right triangle defines sine and cosine only for acute angles. But calculus needs functions such as
for every real number x. The unit circle gives that definition.

subsection.title: Graphs of sine and cosine
subsection.p: The unit circle produces the graphs of sine and cosine as the angle changes.

The cosine graph starts at 1, falls to 0, reaches -1, returns to 0, and then returns to 1.

introduction.p: Trigonometric identities are equations that are true for every angle where both sides are defined.
They are useful because they let us change the form of an expression without changing its value. In calculus, this can turn a difficult derivative or integral into an easier one.

subsection.title: Reciprocal and quotient identities
subsection.p: The reciprocal identities come directly from the definitions:

p.me: \sec x=\frac1{\cos x}, \qquad \csc x=\frac1{\sin x}, \qquad \cot x=\frac1{\tan x}.

subsection.p: The quotient identities are

p.me: \tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, \qquad \cot x=\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}.

subsection.p: Each identity is valid only where the denominators are nonzero.

p.me: \sin x\sec x = \sin x\cdot\frac1{\cos x} = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}.

introduction.p: Completeness of the real numbers supports the existence results used throughout calculus. This appendix develops the least-upper-bound property, monotone convergence, bisection, extrema, and uniform continuity. The main-text Cauchy criterion in gives another formulation of completeness.

The least-upper-bound property states completeness in terms of bounded sets of real numbers. Every nonempty set bounded above has a smallest real upper bound. We will use that property to justify limiting values.

subsection.p: Let A be a set of real numbers.
A number U is an upper bound for A if every number in A is less than or equal to U:
A set is bounded above if it has at least one upper bound.

subsection.title: Finite covering lemma
subsection.p: The proof uses one compactness fact about closed intervals.

note.title: Finite covering lemma for closed intervals
note.p: Suppose every point of [a,b] lies in at least one open interval from some collection of open intervals. Then finitely many of those open intervals already cover all of [a,b].

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: If no finite subcollection covered [a,b], bisect [a,b]. At least one half would also fail to be covered by finitely many intervals. Choose such a half and repeat.
This creates nested closed intervals whose lengths shrink to 0. They trap a point c\in[a,b].

But c lies in one of the open intervals from the original cover. Since that interval is open, it contains a small neighborhood around c. Eventually the nested interval is so short that it lies entirely inside that one open interval. Then that nested interval is covered by a single member of the cover, contradicting how it was chosen.
So a finite subcover must exist.
This is another place where the completeness of the real line is doing hidden work.

introduction.p: This appendix explains graphing windows, finite precision, calculator syntax, and Python experiments. Use reference values and mathematical error estimates to check numerical results, and account for the sampling limitations of plots.
A graph on a screen is not the graph itself.
It is a sampled picture of part of the graph, drawn in a chosen rectangle:

p.me: x_{\min}\le x\le x_{\max}, \qquad y_{\min}\le y\le y_{\max}.

introduction.p: Anything outside that rectangle is invisible. Anything between sampled points may be missed. A good graphing window reveals structure. A poor window hides it.

subsection.title: A window is a mathematical choice
subsection.p: Consider
In the small window
the graph looks mostly like a decreasing curve. In the wider window
we see the full cubic shape: rising, falling, then rising again.

figure.caption: The viewing window can reveal or conceal features of the same function.

Panel 2 of 2. The viewing window can reveal or conceal features of the same function.

subsection.p: The function did not change. The picture changed.

note.title: Window habit
note.p: Before trusting a graph, change the window.
Try a smaller window, a larger window, and a window centered on important points: zeros, critical points, endpoints, and possible asymptotes.

subsection.p: Technology often draws connected pixels. That can hide a missing point.

description.p: A plotted line may hide the fact that the original formula is undefined at x=1.

subsection.p: This is not a failure of technology. It is a reminder that a graphing tool cannot know which features matter unless we ask mathematically.

p.me: \text{The domain is part of the function.}

subsection.title: A graph can hide a sharp feature
subsection.p: A graphing device samples finitely many points. If important behavior occurs between sampled points, the plotted graph may miss it.
For example,
oscillates rapidly. A coarse plot may connect sampled points in a way that looks much less oscillatory than the true function.

figure.caption: Sampling too few points can give a misleading picture of a rapidly changing function.

description.p: Sampling too few points can give a misleading picture of a rapidly changing function.

subsection.p: This matters in calculus because derivatives, roots, local extrema, asymptotes, and oscillations may all be small or narrow enough to be missed in a first plot.

subsection.title: A graphing checklist
subsection.p: When using a graphing tool, ask these questions.

cell.p: A plotted curve may hide holes or forbidden inputs.
Important behavior may lie outside the viewing rectangle.
Connecting across an asymptote can produce false lines.
Have I zoomed in near zeros and critical points?
Local behavior may be invisible at a large scale.
End behavior and global shape may be invisible at a small scale.
Factoring, derivatives, and limits reveal features a plot may miss.

note.title: Graphing principle
note.p: A graph is evidence. It is not a proof.
Use it to form guesses. Use algebra, calculus, and domain information to check them.

introduction.p: A real number can have infinitely many decimal places. A machine stores only finitely many digits.
That difference is small in many calculations and large in some.
Calculus cares about small errors, so we must know how numerical errors enter.

subsection.title: Exact arithmetic and floating-point arithmetic
subsection.p: In exact mathematics,
is exactly one third.
In decimal floating-point arithmetic, it must be stored approximately:
with only finitely many digits.
Similarly,
is an exact number in mathematics, but a decimal approximation in a calculator.
A computer typically stores a number in scientific notation, roughly like
where only finitely many digits are kept. The exact storage system depends on the machine and software, but the main idea is universal:

p.me: \text{Most real numbers are rounded when stored.}

note.title: Roundoff error
note.p: Roundoff error is the error introduced when a real number is replaced by a nearby machine-representable number.

subsection.p: This does not make computation unreliable. It means computation must be interpreted with error in mind.

subsection.title: Subtraction can magnify relative error
subsection.p: The most dangerous basic operation is often subtraction of nearly equal numbers.
Suppose a calculator stores the two numbers
with limited precision. Their difference is
If each input has small rounding error, the difference may have a large relative error, because the true answer is very small.
This problem is called cancellation.
Calculus produces cancellation often. The difference quotient
subtracts two nearby function values when h is small. If h is too small on a computer, roundoff error can overwhelm the improvement we expected from taking a smaller interval.

example.title: a numerically unstable expression
example.p: The original form subtracts two nearby numbers:
The rationalized form avoids that subtraction. Near x=0, it is usually more stable numerically.
are algebraically equivalent for x\neq0, but not equally safe for numerical evaluation.

note.title: Numerical algebra habit
note.p: Algebraic simplification is not only for exact answers. It can also make numerical answers more stable.

subsection.title: Roundoff versus truncation
subsection.p: Many numerical methods have two different kinds of error.

cell.p: The error from replacing an infinite or limiting process by a finite one.
The error from storing and operating with finitely many digits.

example.title: derivative approximation
example.p: To approximate f'(a), we might use
If h is large, the secant slope may be a poor approximation to the tangent slope. That is truncation error.
If h is extremely small, then f(a+h) and f(a) may be almost equal as stored numbers. Their subtraction may lose important digits. That is roundoff error.
So making h smaller is not always better on a machine.

warning.title: Computing warning
warning.p: In exact mathematics,
is the right idea.
In floating-point computation, taking h too small can make the numerical result worse.

subsection.title: Residuals and step sizes
subsection.p: When an algorithm produces an approximate answer, do not ask only:
Ask:
For root-finding, two common checks are:
The number |f(x_n)| is a residual. It tells how close the function value is to zero.
The number |x_n-x_{n-1}| is a step size. It tells how much the approximate root changed in the last step.
Both can matter.
A small step size alone does not prove that f(x_n) is small. An algorithm might be stuck.
A small residual alone does not always prove the root is known accurately. If the graph is very flat or very steep, residual size and input error can behave differently.

note.p: For iterative methods, record at least:
A good computation leaves a trail.

n_values = list(range(1, N + 1))

Check the domain and hypotheses before using a formula, and include an applicable error bound or qualified estimate when reporting numerical accuracy. The tests below are tools for deciding convergence. They do not all give the sum.

cell.p: If the limit is not 0, or does not exist, then \sum a_n diverges. If the limit is 0, the test is inconclusive.
Converges if |r|<1, with sum \displaystyle \frac{a}{1-r}. Diverges if |r|\ge1 and a\ne0; for a=0 the series is zero.
Converges if p>1. Diverges if p\le1.
If \sum b_n converges, then \sum a_n converges. If \sum a_n diverges, then \sum b_n diverges.
Assume a_n,b_n>0 eventually and compute \displaystyle L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}.
If 0<L<\infty, then \sum a_n and \sum b_n either both converge or both diverge.

cell.p: a_n=f(n), where f is positive, continuous, and decreasing for large x.
\displaystyle \sum a_n and \displaystyle \int^\infty f(x)\,dx either both converge or both diverge.
Same hypotheses as the integral test, with a convergent series and N in the region where f is decreasing.
\displaystyle \sum (-1)^{n-1}b_n, where b_n\ge0, b_n decreases, and b_n\to0.
The series converges conditionally. Alternating series often behave this way.
If L<1, the series converges absolutely. If L>1 or L=\infty, it diverges. If L=1, inconclusive.

warning.title: Endpoint warning
warning.p: The ratio and root tests usually decide what happens inside and outside the radius. They usually do not decide what happens at the endpoints.

note.title: Simpson’s rule requires even n
note.p: The subintervals are paired, because each pair is approximated by a parabola.
